Mr. Speaker, in asking that the
report of the committee appointed to inquire into the charges of Major Hodgins with respect to the National Transcontinental Railway be concurred in, I wish to place before the House as briefly as I can some of the reasons which induced the committee to adopt this report. It will be useless for me,
I suppose, to state very minutely the circumstances which led to the appointment of this committee of investigation. I think they are known by every hon. member of this House, and I simply wish to recall that Major Hodgins, who now resides in the city of Victoria, B.C., who had been for some time previously in the employ of the Transcontinental Railway Commisison and who had either left his position or been dismissed by the commission on the 16th April last, wrote a letter which he signed and caused to be published in the ' Daily Colonist' newspaper, published in the city of Victoria, B.C., charging the Transcontinental Railway Commission with undue influence over their engineers, charging them also with undue influence over some members of the government and making other charges which are set forth in the letter, which letter is quoted in the report now before the House. This letter was followed by two alleged interviews in the same paper with Major Hodgins enlarging and repeating in other words the charges that had been made by him in the previous letter. The Transcontinental Railway Commissioners thought it their duty to send a memorandum to the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier) denying all the charges made by Major Hodgins in his letter and these interviews, and asking that a committee of this House be appointed to inquire into these charges, to give an opportunity to Major Hodgins to prove his charges and an opportunity to themselves to disprove them. That committee was appointed on April 29, and commenced its proceedings about that date. Major Hodgins was put on the stand and was subjected to a long examination by his own counsel and by the counsel of the Transcontinental Railway Commission. During the course of this examination, after it had proceeded for some time, on June 3 last Major Hodgins practically repudiated the two interviews which had been attributed to him by the ' Colonist.' I shall quote his exact words to the House to show how emphatic his repudiation was. They are to be found at page 248 of the evidence. He was then being examined by Mr. Murphy, counsel for the Transcontinental Railway Commission, and his examination reads:
Q. Well, it is of importance to know, major, how much or how little of this interview you are now prepared to stand by, because it affects the cross-examination?-A. I am not prepared to be responsible for the interview at all. As I say, if a reporter interviews you and takes down half a dozen sentences, and his notes certainly were not that long (illus-

trating by a gesture) and writes up two columns you cannot hold me responsible for it. Part of the interview, I might tell you, the reporter was trying to find out what an engineer has to do, why he does this, that and the other-in fact I was giving him more or less of a lecture on engineering. There was a whole lot of questions he was working up and he got hoplessly mixed up in the thing.
Q. Prom your answers this morning you would not like to be responsible for other articles that are written nearer home?-A. No.
Q. On the same subject?-A. No.
After this repudiation by the Major of his two interviews in the 'Colonist.' I think about June 16, Major Hodgins repudiated or withdrew all charges he had made previously in his letter to the ' Colonist ' with which we had to deal during the investigation. The question of the classification of materials In district P where he was working, had been the subject of a great deal of correspondence and discussion between the engineers for the Grand Trunk Pacific and for the Transcontinental Railway. The engineers, the commission and the contractors also had obtained from eminent jurisconsults in different parts of the country opinions as to the proper interpretation to give to the specification on that very question which was the basis for Major Hodgins' charges. It was given in evidence that these opinions were all adverse to the contention held by the Major. In the face of this evidence the Major on June 16, withdrew these charges and imputations which he had made in his letter. His withdrawal is to be found at page 386 of the evidence. Major Hodgins was examined by Mr. Macdonald, a member of the committee :
2. You regard that as practically the only question left now?
That is the question of the interpretation of the specification for the classification.
Q. You regard that as practically the only question left now, the question of whether your view of the classification is correct?-A. That is all.
Q. That is all. I understand you to say, from the information that you have gathered since coming into this matter, Major, that you feel that you can not say that you have any imputations to make upon the commissioners in regard to any improper interference, with the engineers for instance?-A. With those legal and engineers' opinions there I do not see that I have.
Q. And you are, not in a position to offer any evidence to show that they exercised any improper interference with the engineers?-A. No.
Q. In regard to that matter in which the statement was made here that Sir Wilfrid Laurier refused investigation on account of the influence exercised on him by Mr. Parent;
I understand , you are not in a position to say, or to offer any evidence that would show that Mr. Parent attempted to influence Sir Wilfrid

in any way, or are you?-A. No, not unless Mr. Parent came up to say he did.
Q. You have no evidence of that?-A. I have none.
Q. And in regard to the question of engineering you apparently as an engineer, with your experience, took a certain view as to how the wording of these specfications should be interpreted?-A. Yes.
Q. Now you find that since you put in the statement here, Mr. Lumsden, on January ID laid down certain instructions for the engineers to follow, which may; be said to be an interpretation from his standpoint of whaf the specifications mean?

A. Yes.
Q. You were not aware of this being in existence at the time you wrote to the ' Colonist' on April 15, were you?-A. No.
Q. J suppose in regard to these opinions of counsel on the meaning of the specifications you had no intimation of them at the time you wrote the letter?-A. Another man's opinion is just as good as mine, as a matter of fact every engineer's opinion is valuable to himself.
Q. And it is a question upon which men may differ quite honestly?-A. Certainly.
* Q. You do not impute to these gentlemen any improper motives in their ideas?-A. Not after reading Mr. Lumsden's letter.
Q. You made use of the expression the other day that you did not regard this committee as the proper tribunal to determine the question at issue?-A. With all due deference to the committee, I do not; it is an engineering dispute and as far as I am concerned I quite believe that the arbitrators who are appointed for the purpose should deal with this question of classification and I think that the board of arbitrators is the only right and proper tribunal to determine it.
Q. And any evidence you have to offer in regard to this matter, to this question at all, whatever is left of it now, is evidence that you would prefer to give to this tribunal of arbitrators that has been appointed under the statute?-A. Exactly.
Q. They are people in whom you have confidence that they can settle this question in the interest of this country fairly?-A. Absolutely.
Q. And you are prepared to accept their judgment on this question of classification as absolutely fair from your standpoint and in the interest of the country?-A. Certainly; I would not put imyself in the way at all; they have to look after the interest of the country.
Q. And you regard this board of arbitration as being the proper tribunal to determine whatever there is in issue in this matter ?- A. They are the proper tribunal.
Q. Personally, Major, it does not seem to me -or have you any desire to go on before this committee through your counsel offering evidence and taking up the time of this committee, or wouln't you prefer to give it all before the aribtrators?
Mr. Lennox.-Would it not be better to hear counsel?
By Mr. Macdonald;
Q. What do you say to that, Major?-A. What is that again?
Q. Have you any desire to go on giving evidence here in view of what you have said now, or do you not think that the proper tribunal

to determine this question is the board of arbitrators composed of Mr. Woods, Mr. Lums-den and a third arbitrator?-A. I do not think it is for me to answer that. I think it is for the committee to decide that.
I shall pass over some of the evidence which is very long as I want to give only answers bearing on the withdrawal of the charges. The examination continued :
By Mr. Macdonald:
Q. I understand you to say you do not desire to press before this committee any charge of wrong-doing on the part of the commission as far as their interference with the engineers is concerned, is that a fair statement?-A. That is right.
Q. And as far as that phase of the inquiry is concerned, you do not offer any evidence for our consideration?-A. It is simply this, that I do not see why I should stand the expense of finding out whether the specification is right or wrong.
Q. Or whether the academic question between engineers should be settled at your expense, that is the position you take?-A. Yes.
This was a withdrawal by the Major of all imputations and charges made in his letter. The question came up afterwards in the committee whether it was proper to continue the investigation. A long argument followed between members of the committee and the majority of the committee thought that it was no use continuing the investigation after the withdrawal of the letter. I submit that the proper guide for us in this investigation was the order of reference which reads as follows :
Order of reference.
House of Commons,
Tuesday, April 28, 1908.
Resolved, that the memorandum of the chairman of the Transcontinental Railway Commissioners to the Prime Minister, of date the 23rd April, and laid on the table of this House on the 24th instant, and the papers accompanying the same, together with the letter of Major Hodgins to the publio press therein referred to, be referred to a special committee of five members, with instructions to investigate the matters and charges therein mentioned, and that the said committee be composed of Messrs. Carvell, Macdonald (Pictou), Geofirion, Barker, and Lennox; and that they have power to send for persons, papers and records, to examine persons on oath or affirmation, and to report from time to time.
Attest.
(Sgd.) THOS. B. FLINT, Clerk of the House.
What was referred to that committee for investigation ? I submit it was properly the charges of Major Hodgins. It could not be the memorandum by the Transcontinental Railway Commissioners to the Prime Minister denying the charges he had to investigate, it must have been the letter, and the charges in the letter in respect to the question of classification having been withdrawn, we thought that the proper
tribunal to continue the investigation was not the committee but the Board of Arbitration which had been created by statute pursuant to agreement between the Grand Trunk Pacific and the commissioners for the Transcontinental Railway. It is for that arbitration board to decide all questions according to the agreement. The agreement says that all difficulties and especially difficulties which appertain to the classification of materials which is probably the most important part to be decided by this tribunal are to be decided by a, tribunal composed of Mr. Woods, chief engineer for the Grand Trunk Pacific and Mr. Lumsden, chief engineer for the National Transcontinental Railway. If these two chief engineers cannot agree on the disputed question, they are to choose a third arbitrator and this tribunal is to adjudicate on the question. All these questions of classification are to come up before these gentlemen. They had agreed after having discussed the question a long time to adopt a certain standard of classification which has been adopted in the work and is being used now. I admit that some complaints as to over classification or under classification have been made by the Grand Trunk Pacific, but the fact that one of the parties to that agreement claims that there has been over classification or under classification does not prove this to be the case until that tribunal has adjudicated on it. That clause providing for arbitration in a contract is not an unusual one. We find very often such a clause in contracts where works of special importance have to be performed, and the fact that it is claimed by one of the parties to the contract that the work has not been properly classified, as I said, does not establish that fact until after the board of arbitration has adjudicated upon it. The very important question of classification was not one to be discussed before the committee. A board has been properly appointed by statute for this very purpose, and all those questions, as Major Hodgins said himself, ought to be brought before that board to be adjudicated upon. After having discussed the matter we came to the conclusion that there was nothing left to be inquired into by your committee. Supposing that Major Hodgins, before the appointment of that committee, after the publication of his letter had withdrawn his letter, no one would pretend that this House would have appointed a committee to investigate. Suppose also he had withdrawn all charges and put in another letter charging that there had been over classification by some engineers, would a single member pretend that a committee should have been appointed to inquire and decide whether that question of classification, which by agreement is to be entrusted to the arbitrators, ought to be discussed any f urthen ? I think iSir, that the .course adopted by the committee was logical, fair

and just, and I move, seconded by Mr. Car-veil, that the report which I laid on the table of the House a few days ago be now concurred in.
Mr. HAUGHTON LEiNNOX (South Sim-coe). Mr. Speaker, I recognize that in appointing a small committee the House expected us to occupy a somewhat judicial position and to endeavour, regardless of what our preconceived opinions politically might be, to arrive at a conclusion which would be in the interest of the country. I am sorry that I cannot concur in the motion of the chairman of our committee for the adoption of the report to which reference has just been made. The order of reference to that committee was made on April 28th last. The hon. gentleman who has just moved the adoption of the report has stated that certain matters were known to the House, certain matters were of public notoriety at the time the order of reference was made. That* is true. At the time the order of reference was made it was known to the House and to the country that Major Ilodgius had made certain charges which reflected very seriously upon the conduct of public business by the Transcontinental Railway Commission and, not only that, but (that his statements had been followed up by comments and editorials in the newspaper's which carried the matter even further than Major Hod-gins' statements went. There was abundant reason why the investigation should take place. It was the motion of the government and not of the opposition. It was a position taken by the government which the government thought was justified by the circumstances. But whilst the charges of Major Hodgins and the editorial and other comments in the press were known to the country, it was not known to the country or the House, but known to the government and the government alone, that statements had been made by the Grand Trunk Pacific engineers which were far more damaging and far-reaching than any charge made by Major Hodgins or the public press. The Grand Trunk Pacific in fact was up in arms against the classification which prevailed, not upon any special section of the eastern division, but from one end of the line to the other. The charge was made by that company-as the government knew, but as the country did not know at that time- that this was not the result of ignorance on the part of the government, but was due to malice aforethought. At the time the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) made the motion it was not known, but it became known in the committee afterwards, that there were attached to the memo, of the Chairman of the Transcontinental Commission the letters which constitute Exhibit No. 38, as filed before the committee, and which contained the dam-Mr. GEOFFRION.
aging statement I am about to refer to. It is alleged and reiterated by Mr. Parent that attached to the memo, laid on the table, and upon which the right hon. gentleman moved, were not only clippings from newspapers, but the bundle of papers which form Exhibit No. 38 filed in the committee as well, and which contained the charges I am about to refer to. In other words, the right hon. gentleman, for reasons unexplained, saw fit to detach from that memo, a portion of the documents which had been transmitted to him with it. I do not wish to read any more of this correspondence than is absolutely essential, but I believe it is essential that this House should know exactly the class of material and how it was classified, in order to be in a position to decide whether the motion I am about to make, namely, that the matter be referred back to the committee for further investigation, should be adopted, or whether the inquiry should be burked at this stage. Before reading the letter of Mr. Wood, Chief Engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific, I wish to make an explanation in order to elucidate certain statements in it. In the specifications in the various contracts on the eastern division we have it defined that earth excavations have a slope of one and a-half foot to a foot; that loose rock excavations have a slope of one foot to a foot, and that solid rock excavations have a slope of only one-quarter of a foot to a foot. Therefore, when we fin 1 in these letters reference to the fact that a slope is one and a-half to one, that means that the engineer is calling attention to the fact that whereas the slope is a slope of common earth the percentage returned for the work is a large percentage of solid and loose rock.
Having said that, I want to read the first letter of Mr. H. A. Wood to the chief
engineer :
Montreal, October 7, 1907.
H.	D. Lumsden,
Chief Engineer,	_
Eastern division of the National Transcontinental.
Dear Sir,-At the request of District Engineer Armstrong, he was furnished recently with a statement of classification for the heavier work on the above section, which were, /when given in detail, so different from his expectations that he requested the writer to visit the work.
During the past week we passed over por- . tions of the work from the Batisoan river west for fifteen or twenty miles, and later from mile 115 to 132.
With reference to the former portion, the classification was given in distances of from three to five miles, and as we did not have total quantities of graduation, could not judge with reference to any particular cutting, although percentages for entire distance seemed excessively heavy in both loose and solid rock.
With the latter portion we had detailed percentage for each cut, and were greatly sur-

prised at the allowances made for solid and loose rock. In nearly every case where the cuttings were not entirely all ledge the estimate given for solid rock is double, or more than double, what it should be.
In fact, the specifications had been entirely ignored and an excessive allowance made, not jjy reason of an error in judgment, but, as I understand, by special instructions from the assistant district engineer.
Let me give you some illustrations:
Take the cutting from stations 5818 to 5826, estimated 71 per cent solid rock and 29 per cent loose rock, slopes taken out li to 1. Very little ledge in this cut. Some large boulders, but a very large percentage is common excavation.
Station 5842 to 5860.-Classified 94 per cent solid rock, 6 per cent loose rock. Slopes taken out li to 1. Solid rock over-classified at least 100 per cent.
Station 5866 to 5875.-Estimated 80 per cent solid rock, 20 per cent loose rock. No rock in place in this cut. Many large boulders, but a large amount of earth.
Station 5882 to 5901.-Estimated 78 per cent solid, rock, 22 per cent loose rock. A large amount of this cut wasted with slip scrapers, and ploughing being done with two horses. There are hundreds of yards of earth here without a stone, large or small.
And yet there is not a foot of common excavation in that. They plough with two horses, and where It can be ploughed even with six horses it is common excavation. But it is all classified as solid rock and loose rock.
Station 6030 to 6046.-Estimated 40 per cent solid rock, 10 per cent loose rock. This is the large sand cut west of O'Brien's camp. Of the 95,000 yards moved to August 31 in this cut, at least 80,000 yards was pure sand.
Station 6071 to 6078.-Estimated 99 per cent solid rock, 1 per cent loose rock. Very little solid rock in place. Slopes taken out li to 1.
So that the solid rock might crumble down.
West of St. Maurice river.
Station 6391 to 6394.-Estimated 46 per cent solid rock, 33 per cent loose rock. Sand cut with few boulders, and possibly 1,500 yards ledge in bottom of cut not yet taken out.
S&ation 6493 to 6504.-Estimated 20 per cent solid rock, 49 per cent loose rock. No evidence of ledge and very few large boulders; nearly all sand.
Station 6506 to 6512.-Estimated 16 per cent solid rock, 44 per cent loose rock. This is purely a sand cut, with very few boulders. Upper slope nearly 100 feet high, material wasted into river. Certainly not 10 per cent of this should he classified.
I may say that it is only ' classified ' when it is solid rock or loose rock. Ordinary excavation is not ' classified.'
Do the specifications declare what is loose rock ?
Yes, they state the nature of each class of material.
May I ask is that an estimate of the quantities taken out, or an estimate of what they were before the work was begun 1

This has reference to the returns actually made by the engineers upon the work to the Transcontinental Railway Commission. The engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company is pointing out how ruinous and absolutely unjustifiable this classification Is. And I am reading for the purpose of showing what these men propose the country shall pay for.
Station 6522 to 6548.-Estimated 26 per cent solid rock, 49 per cent loose rock.^ This is borrowed material from the side. Very little solid rock shown, except what was used for blind drains, but some large boulders not placed in embankment.
On account of heavy rains we were not able to go west of station "6600, but we understand that classification is made about as noted above.
In every case where cuttings were not entirely in ledge we find the material over classified very largely. Mr. Armstrong has been over this work at different times, perhaps quite as often as the assistant district engineer. His estimate and my own are not very different as to the amount of classified material, and until he received detailed quantities he had no intimation that such heavey classification had been given. In many cases, particularly in sand and gravel cuts, he had supposed that no classification would he given, except perhaps for a few boulders as loose rock.
I am informed also that on the work east of the St. Lawrence river heavy classification is being made in borrowed material where ploughing is done with one team and material moved in slip scrapers.
As before stated, these over-classifications are made through error in judgment, not upon the decision of the resident or division engineers, who -are fully acquainted with the character of the work, hut by arbitrary orders from their superior. To such classification as mentioned above, increasing the cost of the work to such alarming extent, we most seriously protest, and respectfully request that either yourself or the assistant chief engineer visit the work and pass judgment upon the classification as made. Please note that the percentages given above indicate the work done to August 31. We are not advised what the September estimate will show.
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) H. A. WOODS,
Assistant chief engineer.
Now that letter, 1 thought it well to read in full, because every word of it is important. But I can economize time in relation to the others. Mr. Lumsden took action. He wrote a letter on October 18 which will be found in the printed evidence at page 395.	1 need not read the letter but merely
refer to it for the purpose of showing that at that time it appeared to Mr. Lumsden, from statements made by District Engineer



Doucet, that Mr. Doucet at that time admitted and recognized that his assistant engineers were over-classifying. It is important to bear in mind that, at that time, Mr. Doucet, to some extent, stood by the country and against the contractors. But Mr. Doucet does not maintain that position afterwards. I need only read from this letter what Mr. Lumsden says to the commissioners. He says : It would appear to me some material may be classified as rock which should be classified otherwise.' He had learned that upon a verbal statement of Mr. Doucet on the 12th instant. More anxiety seems to have been felt about points of etiquette than about the interests of the country. Mr. Ryan, secretary of the Transcontinental Commission says :
Although the procedure

Referring to the letter of Mr. H. A. W. Woods complaining of these matters :
-was distinctly irregular, the commission have taken full cognizance of Mr. Woods' complaint and have given directions that the matter he fully investigated.
This committee, although they do not approve of the manners exhibited by Mr. Wood, have been gracious enough to say that they will take the matter into their full consideration and have it Investigated.
I regret to say that that promise has not been carried out. Mr. Doucet thinks this was not as politely done as it ought to be, and he says in his letter to Mr. Lumsden on October 21:
I may state that such accusations are not only uncalled for, hut most unprofessional, as we in Canada understand professional etiquette.
I am more concerned about this investigation and about some gentlemen stepping out than I am concerned about the order of their going. Now, I refer on page 399 of this evidence to the letter of Mr. Doucet to the chief engineer of the Railway Commission. That I need not read in full, but I want to call attention to one or two sentences. A moment ago I mentioned the fact that Mr. Doucet did not propose to stand in harmony with his subordinates as to the higher classification, but in some way he gets over there, and like the chief engineer he chooses his attitude as time advances, and as soon as the 26th of October we find that Mr. Doucet is prepared to state to the chief engineer that they stand shoulder to shoulder as one man for the Quebec classification. The effect of that upon the chief engineer, upon the fortunes of Canada and upon the amount that Canada will have to pay for this work will be evident to every member of this House before we conclude. Now, he says to Mr. Lumsden :
Dear Sir,-I have already had occasion to state to you verbally that the interpretation

the engineers in district ' B ' have placed on the classification of solid and loose rock, and in accordance with which the progress estimates have been returned since the inception of the work.
I want hon. gentleman to take note of that, that the engineer here announces that from the very beginning of the work the classification which he has contended for as made by these subordinate engineers, and which at first was resisted by Mr. Doucet, and definitely resisted by the chief engineer, that classification has prevailed from the very inception of the work, and prevails to the present time.
Mr, E. M. MACDONALD.	tVou 1 d my
hon. friend be good enough to indicate where he finds this theory of his that Mr. Doucet in his conversation with Mr. Lumsden, as referred to in Mr. Lumsden's letter, took any different position from that which he took in his letter of October 26 ?

I have given the evidence and the references. I had some little experience of my hon. friend in the committee, where I had not as much support as I hope to have here, and I will endeavour to make this clear. My hon. friend can point out a distinction if he sees any between the letters to which I have referred. I have read a portion of this letter, and I have referred to the position which Mr. Doucet is said to have taken, as reported in the letter of 18th of October, and now I wish to add a sentence :
I have never had occasion to force my views on my assistants, all, to a man, have taken the same interpretation of the classification as I have.
So, as I intimated a moment ago, between the 12th and the 26th, for reasons which I cannot explain, Mr. Doucet seems to have advanced along the line on which the contractors were travelling. On the 24th of October there was an examination into this matter. Mr. Lumsden went down and in the letter of the 30th October, page 403, lie points out what was done ; he tells who was there. There were a number of contractors, among others. He points out what they did ; he refers to an interview with them after they had examined the work, and he points out that after this interview he requested Mr. Doucet, the district engineer, to procure statements as to the. interpretation of the specifications from the various engineers under charge of Mr. Doucet and to send these and his own interpretation of the specifications to Mr. Lumsden, the chief engineer. This is a significant letter, the letter of the 30th of October ; it shows the position in which Mr. Lumsden stood on the 30th of October when he communicated with the Railway Commission, and it shows this fact, that at that time, notwithstanding hds subsequent attitude, he stood in comdemnation of Que-

bee classification. After referring to these various matters, and having had these letters from the various engineers on the Quebec section, including the statement of Mr. Doucet, he says :
I can only say that I do not concur with the interpretation placed on clauses 34, 35 and 36 of the general specifications, by Mr. Doucet or the engineers under him. In my opinion solid rock excavation, clause 34, covers all material that should be classified as solid rock, etc.
He goes on to define for the purpose of pointing out that he does and will not agree with the classification prevailing in Quebec. What are you to say to the members of the committee? 'What are the members of this House to say to the members of the committee as to staying their hand now when we find that subsequently the chief engineer of this work, for reasons not appearing, now says that that bind of classification is to prevail, and that kind of classification is prevailing from one end of the eastern division of the Transcontinental Railway to the other at the present time? After pointing out what he regards as proper classification, he says :
Such being my views and as stated to you in my letter of the 18th instant, I must decide to certify to any future estimates, except upon classification in accordance with my interpretation of the specifications above mentioned, unless both parties to the contract agree to amend the contract formally, with due concurrence of t>he government, o,r until the estimates are corrected and conform with my interpretation. In any event, I ask that this correspondence be at once submitted to the government.	[DOT]
So the matter stands on the 30th October. The chief engineer, the gentleman by whose decision we are bound, the gentleman whose word is final, as has been said by a majority of this committee, the gentleman who is the sole arbitrator on the question of classification, stands firm with his back to the wall deifying all the subordinate engineers of the eastern division of the Transcontinental Railway. Yet strange to say, he changes his opinion later on. How does he do it? Well, he does it at the instance of an honourable class of men, but not the best class of men to invoke in a case of this kind. He has the engineers on the one hand, he holds them down ; he seems for the time being to be the strong man. Then a greater influence comes in, and lawyer after lawyer is introduced to argue this question-in the interest of the Grand Trunk Pacific xvho are complaining? Not at all. In the interest of the people whose money is being paid out? Not at all. But the ex-parte argument of the contractors who are clamouring for more is introduced to shape and guide the judgment of the chief engineer of the Transcontinental Railway Commission.
Before whom did the lawyers argue?
They are asked for opinions for which they are paid $500 each. That is all right.
Paid by whom ?
By the contractors, I presume, but I am not going to swear to that
Who asked for that opinion?

I presume the contractors asked for that opinion and the opinions rendered should have bean to the contractors and should have been reserved toy the contractors, but when these opinions were used as an argument ex parte, 'behind the backs of the people-and the Grand Trunk Pacific who were, incidentally, protecting the people -to shape and warp the judgment of the chief engineer, who was to have been independent judge in this matter, a great wrong was done to the people of Canada. Here we have Mr. Lafleur-all right; Charles H. Ritchie-all right; Mr. Lacoste-all right ; all good lawyers, all prominent men-
Not Mr. Lacoste; Sir Alexander Lacoste.

It is A. Lacoste here. I did not know that he had a title-Sir Alexander Lacoste, K.O. He is no better lawyer on that account. You see etiquette in it all the way through. I do not think the people are so much concerned in that matter as in the question whether or not they are, through fraud or otherwise, paying too much for the construction of this railway. Mr. Donald McMaster, Mr. George F. Shep-Igy-\yhave heard of him before and Messrs. Aylesworth & Company, inclosing the opinion of Mr. Wallace Nesbitt. What happens? We had the opinion of the chief engineer on the 18th October, a pretty strong opinion; we had the deliberate, considered opinion of the chief engineer, on the 30th October, sure, firm and defiant; we had a subsequent reiteration of that opinion slightly emphasized on the 16th December, which is found at page 426, and we have bis opinion on the 9th January.
Did the Department of Justice give an opinion?

That is what I am coming to. Before referring to that I may say that the matter was referred to the Justice Department and that Mr. Newcombe was asked for an opinion but Mr. Newcombe did not give one. I want that to be clearly borne in mind. It is alleged that Mr. New-combe gave an opinion, but Mr. Newcombe ' appears to have recognized this fact-
What about bis letter on page 429?
Page 429 is what I have here.
What is it if it is not an opinion?
My hon. friend can read it to the House.
You had better read it to show that it is an opinion and in that way contradict yourself.

Mr. Newcombe writes a letter which I say is not an opinion except in this that he tells the engineer : You are the party appointed to decide, you should decide and you should decide without outside interference. I shall read, in order that we may be clear upon this matter, the order of reference:

But what did the majority of the committee do ? I do not think that was right. I am not anxious to spend my time there: but I think we had a duty to perform. Everything that was known the day we ended our labours was known on April 28, when the Prime Minister moved the reference to the committee. That being so, I fail to see why, after we had elicited a certain amount of information, and after it had abundantly appeared that a vast amount of information material to the country's interest could be elicited, we should he told that we should not proceed.
Now, just one more point, as I wish to close before one o'clock. I wish now to refer to the statute, and the point I want to make clear is that it was a misrepresentation to say to Major Hodgins that we had a board of arbitrators investigating this matter. The otlier day the Minister of Railways answered a question that I asked by saying that, under section 7 of the agreement between the country and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway the reference was taking place. What I want to submit is, thait, as a matter of fact, that inquiry, which is progressing now, has absolutely nothing whatever to do with this question of the cost of construction of the railway or with the question of classification or over classification-that is not a matter that can be investigated under the terms of section 7. Section 7 is a provision that the chief engineer of the railway company and the chief engineer of the Transcontinental Railway Commission shall determine two things, two things only, and they shall determine them as experts. First, the kind of specifications that shall be adopted in reference to the building of this road, in other words, defining what class of road shall be built. Paragraph 7 of the agreement provides that before any work is done these two chief engineers shall determine the kind of road and the kind of specifications that shall be adopted. They provide, in addition, that when these specifications have been adopted by joint action of these two ex-

perts, the question whether the road is being built according to the terms of these specifications, in other words, whether the contractors are living up to the contract, shall also be determined by these two men, and in case they differ, the question shall be referred to the party selected by them, or if they do not agree, the third one shall be appointed by the court. But there is not one word in that clause 7 which justifies the argument that these men can determine the question of classification, or the cost of construction. That matter is defined by paragraph 15 of the contract, where the meaning of cost of construction is defined, and by paragraph 47, which deals with the question of cost of construction. Paragraph 47 I will read, because it covers exactly a difficulty of the kind which has arisen between the Transcontinental Railway (Commission and the railway company:
Any dispute which may arise as to the meaning or construction of this agreement, or as to the performance of any of the obligations of either of the parties to this agreement, or as to working expense or cost of construction, should, if not herein otherwise provided for, be determined by the award of a single arbitrator, if the parties concur in his appointment, or if not, by the award of three arbitrators, one of whom shall be appointed by the government, one by the company, and a third by the two so appointed, or, in the case of their being unable to agree, by the chief justice of the Supreme Court of Canada, and the award of a majority of such three arbitrators shall be final.
I wish to point out that no action has been taken, and only by action under section 47 can the question in dispute between the railway company and the commission be determined. This is important, because in this case they are not necessarily experts, and it was in view of the pretense that there was a pending arbitration that Major Hod-gins was compelled-I might almost use the word compelled-to retire. Now I argue this, because I think it is important to the country, because I think that inevitably an enormous loss will result to the country by the action taken by the majority of this commission. It is idle to say that the determination of this body, if it did determine it, would protect us from loss. In the meantime money is being paid out, and must be paid out, and an arbitration between the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental Railway Commission cannot decide the matter of the contract. The matter has to be decided by the chief engineer. Once the money is paid, if it is improperly paid, it is lost to the country. Therefore it is all important that this matter should be investigated now. I therefore move :

Mr. Speaker, I am very sorry that I find it necessary to take up any portion of the time of the House at this late stage of the session in discussing a question which, I may say, was dead and buried something like three or four weeks ago, but as our hon. friends on the other side have decided to discuss it we find it necessary, in order to place the case fairly before the country, to take up some of the time and I will proceed to do so as speedily as possible. This question arises entirely on account of a letter which Major Hodgins, at one time district engineer in the employ of the Transcontinental Railway Commission, wrote to the Victoria ' Colonist,' somewhere about the 16th April last, followed by two interviews, I think, on the 17th and 19th April. When this letter and these interviews were brought to the attention of the chairman of the Transcontinental Railway Commission he immediately sent a note to the right hon. the Premier (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) accompanied by all the correspondence bearing upon Major Hodgins' dismissal and asked that a parliamentary committee be appointed in order to have the matter thoroughly investigated. That was done and even before. the full text of Major Hodgins' letter had had time to come from Victoria here, a meeting of the committee was held, we took evidence for two or three weeks, interspersed with a good many adjournments and finally we were able to bring down a majority report with which I am very sorry to say two members of the committee were unable to agree. My hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) discussed this matter for an hour and a half and in the main, as far as he discussed it, he was very unfair. There were one or two instances, which 1 might almost call glaring instances, of unfairness to which I will be compelled to refer and then I will proceed, as I feel it to be my duty to do, to discuss this matter to some extent upon different lines from those followed by my hon. friend, or rather on lines in regard to which my hon. friend conveniently forgot to discuss it. My hon. friend forgot to discuss the charges made by Major Hodgins, and I do not wonder, because I would think that if there is a man in Christendom whom the Conservative party in Canada to-day want to forget and to imagine never existed it is Major Hodgins. We know the glee with which they looked forward to the investigation of these charges and we can appreciate to some extent their disappointment at the outcome. However, rather than let him die-I mean figuratively

or let his charges die, they have decided to bring the matter up in the House and they have devoted their whole attention to the question of classification and have attempted to make out the charge that a grave fraud is being committed upon the country by means of the classification in the construction of this railway. I must insist and I think I am logical when I do insist, that Major Hodgins' statements are the foundation of the whole case, and that but for this letter and these interviews, we never would have heard of the matter. The press comments upon the letter are only carrying out the |ame ideas as those which are embodied in the letter itself. The letter, as I understand it, practically charged four things. It did not raise the question of classification in any distinct instance excepting in district 1F ' which I will take occasion to refer to a little later on. The first portion of the letter charged that there was trouble in connection with the work in district ' F ' and that Mr. Young, one of the commissioners, suggested to Major Hodgins that he should go down to Quebec, take an object lesson and see how matters are run there. The second statement is that Major Hodgins went to Quebec, went to a certain cutting called La Tuque, a cutting originally intended to be a tunnel, but a cutting which they afterwards changed to an open cut, and he there saw that they classified material as 86 per cent soiid rock which, in his judgment, should only have been classified as 40 per cent. He at once came to the conclusion that all

the work in the province of Quebec was being classified upon that basis, or that there was about twice as much solid rock as there ought to be. When I point out to the House that under the contract of Mr. McArthur he was paid $1.70 per cubic yard for the removal of solid rock, 60 cents per cubic yard for loose rock and 30 cents per cubic yard for common excavation, it is not necessary to be an engineer to see what a huge fraud would be perpetrated upon the country if the facts alleged by Major Hod-gins were true, and if the classification of material in Quebec was as Major Hodgins claimed it was. The third statement is that if he had gone back to his district and had classified the work according to the Quebec classification it would have amounted to a difference of about $4,000,000 on the 400 miles of district ' F' and If applied to the whole line it would have amounted to a difference of $2S,000,000 in the cost. The fourth statement in the letter is that because he would not adopt the Quebec classification his services were dispensed with, and that Mr. Poulin, a friend of Mr. Parent, was appointed in his stead. Then he said he construed solid rock to include rock in ledges, boulders of one yard and upwards, masses joined together, provided the individual pieces composing those masses were of one cubic foot up to one yard in size. That was handed to the Deputy Minister of Justice, and the Deputy Minister of Justice said :
I do not understand upon what principal the chief engineer limits the size to pieces ex ceeding one cubic foot. If ' rock assembled * may be regarded as a mass of rock, and if it may be best removed by blasting, I do not see why under the specification it is material whether the individual pieces exceed or are less than one cubio foot in size, and if ' rock assembled' is not regarded as a mass, the minimum limit of size which can be classified as solid rock exceeds one cubic yard.
After receiving this letter Mr. Lumsden again changes his opinion and sends out a third interpretation of this clause in the specification, and the third is practically the same as the second, excepting that he tells his engineers if they find rock in masses joined together, no matter what the sizes of the individual pieces may be, if, in the opinion of the engineers, it may be best to remove it by blasting, he classifies ic as solid rock.
This brings us down to the 10th of January, when that is finally decided as being the proper construction of these clauses in the contract, and from that forward every engineer was told to classify according to that interpretation. Supposing Mr. Lumsden took a certain view of a certain cut down in the province of Quebec, his view as to whether that cutting should be classified as so much solid rock or so much loose rock, that would have nothing whatever to do with the language in the specifications or their general interpretation.
What were all these legal letters about and letters of opinion?

Legal letters, because they were dealing with a concrete case. These legal gentlemen were undertaking to deal with the question as to the proper interpretation of the specifications, because the question of classification was entirely in the hands of the chief engineer. Sir Alexander Lacoste, who I understand is one of the legal gentlemen our hon. friends have consulted, is not a gentleman who, as insinuated, would give an opinion merely to please a client. I am sorry the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) is not in his seat, because 1 would like to commend him the task of reading the opinion of Sir Alexander Lacoste, to find out in it how little there is in all the squabble over this question, because when Sir Alexander Lacoste deals with these questions, it is in such a clear manner that it makes my hon. friend's argument absolutely untenable. Therefore; we have established now that even if the allegation is that interpretation of these specifications was altered it does not avail them, because there was never any original interpretation to alter. But finally, on .January 9, Mr. Lumsden Issues a document in which he finds there were six conditions under which you can class solid rock: First, rock and ledges; second, rock and boulders over one cubic yard; third, conglomerate rock or plumb pudding stone; fourth, detached ledge rock in mass over one cubic yard; fifth, rock in masses of over one cubic yard; sixth, shale rock; six different defined conditions which can be classified as solid rock, and since that time they have been interpreted in that way. My hon. friend from Hastings undertook again to distort language with a view of endeavouring to show that Mr. Lumsden took that position under pressure. There is not any evidence of that. Mr. Newcombe, the Deputy Minister of Justice, pointed out when the matter was referred to him, that Mr. Lumsden had evidently overlooked the use of the words ' cubic foot ' instead of the words ' cubic yard.' As a result, Mr. Lumsden corrected his interpretation which he had previously given on December 9, and used the words ' cubic yard ' in deference to the suggestion of the Deputy Minister of Justice. But in no other respect did his interpretation differ from that made on December 9, as he stated at the end of it that he had made it after consultation with Mr. Schreiiber, who was the consulting engineer in the western country. Now this is what the chief engineer did, and since January 9 of this year these uniform instructions as to interpretation have been in existence all over the Transcontinental. There never was any complaint made by the Grand Trunk Pacific in regard to classification previous to October 7 of last year, when Mr. Woods wrote on that subject. The hon. member Mr. BARKER.
for Simcoe endeavoured to deduce some argument from the statement in Mr. Lums-den's letter that Mr. Doucet at one time had taken a position in which he agreed with Mr. Woods. My hon. friend from Simcoe was not fair, or he overlooked the letter of Mr. Doucet which is to be found on page 399, in which he expressly states that he affirms the very position he took in the verbal discussion he had with Mr. Lumsden. But this letter of Mr. Woods, which has been made so much use of by the Conservative press, has been completely disposed of. It is disposed of by the letter of Mr. Doucet on page 398, it is disposed of by the letter of Mr. Huestis, on page 400, in which Mr. Huestis says:
Although Mr. Woods distinctly stated on the trip to La Tuque just completed that his interpretation was different to that as expressed by me, yet Mr. Armstrong told me that when he and Mr. Woods visited the work in the early part of October cut from station 59505969 which is classified by Mr. Bourgeois to be 88 per cent solid rock, 12 per cent loose rock was judged by Mr. Woods to be 100 per cent solid rock, which he could not possibly state on his declared interpretation of the specifications, as the eastern end sho.ws a cut where masses of material rather than ledge rock occurs.
Also by Mr. Bourgeois' letter on page 402, where Mr. Bourgeois, who is the local engineer, states that he had kept gangs of men in these cuts measuring the boulders that came out in order to verify their size, and to make it clear whether or not they should be classified as solid rock. As a matter of fact, I am prepared to state that Mr. Woods does not pretend to suggest that this error in classification, which he claims existed in October, occurred through any instructions that came from any superior.
All the more reason why that should have been done.

Mr: Lumsden was there, who could speedily correct it. My hon. friend from Simcoe knows as well as X do that the decision of an absolutely technical question as to whether any cut should be classified one way or another, is a matter peculiarly for engineers, and not for lawyers or members of parliament. Not only that, but you will find Mr. Woods' letter written in February 20 of this year, on page 469, in which he absolutely accepts the interpretation which was put upon the specifications by Mr. Lumsden in the previous January, and in which he says:
We are quite satisfied with your interpretation of the specifications and with your instructions, which are explicit. I do not know the date of these instructions or when they are supposed to become effective, but from reports from my assistants at Winnipeg and Quebec, there does not seem to have been any change in classification of work previous-

ly estimated was not classified according to your recent instructions being over estimated in both loose and solid rock.
Mr. Woods and Mr. Lumsden know better than the member for Simcoe and the member for Hamilton what is right, and they will so decide, if they are honest men. I do not think it is necessary to detain the house any longer. The conference between these arbitrators is now going on. If any interpretation of the classification upon any portion of this railway should, upon investigation by the chief engineer of the Transcontinental, appear to be incorrect, he will deal with the matter. There is no use talking moonshine about the people of Canada losing thousands and thousands of dollars. There is not a contractor who has not got 20 per cent, or 10 per cent of all the money that can possibly be given to him and 10 per cent of the whole value of his contract in the hands of the commission. Not one of the commissioners, not Mr. Mclsaac, not Mr. Eeid, not Mr. Young, not Mr. Parent, not one of them, can give to any one of these contractors a five cent piece unless Mr. Lums-den, the chief engineer, says so, and if any one of these men has got a five cent piece as a result of any incorrect classification, every five cent piece, every dollar, every thousand dollars that he has got incorrectly can be got back from him in consequence of the required certification of the chief engineer. The whole tiling is in his own hands ; the responsibility is his. It is part of the political game of hon. gentlemen opposite, as they play it, to make the people believe that the gentlemen composing this commission have something to do with the question of classification. I do not know that I could conclude very much better than by asking1 the hon. member for Hamilton to show how a member of the commission, or a member of the government, could give to a contractor, or a sub-contractor, one dollar unless the chief engineer said not only that he should have it but that if he had got it he had a right to keep it. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that while we have had under the consideration of this House and of the committees various absurd and ridiculous charges which have emanated from hon. gentlemen opposite, who have deserted every tradition of their party, abandoned every alleged policy, the absolute fiasco which has followed their attack upon the management of the Transcontinental Railway is the worst that has marked their whole career, and this fact is so apparent that I need not argue further. My hon. friends are simply covering their retreat, and I should apologize to the House for detaining it so long.

nesses. It was a very plain position. There is not an lion, gentleman on the opposite side of the House who will say that we were not perfectly reasonable in that. cent. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Carvell) went on to add that in fact it was not classified at so much as 40 per cent but at only 32 per cent and had been on a previous occasion classified at 29 per cent. The facts about that are very simple and the hon. gentleman knew them as well as any member of tlie committee. Major Hodgins was taken down to section ' B ' in Quebec; he knew nothing about the country, he had no plans and no profiles; he was just taken there to look at the work. He was shown a particular piece of work, and asking how it had been classified he was told by one of the men on the spot that it had been classified at 86 per cent solid rock. Major Hodgins may or may not have been correct in his recollection of that. He left shortly after for Ottawa, he had no memoranda about him, but nobody who knows Major Hodgins believes that he would wilfully misrepresent. I would not say that Major Hodgins may not have been mistaken; he may have made a mistake in describing the exact location of the piece of work he was speaking about.

That cutting is the only cutting on the eastern division of the Transcontinental that has 100 feet in depth. I know well what I am speaking about and I may say that the cutting is not all out yet and they were only working upon a very small portion of it at that time.

La Tuque is a general designation of the place Major Hodgins went to, but he went over several places in the neighbourhood and he did not confine his walk to that particular cutting. He had firmly in his mind one spot which was represented as being classified at 86 per cent.
He specially mentions a cutting 100 feet deep and La Tuque is only one of that depth.

It is clear that Major Hodgins is not alone in referring to 86 per cent classification in that neighbourhood, because the Grand Trunk engineers find a similar classification, and what Major Hodgins says is that it was quite possible for him to have made an error as to the exact spot when he was speaking several months afterwards. I assert, that when the member for Carleton ((Mr. Carr veil) tells us that Major Hodgins is an honourable man and a straightforward and a truthful man, it is neither fair nor right for that hon. gentleman at the same time to represent him as wilfully misrepresenting the classification. That is all I have to say on that subject.
The hon. member (Mr. Carvell) went on to refer to force account, and he very strongly condemns Major Hodgins for the advice he gave with regard to it. But Mr. Lumsdeu the chief engineer expressly stated that he did not find fault with Major

Hodgins as to his advice about force account nor was he dismissed on that ground, and I shall show later that Major Hodgins was treated most unfairly and most unjustly by the commission with regard to that matter. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr* Macdonald) claims that Major Hodgins unreservedly withdrew his charges. That is putting it very strongly indeed as any one who has heard or read the evidence of Major Hodgins must nd-of Major Hodgins was confronted, with these legal opinions that we have heard so much about and. in reply to the member for Pictou he said lie did not know of those opinions when he wrote his letter. He was then asked if he would have modified his own judgment as to what he said in his letter, had he known of these legal opinions. Major Hodgins confessed that it would have had an effect upon his mind and might have altered his opinion as to the acts of others, but as to his own division and as to the cases in which he found fault with classification he never withdrew one he had uttered, aud he had remained of precisely the same opinion. He was manly enough to say that if the engineers acted upon legal advice, accepted by the chief engineer, that certainly would modify his opinion as to the conduct of these engineers. But the hon. gentleman (Mr. Macdonald) carefully concealed the fact that the over classification as to which Major Hodgins gave evidence was all done before the change was made in the interpretation. The action taken by McIntosh had altered the estimates from January to June and July, 1907, but the legal opinion were later so they could not affect the charges made by Major Hodgins himself. The hon. member (Mr. Macdonald) went on to speak of obstructors and the press, but there is no question of obstruction before us here and it would be useless to follow him in that line of argument. The simple question is : The House having referred a certain subject to the committee, whether the committee should deal with it or whether they should take the opinion of Major Hodgins that another body could deal with it better than the committee. It is not for the committee, it is not for Major Hodgins to decide that. The House, knowing the facts, knowing the statute which provided for arbitrators, the government knowing all about that agreement of January 10, 1908, knowing every fact that we know today, appointed the committee and directed us to investigate. By what authority does the committee accept from Major Hodgins who is a mere witness the opinion that some other body can deal with it more satisfactorily than a committee appointed by this House. Then the hon. member (Mr. Macdonald) tries to make out there is some excessive verbiage and he says we charge over classification, excessive allowance, and undue payments. There might be over
classification by the resident engineer and it might go no further, but still that might be a matter for proper inquiry. But there was not only over-classification, it was allowed, and undue payments given.
Those are the specific charges made and the amendment urges that we ought to continue the investigation of these subjects.
The hon. member also comments upon the fact that in putting in before the committee the various letters that have been referred to to-day I had said that those letters did not charge or prove fraud against the commissioners ; I say so still. There is nothing in those letters that indicates any fraudulent conduct on the part of the commissioners. That has never been pretended. The letters do not say there was any fraud, but they prove what is on their face, that over-classification was allowed by the resident engineers. That is all the letters say, and that is all we put them in to show. If the inquiry had gone on, the committee would not have rested with those letters ; we would have sent for those Grand Trunk engineers, would have sent for Mr. Armstrong and Mr. Woods, and would have heard all the evidence, we would have brought these witnesses face to face with the government engineers, and would have found out what the truth is about all this. But when the committee got to that point, and with those letters before them, showing most grievous errors apparently, certainly enormous amounts at stake far beyond anything that Major Hodgins knew as to his own division, tiie committee shut down and said they would investigate no more, although they were ordered to investigate by the House. That is all I have to say in answer to the speech of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. K. M. Macdonald).
I propose to take up what I -understand to be the real questions submitted to us and to deal with them in as brief a manner as I possibly can. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. E. M. Macdonald) says : What is the question which was submitted to us? That can be answered very simply. In April, 1908, certain letters, interviews and comments appeared in the newspapers commenting upon charges affecting the commissioners of the National Transcontinental Railway, and these were of such a character that the commissioners considered it their duty to bring the matter before parliament, which they did by memorandum to the First Minister, appearing at page 15 of the printed evidence. That is the starting point, the bringing up of that memorandum of Mr. Parent by the First Minister. The First Minister made a motion to refer that memorandum and other papers to a committee. The motion is printed at page 5 of the evidence, and as it appears here is somewhat altered from the form in which it was at first introduced by the Prime Min-

ister, the words ' together with the letter of Major Hodgins to the public press thereto referred to,' haying being Inserted before the motion passed. It is dated 28th April, 1008, and reads :
Resolved, that the memorandum of the chairman of the Transcontinental _ Railway Commissioners to the Prime Minister, of April 23, and laid on the table of this House on the 24th instant, and the papers accompanying the same, 'together with the letter of Major Hodgins to the public press therein referred to, be referred to a special committee of five members, with instructions to investigate the matters and charges therein mentioned, and that the said committee be composd of:	_
Messrs. Carvell, Macdonald (Pictou), Geof-frion, Barker, and Lennox-; and that they have power to send-
Not to send for Major Hodgins, but
-to send for persons, papers and records, to examine persons on oath or affirmation, and to report from time to time.
That was the reference, but when you come to the papers themselves which were referred to the committee you find that to the memorandum were appended Major Hodgins' letter and various newspapers and other papers. For the letter Major Hodgins of course accepted full responsibility. As to the interviews he did not repudiate them to the sense that the repudiation has been represented here. He simply said that he had an interview with a newspaper reporter ; that the newspaper reporter took a short memorandum from him, perhaps as he described it, it would occupy a space of two or three inches, and having got, in newspaper reporter fashion, the substance of what he wanted, the reporter elaborated that out into a rather lengthy article, and so Major Hodgins says : I do not accept responsibility for the elaboration, I only accept responsibility for what I told him. That is not withdrawing the charge, that is not repudiating anything he said; he over and over again repeated that he stood by whatever he said, and especially he stood by the letter. In that letter Major Hodgins made very distinct charges about which there could he no mistake. First of ail he said that the root of all the trouble between the commissioners and himself was the question of over-classification ; that is, his refusal to certify work done as of a higher and more costly class than the facts justified. There was a distinct charge that he had been in trouble with the commissioners, and because be refussed to certify for a higher class of work than the facts justified. That charge would be confined to his own district. He had, he said, refused to be more liberal in classification than he was allowing, and he had suggested that the commissioners, not being railroad men, should leave the engineering department alone. That was charge No.

2. He also said that one of the commissioners had advised him to go to Quebec and see how things were managed in that respect where the (contractors were not kicking and get an object lesson. That was charge or statement No. 3.	*
In his letter he alluded to the interview of Mr. McArthur, and this brings up the statement with which I find fault to the speech of the hon. member for Carleton, N.B. McArthur was the contractor for 250 miles of district ' F ' near Winnipeg. A statement had appeared in the Toronto 'World' of March 14, as coming from McArthur, that whereas the first estimate of the cost of the 230 miles had been $13,000,000, the actual cost would be close to $16,000,000, because so many changes had been made. That was the statement of Major Hodgins, as the member for Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell) put it, but it was a statement made by McArthur, the contractor. As to this Major Hodgins replied, in his letter, that changes in location had really reduced the probable outlay by almost $1,000,000. So that the total cost should be reduced to about $12,000,000 instead of being increased to about $16,000,000. He did not say, and did not pretend to say, that the probable cost had increased to $16,000,000 ; that was Mr. McArthur's statement. All that Major Hodgins said was that the alterations in location really reduced the $13,000,000 by about a million and that there should be a reduction to about $12,000,000 instead of an increase to $16,000,000. Commenting upon the McArthur interview, Major Hodgins in his letter said :
If Mir. Poulin, the engineer appointed by Mr. Parent to replace me on the western district, has allowed the introduction of classification similar to that in the province of Quebec, this will account for an increase in the estimated cost of the line.
He did not say that Mr. Poulin had allowed that, but that if he had, that would
account for an increase.
If this increase amounts to three or four million dollars '(33J per cent), it is time the public demanded some explanation from the government.
Mr. Hodgins made no assertion there except based upon what had been said by Mr. McArthur. What he said was that if the increase was caused by using the Quebec classification, as it was termed, it was about time the government should inquire into it. Major Hodgins, in his letter, went on to say :
The quickest way for the government to find out if the classification allowed ,is extravagant or not will he for the. Minister of Railways to ask for the monthly reports of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway engineers, who

are stationed on the Winnipeg district and the Quebec district, Messrs. Mann, Heaman and Armstrong; these reports are, I think, sent to the assistant chief engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific in Montreal. These engineers are well known in the west, and their reports contain much more information on the subject than I have.
Here we have a clear statement involving, not merely district ' By near Winnipeg, but district ' B,' in the province of Quebec. Major Hodgins made no pretense of knowing anything of district ' B ' of his own knowledge, but he did know about district ' F.' It must be borne in mind that Major Hodgins did not know what Messrs. Heaman, Armstrong and Mann could prove; and he could not, by this statement, have expected anybody to believe that he was himself in a position to prove anything about excessive classification in the province of Quebec. But the engineers of the Grand Trunk Pacific could give that evidence. Major Hodgins could give evidence as to district ' F.' It was as to these charges among others, appearing in the papers appended to the memo, which the chief commissioner wrote to the First Minister, that an inquiry was ordered. These charges involve, not merely the Winnipeg end, but district ' B '-not merely information within the knowledge of Major Hodgins but information that could only be obtained from the Grand Trunk Pacific and their engineers.
Now the chairman of the Transcontinental Commission used these words at the close of his letter to the Prime Minister :
In conclusion, the commissioners would respectfully request, as they do not wish to remain under the aspersion which such reports cast on them

Those reports include not Major Hodgins' district alone but district ' B ' as well.
-that the whole matter be referred to and looked into by a committee of the House and that Major Hodgins be assigned to appear before the same to repeat his charges in a specific manner in order to substantiate them if he can.
Thereupon the House, on April 28, referred all those papers to a special committee with instructions to investigate the matters and charges therein mentioned. I have stated the matters contained in that letter, not with the view of discussing whether they have been proven or not but to bring clearly before the House what was the subject matter referred to the committee. It is absolutely clear that what was recognized by the commissioners as affecting their reputation was not merely the charges as to district ' F,' not merely things within the personal knowledge of Major Hodgins, but the matters also referred to re-393
garding district 1 B,' and the evidence that could be given by the Grand Trunk Pacific engineers. It must be quite clear to hon. members, when they have read the evidence, that it was absolutely impossible for Major Hodgins to have known all the facts contained in these charges. He had reason to suppose there was foundation for the charges when he made them, but he could no more prove them on oath than he could prove what was going on in China. He had nothing to do with district * B,' but he had reason to believe that things were not going on as they should in that district ? He knew that the Grand Trunk Pacific engineers were finding fault with the classification there, but he knew none of these things of his own personal knowledge.
If the House desire to understand exactly what occurred with regard to Major Hodgins, they should know precisely what his position was and what were the relations between him and his chief and the commissioners. He had been district engineer, at first in charge of location, and then of the construction of about 380 miles lying immediately east of Winnipeg, known as district ' F.' He had under him the usual staff of engineers, and they apparently were quite satisfactory to him until the troubles arose to which I shall refer. Mr. McArthur was contractor for 250 miles of that district and had sub-let portions to other contractors. The classifications on which the contract prices were based were ordinary excavation, loose rock, and solid rock, and the prices were solid rock, $1.70 per cubic yard, loose rock, 60 cents and ordinary excavation, 30 cents. Mr Hodgins was under the impression-and I think that was generally understood-that McArthur had taken his contract for ordinary excavation at too low a price, and no doubt the sub-contractors were lower still. After McArthur began his work labour became scarce and wages increased which made it harder for all of them as regards common excavation. There are some gentlemen in this House who have had some practical experience of this sort of thing; but anybody who knows anything about it is quite aware that these conditions are sure to breed trouble, and the position both of the district and subordinate engineers became an exceedingly difficult one. That was the position of Major Hodgins. The progress of Mr. McArthur and his sub-contractors was very unsatisfactory. Major Hodgins seems to have found serious fault with him, but he rather sympathized with the difficulties Mr. McArthur was in. It was very difficult to get labour, the prices were known to be low, and it was supposed that some of the sub-contractors were losing money.
In December, 1906, and again a few months later, Major Hodgins had formally notified the contractor that he must increase his force, and had forwarded this notice to



the chief who had also given similar notice. In May or June, 1907, the chief engineer met Major Hodgins in Winnipeg. The commissioners were there, all of them, and it is curious to see how soon these commissioners began to meddle with the engineers. I shall not take the time to read these letters. The evidence shows the conversations with the commissioners, and the hints received by Major Hodgins that he should try and relieve matters, and the difficulties he had generally, so that he finally said to one of the commissioners, ' You don't understand the matter; you had better let the engineers alone.' I mention that as indicating that there was an interference by the commissioners that was certainly likely to lead to insubordination. Anybody who knows anything about these matters must see that it was a most improper thing for these commissioners to meddle between the contractors and engineers. It should have been left for the chief engineer. Nobody would expect to see the board of directors of the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Grand Trunk going out and interviewing contractors, engineers and subordinate engineers, consulting with or directing them apart from or otherwise than through the chief engineer.
Then, in June, Mr. Gordon Grant was sent up to Major Hodgins' district, as it was said, to report. Apparently, he was sent as an inspecting engineer over the whole district ' F,' but it was not intended that he should do more than inspect and report to headquarters. In fact, at page 116, Major Hodgins is asked :
Q. Did Mr. Lumsden tell you what instructions he had given to Mr. Grant?-A. I asked him whether we were to take instructions from Mr. Grant and he said no. Mr. Grant had been appointed against his wish and he would see that he did not give any instructions to the engineers.
Now, it has been said that there was a feeling of hostility on the part of Major Hodgins towards Mr. Grant. I think that is not improbable. Major Hodgins was in charge of District ' F.' Mr. Gordon Grant, without any communication to Major Hodgins, was sent up to be inspector of the whole district in Major Hodgins' charge. And it is here in evidence that the chief engineer said that Mr. Grant had been appointed against his wish and that he was not to interfere with the engineer, but to report direct to bim, the chiet. This is confirmed in a rather singular way by a letter which appears at page 93, a very significant letter, showing how, at that date at all events, the commissioners or some of them had begun to intermeddle with engineering matters, going behind the back of the chipf. A. E. Hodgins, Esq.,
District Engineer,
Kenora, Ont.
