House resumed adjourned debate on the motion of Mr. Oliver for the third reading of Bill (No. 181) to consolidate and amend the Acts respecting the public lands in the Dominion and the proposed amendment of Mr. Lake thereto.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Since Saturday I have considered whether the amendment then moved by the member for Qu'Appelle to the motion for the third reading of Bill (No. 181), is in order or not. The said amendment plainly contemplates the setting aside, appropriation and transferring to the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan of certain of the Dominion lands.
In the last edition of Mr. Bourinot's work on Parliamentary Procedure at page 628, in a foot note, it is stated that since 1874 all grants of public lands are initiated in the Commons. This is upon the theory that public lands are in the same position as public revenues. (See page 627).
At page 56S of the same work it is expressly stated that:
No cases can be found of any private member in the Canadian Commons receiving the authority of the Crown through a minister to propose a motion involving the expenditure of public money. No principle is better understood than the constitutional application that rests upon the executive government of alone initiating measures imposing charges upon the public exchequer.
I must, therefore, rule the amendment as out of order.
In connection with the same point of order a question was raised on the Bill, which I might as well dispose of now.
A discussion also arose as to whether in view of certain clauses in the Bill a previous sanction of the Governor General should not have been obtained and announced to the House before its introduction, and such Introduction preceded by a resolution.
Having regard to the precedents in the House, I find that this has not been considered necessary. In the year 1883, a similar Bill was passed, which now appears in the statutes for that year as chapter 17, intituled: 'An Act further to amend and to consolidate, as so amended, the several Acts respecting the Public Lands of the Dominion therein mentioned.' This Bill was introduced by Sir John A. Macdonald. No consent of the Governor General was announced at any stage nor was any resolution passed previously to the introduction of the Bill. This seems to be a precedent exactly in point.
This Bill is a consolidating and amending Bill and in the case of such Bills it is only when there are clauses imposing new burdens that it is necessary to consider these first in a Committee of the Whole.
The object aimed at in such Bills is to give the old law a new and more convenient form.

This Bill is not only an amending and consolidating Bill, but distinctly provides for the granting of preemptions and purchased homesteads not provided for by the Act as it stood before. It is in part an amending and consolidating Bill but it is in many respects, an entirely new Bill and contains entirely new provisions for alineation of the public domain.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not find that it provides for the setting apart for the purposes of the Bill of any wider area of lands and I think it will be found that the Bill of 1883 to which I referred, also provided for an extra homestead in certain cases as this one appears to do. I cannot find any very substantial difference and following the rule laid down by Dr. Bourinot in his work, relating to consolidating and amending Acts, I would rule that this Bill does not require any preliminary resolution or consent.

Of course it is true that the Bill does not cover a wider area of land than was provided in the enactments previously on the statute-book. The same observation is also true of the amendment of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Lake). It does not propose to go outside the area of land previously dealt with (by the enactments on the statute-book.
I beg to move then, seconded by Mr. Chisholm

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have ruled, of course, that the first amendment is out of order, and now this, I assume, is a new amendment.

I beg to move :
That the said Bill be not now read a third time but be referred back to Committee of the Whole House with instructions to amend the same by providing,
That the Governor m Council shall forthwith institute such proper inquiries as may he necessary for the purpose of ascertaining what quantity of Dominion Lands in each of the provinces of Alherta and Saskatchewan should he set aside and appropriated for the purposes of higher education with a view to setting aside, appropriating and transferring to the said respective provinces the said lands so ascertained for the purposes aforesaid.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think that probably that amendment is in order although it comes close to the line too.

Before the Bill receives its third reading, I wish to draw attention to clause 16. That clause provides :
16. Every entrant .for a homestead shall, except as hereafter otherwise provided, he required, before the issue of letters patent therefor (a) to have held the homestead for his own exclusive use and benefit for three years from the date of entry, (b) to have resided thereon at least six months in each of the three years from the date of entry, or the date of commencement of residence, (c) to have erected a habitable house theron, (d) to have cultivated such an area of land in each year upon the homestead as is satisfactory to the minister, and (e) to be a British subject.
I would draw attention to the fifth line of this clause : ' to have resided thereon at least six months in each of three years from the date of entry, or the date of commencement of residence.' 1 have seen a good many cases of great hardship to settlers coming from any part of the empire or even from foreign countries to the Northwest owing to this particular clause. I have always considered it a great mistake to have this clause dealt with in the arbitrary manner in which it is. The head of a family has to reside on the homestead six months of each year during three years before he can obtain his patent. But what better proof can you have of the good faith of the homesteader than in the fact that he has left a foreign country or even some portion of our own land, and has gone out to the prairies and taken up a homestead there in order to provide a home for his family. It may be argued that if you allow any leniency in the regulations, he may sell the land just as soon as he obtains his patent and go back to the country from which he came. But I would draw attention to the letter of the law which provides that the head of the family must reside on the land during six months of each year for three years before he can obtain a patent. A man might leave his family and come even from a foreign country, enter for a homestead in our country, to which he was attracted by the prospects of bettering himself ; he might leave his family in a foreign country, enter for a homestead, comply with the letter of the law by living on the homestead
six months in each year for three years and perform homestead duties, and then he might sell his homestead, put the money in his pocket and go back to his own country. So that there is nothing under this clause to prevent his selling out any more than there would be if this residence obligation were not required. I admit that it is necessary to impose some restrictions so as to have some evidence that a homesteader has the neces-ary qualifications to entitle him to a patent. But I claim that we often work out hardship by insisting that the head of the family must reside on the land the precise time of six months each year during three years. That same point has been drawn to the attention of this House before now and has been considerably discussed in the country. I would recommend a change in the regulations to this effect. If you were to provide by your regulations that either the entrant for a homestead or his family should reside continuously on the land for three years, I would see no objection to that. What I object to is that the man himself must reside on the land so that even if he left his family on it, while he himself was working elsewhere, he could not obtain his patent. What better evidence could you have of his sincerity than the fact that he has put his family on the land. He might be so situatetd that he could not comply with the condition of personally residing on it himself.
But I say that the very fact of having the head of the family live on the homestead for six months in each year has worked great hardship in many cases in our new country. There is- another very important factor in this question. There is a great portion of our population which should be seriously considered in this relation-the female population of our country. If the law which I suggest were put in operation, it would encourage young men to marry and would give our young women opportunities to assist in providing homes for themselves, their husbands and their children. This is a very important subject as every intelligent person will agree. In my observation of conditions in the west for the last thirty or thirty-five years, I have known men. even from outside our own Dominion, enter for homesteads, erect homes for their families, bring their families to this country and place them on the homestead. Then, through unforeseen and unavoidable misfortune they found themselves unable to maintain their families on the homestead, and so were compelled to go to the town, perhaps a short distance, perhaps a long distance away, to get employment. Perhaps they get into debt, perhaps further into debt, as I have suggested, through circumstances beyond their own control, and so were unable to go back and live on the homestead as required by the regulations and the law

providing that they had to live on the homestead for six months of every year. The result being that his homestead was cancelled and thus Canada lost a good citizen, settler and his family. I agree that the government, in days gone by, has. been lenient in many cases. Still, there was a limit to what could be done under the law. I consider there never was a more iniquitous law upon the Canadian statute-book than this clause 16 which provides that the head of the family must reside upon the homestead for six months in each year for three years before he can obtain a patent. For these reasons, I move, seconded by Mr. Staples :
That the said Bill he not now read the third time, hut that it he referred hack to Committee of the Whole House for the purpose of amending section 16 and other relevant sections of the said Bill by providing that the residence of the wife and family of any entrant for a homestead shall he accepted as equivalent to the residence of the entrant himself, subject to such regulations necessary or expedient for the purpose of securing actual permanent settlers.
Amendment negatived on the same division last recorded.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the third time and passed.

Bill (No. 190) respecting Juvenile Delinquents-Mr. Ayiesworth-was read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
Mr. It.' L. BORDEN. We passed the second time, and House went into committee I presume because it comes from the Senate. Perhaps the Minister of Justice will be good enough to state the purport of the Bill and explain what its effect will be.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. B. AYLESWORTH (Minister of Justice).
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The general effect of this Bill I think I may summarize by saying that it is intended to obviate the necessity for children, when accused of crime, being tried before the ordinary tribunals. The provision at the conclusion of the Bill is that the Act may be put in force in any province, or any portion of a province, by proclamation after the passing by such province of a Bill providing for the establishment of juvenile courts. And the intention is that wherever any province has established, or may hereafter establish, a special court for the trial of young persons, under the age of sixteen years, all offences against the criminal law by children under that age shall be disposed of by these juvenile courts. The case of an indictable offence committed by a young person over fourteen is excepted, but with that exception the provision of the Bill is in short, that all infractions of the criminal statutes, whether of the Dominion, of the province or Mr. HERRON
municipal by-laws, shall be dealt with by this special court, instead of being tried in the ordinary way. There are many details, which are self explanatory, governing the trial. It is to be of a summary character. Notice is to be given to the parent or guardian and to the probation officer, he being an officer appointed under the provisions of the provincial statute in that behalf, or, where there is no provincial statute on the subject, he may be appointed under the provisions of this Act. Instead of the juvenile court imposing sentence of imprisonment, as of necessity under the existing criminal law, the child may be released on probation.
Under no circumstances is it to be sent to jail, but if not released on probation, or a home found for it, either in some public institution or with some private family, provision is made with regard to the disposition that the court can make of the child. The court is empowered to appoint in any community a small committee, to be called the juvenile court committee, the duty of which is to assist the court in the way of suggestion, advice, and looking after the child, who is treated, from the time when found guilty of an offence, as a ward of the court, with the idea of being reclaimed rather than punished by imprisonment. In some of the provinces there is already legislation with regard to the care of neglected or abandoned children, to which this legislation is necessarily of an ancillary character. In the province of Ontario there is elaborate statutory provision designed for the protection and reformation of neglected children, and an officer of the government, a superintendent, having charge of such matters appointed by the government, and children's aid societies established in a great number of communities. These children's aid societies have felt the necessity of legislation of this character. I want to prevent the possibility of children who might be reclaimed if treated otherwise than as criminals, being sent to the ordinary prisons of the country with the older and possibly hardened offenders.
On section 17,

I am going to protest against the passing of a serious law like this in this hasty way. Here is a statute which is going to affect the character and the liberty of every little child, and I protest most seriously against the levity that is going on in this chamber.
The hon. member for Simcoe is the only one who made a joke about it.

This levity is altogether out of place. Just because the Minister of Justice, who cannot hear a word, wants this Bill to go through it is to be laughed through as a joke. Here is an Act resepeeting juvenile delinquents, a brand new law, brought in during the dying

hours of the session by the Minister of Justice, containing thirty-five sections, and after midnight we are asked to pass, but not consider it. It affects the liberty, the character and the treatment of every little child in this country. I am not going to stand for this Bill going through with this most uncalled for haste, and I think the Minister of Justice is not doing his duty in trying to rush it through in this way.

I was the one who asked the chairman to read the side notes instead of the clauses, because I had been looking at the Bill -and I saw there was no amendment to it. I supposed it was well considered by the Senate.

If the Senate passed this Bill, that is all the more reason why we should consider it carefully. Are we going to rush a law through this House simply because it has come from the Senate? I think that is a reason why it should be twice considered instead of being put through with this undue haste. My experience of legislation which has come from the Senate would lead me to the conclusion that it should be kicked out body and bones.
Has the hon. gentleman any amendment to propose?
If the hon. gentleman will tell me what the Bill is, I will tell him what amendments I have to propose.
Read it.
The hon. gentleman had better read it himself and not try to laugh the Bill through the House. I want, to understand every clause of this Bill before it passes.
Then it will never be passed.	_

I do not say that it never will pass with the majority that the government has to force it through, but, speaking for myself, it never will pass if It is going to be put through in this ill-advised, hasty and deplorable way in which it is attempted to put it through to-night. It is an outrage upon common decency and upon the respect that we should have for the little boys and girls of this country.
Will the hon. gentleman explain his anger about the matter?
If the hon. gentleman -chooses to call it anger, my anger is caused, if it is anger, by the fact that the so-called Minister of Justice brings into this House
Order, order.

speechtext: That tern should not be used.

speechtext: He has withdrawn it.
He has not withdrawn it.

I have withdrawn the word 'so-called.' This Bill may be all right, but I am not going to allow the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Talbot) to assume that this Bill is all right and to swallow it holus bolus because It is brought in by the Minister of Justice or anybody else. I am responsible to my constituents for what goes on here. This Bill is dealing with <x most serious matter. I do not see one word in it, for instance, in the hurried glance which I have been able to give to it, providing for the protection of the child or as to how he is to be defended. He seems to be entirely at the mercy of a person called a probation officer. There should be some provision for the child being -able to say he is not guilty If he is not guilty. Whatever the probation officer chooses to do with the child is to be done. It mav be all right if we had time to consider it carefully, but what I am pleading for, and I do not care if the whole House gets angry with me for doing so -
You are the one who is angry.
I do not care whether the hon. member for Cape Breton is angry or not.

He may be sorry for you but he is not angry.
' Mr. LANCASTER. The hon. gentleman's sorrow does not amount to anything. His are crocodile tears. 1 am going to protest against this Bill going through without being carefully considered. We might do it In five or six hours but we cannot in five or six minutes. I think the Minister of Justice will be well advised if he moves that the committee rise and report progres and let us take it up when we have more time. Is there any provision in this -Act corresponding to the amendment made by a Bill Introduced by me some years ago, providing that when a child was charged with any indictable offence no election for trial could be made without the parent or guardian being notified so as to advise the child.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: -Section 8 provides for that.

Is this Bill modelled on some other law as to which there has been experience ? I presume that a Bill of this kind consisting of a mass of detail Is not

put upon the statute book simply as an experiment.	'

I can only answer in a very general way as I have not prepared the Bill myself. The whole subject is one to which those interested have given a great deal of attention and I have been favoured during the past 12 months with a mass of literature dealing with this question. It is stated by writers on the subject that Canada is almost alone among civilized nations in being without legislation of this character. That assertion is too sweeping because there is in Ontario a very elaborate statute going no doubt as far in the direction of this legislation as the provincial legislature felt itself constitutionally empowered to go. There is legislation of a more or less similar character in other provinces. I understand this measure has received very careful consideration from the Senate and has been passed with a view to filling a need, in order that the provincial legislation might have its full effect. The enactment goes into only as and when it is proclaimed in respect of some section of the country which asks for it and where there will be some general feeling of the necessity if it. It must be borne in mind that where this Act is not in force, if any one under the age of 16 years commits an offence, the only recourse under the present law is prosecution leading to fine and imprisonment. This statute will confer upon the court a much wider discretion so as to avoid going the length of imprisonment where it is a young offender.

Probably sections 34 and 35 will remove any objection to the Act that I am aware of.
since Magna Charta, and which cannot be denied to even a hardened criminal. The right to elect as to trial by jury should be vested in the person accused and not in some other person, in this case this levelheaded judge.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend is right in the view that this Bill would prevent the advantage of trial by jury, but possibly there are countervailing advantages to the person accused which would be of even greater value. The provision is distinctly made that a child is not to be sent jto a, common gaol before or after sentence. That in itself is a greater privilege and protection against the danger of the child being destroyed by what is perhaps a comparatively venial offence than the privilege of trial by jury. Cases are continually arising, I have one in mind which has occasioned a great deal of anxious consideration to officials in the Justice Department and actual distress to the judge before whom the child was convicted. A child of some twelve years of age killed another while at play. The jury convicted of manslaughter and there was no other recourse to the judge than to sentence, and feeling that he was obliged to sentence he felt he could not do otherwise than sentence to a substantial term of imprisonment and that youngster is possibly having its life destroyed at the present time in a penitentiary because it was impossible to treat it otherwise than as if it had been a grown man.
In such a case you could provide for a less severe penalty without depriving the child of the advantage of trial by jury.
Is there any discretion left to the magistrate as to whether proceedings shall be taken under this Act or under the general criminal law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: When it is an indictable offence and if the child is over 14 then by section 7 the court may in its discretion order the child to be proceeded with in the ordinary way, but unless such an order as that is made all offences of a criminal nature by children under 16 will be tried under the provisions of this Act and not in an ordinary public court.

If section 7 means that the child is deprived of the right' to have a trial by jury I protest against it. That is although it is an indictable offence and the child is over fourteen years, the court may in its discretion let the case go to the criminal court with a jury, to the assizes or to the sessions. That magistrate ought not to have the discretion to say a' child shall not have the right to a jury when it is over fourteen. My objection is to denying to that child the inherent right to trial by jury which we have all enjoyed

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The objection to trial by jury is the publicity; the whole idea is to avoid that. There is even a provision to prohibit the publication of offences of young people in the newspapers.

This clause 7 is at the discretion, of course, of the magistrate and the enforcement of the law will depend altogether on his judgment. The Act strikes me as one which will be of great benefit. Any one who has read the record of Judge Lindsay's court at Denver cannot but bie impressed with the great good he has done for boys and girls of that city, in fact he is known the world over as the children's judge. It is just on the lines of this Bill that he acts, but of course the usefulness of such Acts depends altogether on the men enforcing them. He must be a man who is trying to reclaim rather than to condemn the child. In Ontario we have Mr. Kelso the head of a department and the work of the department has resulted in the emptying of at least one institution for boys in the province, these boys have all been placed in homes and the latest reports I have is that only two have turned out badly. The

Act will accomplish as much good comparatively as Judge Lindsay has in his vicinity.

If the child is allowed the inherent right of trial by jury, which he undoubtedly has under the British constitution, it is put in the hands of the child to do away with the entire benefit of the Act. We are passing extraordinary legislation for the protection of the child, and to amend that as my hon. friend suggests would be to do away with the benefit of the Act.

You are providing that the parents shall be notified. On being notified, if the case is a serious one, the parent will employ counsel, and the child will have the advice of both the parents and the counsel, and the decision can be safely left to them. But you are leaving the decision entirely in the hands of some one who has no direct interest in the child's welfare.
It is the converse of the case which the hon. gentleman puts. We are passing an enactment for the benefit of the juvenile delinquent.
How do you know it is ?

W the hon. gentleman thinks it is not, he should have moved the six months' hoist on the second leading. Having read the Bill the second time, we have admitted the principle and we are providing a special court where the juvenile delinquent will be guarded against publicity and from being sent to the common jail. We are providing a special place for his incarceration. Assuming that this is for the benefit of the juvenile delinquent, we still provide-which is the converse of the case the hon. gentleman puts -that the magistrate shall have the discretion of giving a trial by jury where he thinks the seriousness of the case demands it.

By section 7 you are taking away the very thing which my hon. friend says is such a wonderful benefit that this wonderful Bill is going to accomplish. Instead of leaving the discretion to the whim of the magistrate, who has no experience of trials by jury and consequently knows nothing about them, I would leave the election to the parent of the child assisted by counsel.

My hon. friend assumes that every criminal case in the Dominion is tried by jury. We have heard him declaim about this inherent right of trial by jury conferred by Magna Charta, but does he not know that ninety-nine cases out of a hundred, where youths of fourteen years and under are brought before the court, they are tried by the magistrate without a jury? There are numberless instances all 394J
over Canada of criminal cases tried without a jury.
When the accused elect for summary trial?

Without any election at all. The hon. gentleman does not know what he is talking about. For the last hour he has been trying to get his friends to help him out of his wrangling over this matter. Does he not know that more than three-quarters of the cases of assault tried in this country are tried by a magistrate without a jury and the accused has no right to a jury?
They are not indictable offences.

I know they are not. The hon. gentleman is simply talking against time, and I want him to try and have a little sense.
On section 35, any city or town may ask for this law.

Taking section 35 in conjunction with section 34, it would strike me as being rather repugnant. Perhaps the Minister of Justice will explain how it would work out. Section 34, apparently, makes it a condition precedent that the province shall issue a proclamation bringing the Act into force. But under section 35 the Act may be brought into force by proclamation, notwithstanding that the provincial legislature has not passed an Act, if the Governor in Council is satisfied. The Governor in Council would be the Governor in Council of the Dominion, I presume, and the proclamation under the section would be the proclamation of the Dominion government.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) is going to move a section to meet that.

speechtext:
Sir WILFRID LAURIER rose to move the following resolution ;
That at the Imperial Conference lately held in the city of London, England, the following resolution was unanimously passed:
That -in the opinion of this conference the interests of the empire demand that m so far as practicable, its different portions should be connected by the best possible means of mail communications, travel and transportation ; and that to this end it is advisable that Great Britain shoud be connected with Canada, and through Canada with Australia and New Zealand, by the best service available within reasonable cost; that for the purpose of carrying the above project into effect, such financial support as may lie necessary should be contributed by Great Britain, Canada, Australia and New Zealand in equitable proportions.
That it is desirable that steps should be taken with all convenient speed to achieve the results aimed at in the said resolution.
That this House doth hereby endorse the terms of the said resolution, affirming that Canada is prepared to assume her fair share of the necessary financial obligations.
That in the opinion of this House it is desirable that the governments of Australia, Canada and New Zealand should, with as little delay as possible, agree upon a definite plan for carrying into effect the terms of the said resolution of the Imperial Conference, the same to be submitted for the consideration of the imperial and colonial parliaments.
He said : Of the advantages which would accrue to Canada if such a scheme as is here outlined were to go into effect I do not propose to speak. I have followed pretty carefully the expressions of public opinion

on this subject from the time, now twelve months ago, when it was first brought to the attention not only of Canada, but of the whole British empire; and, so far as my own observations have gone, I may say that though there have been some carping criticism, on the whole the scheme seems to have commanded universal approbation-I do not say unanimous, because I must recognize that some expressions of dissent have been heard. But while the expressions of opinion have not been unanimous, they have been pretty generally in favour of such a scheme. One thing at all events seemed to be certain: if such a scheme were to become a fact, its advantages to Canada would not be disputed. Canada would undoubtedly be on the highway, not only between Great Britain and her distant possessions on the other side of the globe, but also between Europe generally and the Orient. This scheme, which would primarily affect the British empire, would not in its usefulness be confined at all to the British empire ; but all the countries of Europe and all the countries of the Orient would necessarily seek this route as a means of communication between each other. Canada has the advantage of geography in this matter. We have the shortest route, I believe, both on the Pacific and on the Atlantic. At present the only available route between Great Britain and Australasia is by way of the Suez canal, and the disadvantages of this route as compared with the Canadian route are manifest. First of all, the duration of a trip from London to New Zealand by the Suez canal is no less than 29 days, and the discomfort of the trip to one of European blood is pretty severe. A trip through the Suez canal, and then through the Red sea and then east by way of Colombo is a very trying one to Europeans. A similar trip by way of Canada would certainly obviate all these discomforts. There is, I may say, an alternative route by way of San Francisco, and at the time of the conference Sir Joseph Ward, the Prime Minister New Zealand, who spoke with authority on this subject, stated that he had made a trip from New Zealand to England by way of San Francisco in 29 days. I think, however, that this route is practically no longer in existence ; since the earthquake at San Francisco some two years ago, I believe it has been abandoned. I speak under correction on this point, but I think I am correct. At all events, if that route is not now in existence, it may be revived at any moment. So that, in all our calculations, wo have to take into consideration not only the route by way of the Suez canal, but also the possibility of having a line of communication at any time from Liverpool, by way of New York and San Francisco to Australasia in 29 days. Therefore, it behooves us, if we are to attain what we have In mind, to make the journey by thv, line we have organized inside of 29 days and some days Sir WILFRID LAUEIER.
more. The line may be divided into three parts-the Atlantic part, the continental part and the Pacific part. When we speak of the Atlantic part, we know exactly what we can do; we know the conditions that prevail to-day between Europe and the American continent; and we know that it is possible, with a line of steamers of the highest type afloat, such as the ' Mauretania ' and the ' Lusitania,' to cross the Atlantic from British territory to Canadian territory within four days. We have the advantage on our side of distance to the extent of some about 1,000 miles, which would enable us to have easy communication from land to land with vessels of that type in four days. I do not, however, lose sight of the fact that vessels of the type of the ' Mauretania ' and 1 Lusitania ' are still in the experimental stage, commercially speaking. So far as navigation is concerned, the stage of experiment is past. These vessels have proved their adaptability to the service in which they are engaged; but, so far as the commercial aspect of the case is concerned, we are still in the dark, and no one can say yet that these two vessels, which have been heavily subsidized by the British government, will prove a success commercially. It is a well-known fact that all such high-class steamers have not been a success commercially, and it is an essential in all countries that they should be assisted out of the public treasury. The Germans do it, the Americans have done it, the English have done it, and the Canadians have done it. But although all these high-class steamers have been subsidized by their respective countries, there is a limit beyond which such assistance is not possible, and it is a question whether or not vessels of the type of the ' Mauretania ' and the ' Lusitania,' even with the assistance they have received from the British government, can be called a commercial success. Their owners say that the time will never come when they can dispense with such assistance.
Even if at the present moment we are not prepared to provide vesels like the ' Mauretania ' and the ' Lusitania ' it is possible for us to entertain the hope that we can have twenty knot or twenty-one knot steamers and these will easily cross the Atlantic within five days. Assuming that even it should take five days to cross the Atlantic I think I can hopefully if not confidently say that we can secure a train service which will cross the continent in at least five days ; may be in four days but as to that I would not speak positively. We are, however, on absolutely safe ground when we say that the train journey across the continent can be accomplished in five days. There then remains the service on the Pacific and as to that we are to a large extent in the dark. At present there are two Pacific services subsidized by the Canadian government, one to China and Japan, and the other to Australasia. The Pacific service by

the Empresses is in every respect excellent, but the steamers have a speed only of thirteen knots and consequently the voyage from Vancouver to Hong Kong is considered somewhat slow in these days of fast transportation. The service between Vancouver and Australasia has not up to the present time given the satisfaction we had reason to hope for, and we are now negotiating for its improvement. For this service we have been paying something like $40,000 a year. The mail service on the Atlantic costs us at the present time about $500,000 a year, and, therefore, for the ocean mail service on the Atlantic and the Pacific we are paying about $540,000. It is for us to consider to what extent we will have to implement the present service in order to achieve what we r.ow contemplate. Sir Joseph Ward, Prime Minister of New Zealand, expressed at the conference his decided preference for a Pacific service equal to the service now on the Atlantic, namely, steamers of twenty-knots or twenty-two knots, in order that Auckland may be made in ten or twelve days from Vancouver. Such a scheme is perhaps too ambitious for us now. I wish for my part I could view the matter with the same enthusiasm as my friend Sir Joseph Ward, who stated that New Zealand would be prepared to pay a subsidy of £100,000 sterling to such a line as that. This is a very large subsidy, indeed, for a country Ike New Zealand with a population of less than 1,000,000, but Sir Joseph Ward attached so much importance to a fast allBritish line that he was prepared- to advise the parliament of his country to grant this very handsome subsidy to secure it. Whether or not it is possible to have such a service on the Pacific seems to me of somewhat doubtful possibility. We must recognize that these mail subsidies have to be calculated largely upon the basis of the population which is served. The population of New Zealand is about 1,000,000, the population of Australia is under 5,000,000 and the population of our Pacific coast is not much more than 200,000. It may be that this population is not so large as to justify a twenty knot or twenty-two knot service on the Pacific, and so we have to consider if we cannot do with less. It is quite possible I think that we might have an eighteen knot service from Vancouver to Auckland and from Auckland to Sydney, and with steamers of that speed they ought to make the voyage from Vancouver to Auckland in about sixteen days. From Vancouver to Auckland is about 6,355 miles, from Vancouver to Sydney the distance is 6,824 miles and from Auckland to Sydney the nautical distance is about 1,200 miles. That means that the voyage between Vancouver and Australia could not be covered in less than twenty-two days by eighteen knot steamers and this is not entirely satisfactory from the point of view of Australia which has perhaps the right to ask for a more expeditious service. It is, therefore, for us to consider whether it is possible to come to an agreement for a twenty knot service on the Pacific. I am not prepared now to give an opinion as to whether or not such a service cannot be attained ; it is a question which has to be very carefully considered and so for the present we do not propose to ask the House to give us endorsation to this scheme in any concrete form. The only thing we ask the House now to do is to authorize us to approach the subject with the governments of Australia and New Zealand so as to give the best possible consideration to the question and at a later day to come before the House with some concrete proposition if that be possible. That the idea is an excellent one every one admits ; that the idea is one which will commend itself to the best judgment of every pne in this country we all recognize, but at the same time the government does not close its eyes to the fact that the scheme may present so many difficulties as to render it impossible of absolute accomplishment.
And so the question has to be considered very carefully and looked into in all its details. We know where we are on the Atlantic, we know where we are with regard to the train service across the continent, but so far as the Pacific is concerned, the matter is still in the dark and, although the idea is one which should be exploited, we do not say that it is absolutely sure or feasible. That is the reason why we are asking the House to ratify the idea of the resolution which was passed by the conference. We have no intention of saying that the thing is absolutely beyond per-adventure, that it is an absolute certainty. We do not want, in approaching this subject, to give to the House more confidence than we have ourselves ; we do not want to lead the House to understand that we are sure that the project is absolutely feasible, because there are things which have to be taken into consideration, which have to be determined and which must engage our best attention. There are on the Pacific ocean physical conditions which have to be looked into very carefully and which, if possible, have to be overcome. The climatic conditions are such that it is perhaps possible that the complete execution of the idea may not be feasible. I understand that vessels have the same difficulty there that we have in winter in making steam, that climatic conditions exercise nearly the same influence over the making of steam on the equator as on the frozen ocean, and, for all these considerations, whilst we bespeak the sympathetic attention of the House to the scheme, we do not in any measure commit ourselves to it as a scheme as to which we may have an absolute condition of certainty. The House will remember that all we are asking is that it shall endorse the

terms of the resolution. All we are asking it to do at the present time is to authorize us to enter into negotiations with our fellow subjects of Australasia in order if possible to find the means of having such a line as is now contemplated, and if it is feasible then to bring it before parliament for its consideration.

Mr. Speaker, we have all listened with a great deal of interest to the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) who introduced this resolution. I think the House and the country will agree with me that the mover of the resolution has not been at all as positive in his statements in this House as he was in the imperial conference of 1907 when he moved, not this resolution, but a certain resolution with the same object in view. At that time my right hon. friend had no doubts. He was not only in favour of the idea, he not only believed that the idea was practicable, but, if I mistake not, his demand upon the conference at that time was to at once establish a service between Great Britain, Australia and New Zealand through Canada. I think it is of sufficient importance that, just at this point, in view of certain expressions and of the assumption that has been made, to take up a little time In presenting the history of the growth of the idea of improved steamship communication between Canada and Great Britain, between Canada and Australia and between Great Britain and Australia through Canada as a land route. It is not true that the idea, which was broached to the conference in 1907 and which the right hon. gentleman spoke of when he came to Quebec in the latter part of that year, was a newly discovered idea. It is well just here to quote what the right hon. gentleman said in his Quebec speech. He said :
During the last five days of the conference I announced a new idea which has almost become historic-the All-Red Dine. My proposition was the establishment at once -of fast boats on the Atlantic and the Pacific. I am thoroughly convinced that my ideas are in the interest of Canada and the empire and, although I have grown old and white in the service of the country, I am prepared to work with all my energy to further the cause.
The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sif-tou), who made a very exceedingly comprehensive statement in reference to this idea a few months ago in this House, also declared, iu express terms, that the resolution of Sir Wilfrid Laurier in the conference of 1907 included the genesis and included the history of this idea of intercommunication between Great Britain and the overseas dominions. Another point I want to call the attention of the House to in connection with it is the extremely different imsition which my right hon. friend occupied in the conference of 1907 and oc-

Every idea is taken in that my right hon. friend contemplates in the resolution which the Prime Minister has moved to-day.

conference of 1907. The Prime Minister said : Without experts, without the information required for the establishment of the service, he would pledge Canada to take her share even up to a million and a half a year. We have information by actual experience of what the country has spent and is likely to spend by reason of taking my hon. friend at his own estimation in 1903. He estimated that the total money cost to this country of the National Transcontinental Railway would be $13,000,000. The Minister of Customs followed in his wake and used the argument throughout Ontario. The Minister of Finance made a carefully revised statement of the cost and placed it at $52,000,000. The Minister of Railways comes down today and leaving out terminals and interest and a lot of other things, he tells us it will cost at least $114,000,000. My friend to my right (Mr. R. L. Borden) by a most temperate and I think careful statement, placed the cost of that completed road from Moncton up to the city of Winnipeg at $170,000,000 or $180,000,000. Leaving out of account $11,000,000 which he has calculated for, which might be disputed by some, although 1 do not think it is at all liable to any dispute, and basing the figures on government records and information, that line of railway will cost us from $160,000,000 up to $170,000,000. We are therefore suspicious and we would not like to and do not propose to vote for any scheme that my right hon. friend brings down in this eight month of the session involving the laying of a possible $15,000,000 additional burden upon the people without making sure that no contract will be signed in the recess, and that when we meet next year we may not have the Prime Minister present to us, as he has done in the Yukon and other cases, a hard and fast contract and say to his followers : We are pledged to that, pledged to Australia, pledged to New Zealand, pledged to Great Britain, you are to see us through-and his obedient following would see him through as they have done heretofore. The financial conditions of this country are such that it is necessary to scan with the very greatest particularity any scheme by which it is proposed to place on the shoulders of an already overburdened people an additional possible tax of $15,000,000 during the next 10 years. The Finance Minister knows something of the condition of the London money market. He boasted the other day that we got our money but he was not very particular in explaining that we got it because the promoters had to put up the money, and now to hold 50 per cent of the whole subscription. Although we got our money from the underwriters, then, does he think that he has made it easier for us to go on the London market and ask for another loan of four, six or eight millions as he will have to in the course of this Mr. FOSTER.
and the early part of next year ? To-day the revenues of Canada are falling off by over a million dollars a month ; to-day the taxes are rising at the rate of 16- per cent in ten years and other obligations in addition to what we already have are promised to be loaded upon the people sometime during the few remaining days of this session, some of them may be necessary, some of them I am bound to say not at all necessary. With all this in prospect we do not propose as an opposition to pin ourselves down to a position where we will be met with an added obligation of $10,000,000 or $15,000,000 facing us when the next parliament assembles at Ottawa.

The unusually late date at which this motion has been brought down, when it is anticipated that parliament shall prorogue on a week from Saturday next, is an indication that the government do not expect any very lengthy or adequate discussion of so grave and important a proposal. However, if the Prime Minister had followed the exact analogy of his course at the Imperial Conference of last year, he would have brought it down on the very last day of the session. So, I think, we may be thankful that it has not been postponed until a still later date.
There is not the slightest doubt as to the absolute importance of better means of intercommunication between the different parts of the empire. That has been an article of Conservative faith and Conservative policy for many years. I need not go over the ground already traversed by my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster), who has pointed out that what is now known as the ' All-Red route ' in Canada is practically that which for many years had borne the same name in Australia and New Zealand, and is but the ordinary development of ideas and proposals that were debated in this House long before the right hon. gentleman came into power in 1896.
I do not desire to detain the House at any length, but let me point out that since 1896 conditions have changed a great deal in this country. What were essential and necessary features of any policy in 1896 may not be so essential and so important to-day. The Conservative government of this country in 1895 looked forward to a 20-knot service on the Atlantic. (Since 1896, the service on the Atlantic has advanced from 14 or 15 knots to 18 knots. We have to-day on the Pacific, as well, a 14-knot service.' My hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) in speaking on this question a few years ago in Montreal used some language which is singularly like that what the Prime Minister used to-day, but singularly different from the attitude taken by the right hon. gentleman at the imperial conference and from the view expressed

in very forcible and eloquent terms by the bon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) when he addressed this House on this subject during the budget debate. The Prime Minister's proposal at the imperial conference was for a 24 or 25 knot service ; and X think the hon. member for Brandon put the case for a service of that kind as strongly as it could be put when he addressed the House during the debate to which X have just alluded. My hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture, speaking on this subject not long ago, in Montreal on the occasion of a banquet to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, then Minister of Justice, said :
Personally, as far as the fast line is concerned, I would like to see a line of ships built to steam 18 or 20 knots, carrying 10,000 or 12,000 tons of freight, and accommodating about 250 passengers with comfort. That type of boat is both profitable and comfortable. I would rather travel across the Atlantic in a steady commodious boat than in the speedy ones. The record breakers made good time, but there is more ease and comfort in crossing on the cargo boat. I think these boats could touch at some coast port for the convenience of passengers who were travelling in haste, after which the journey could be continued to an inland port. It is easy enough to get a fast line, but it costs a lot of money, and I do not see why we should be held by the nose for such a service. At present, there is an inclination on the part of some Canadians to plunge into any expense, and this must not be allowed to go too far.
That would seem to have been a rather severe stroke in advance at the statements of the right hon. Prime Minister at the imperial conference, and at the same time a somewhat forcible retort to the argument put forward by the hon. member for Brandon during the present session.
I should pause to mention the great interest which the High Commissioner for Canada has taken in this project of better communication between parts of the empire; and whether we accept or do not accept all the views which have been put forward by Lord Strathcoua with regard to the rate of speed which is practically attainable under present conditions between Canada and the mother country, we must all acknowledge with gratitude and appreciation the great services which that gentleman has rendered to the empire in this and many respects, and the deep interest he at all times has shown in everything that tends to the welfare of this great country and of the empire as a whole.
My hon. friend the member for Brandon, in debating this matter during the present session, and the right hon. Prime Minister in' his speech to-day, have touched this question solely from the standpoint of passenger and mail service, except in one respect to which I will allude for a moment, In which my hon. friend from Brandon did mention the subject of freight. I regard that 395
as a rather serious omission. I am not inclined for one moment to minimize the importance of the best service for passengers and mails that can reasonably be attained, within the resources of this country, between Great Britain, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. I appreciate to the full what has been said in support of that view, especially what has been said by the hon. member for Brandon. There is a great deal of force in all that he has urged upon our attention on that subject. As a matter of sentiment, as a matter of bringing together citizens from different parts of the empire, as a means of enabling them to discover the enormous resources of this country, and, in that way, to promote the development of these resources-for all these considerations and many others that time does not permit me to dwell upon, I acknowledge the importance of that aspect of this great question. But let us remember

and it seems to me that this point has been entirely overlooked- that, after all, the transmission of passengers and mails does not constitute what is really commerce between. Canada and Great Britain or Canada and the other parts of the empire. When you analyse what is meant by the promotion of trade and commerce between the different parts of the empire, you must acknowledge that, in the end, it depends upon the free interchange of commodities and upon our being able to transmit to their market in the mother country and in Europe the rapidly increasing, and already very great, natural products and manufactures of this country. It is in this that trade and commerce consists. And, without for one moment minimizing the other considerations that have been urged, I venture to regret that those who have at heart this great project do not seem to have taken that aspect of the subject sufficiently into consideration.
Jf you put aside sentimental considerations and the possibilities of attracting capital to this country to which I have just now alluded, what do we find to be the chief benefit that can be derived by the people of this country from better communication between different parts of the empire? How many farmers and producers of this country have occasion to cross the Atlantic in any year? But how many farmers and producers are there who are not vitally interested every year in the transmission, by the cheapest and most expeditious modes of transportation of their products to the mother country? Seventy dive per cent to eighty per cent and perhaps eighty-five per cent to ninety per cent of our people are vitally Interested in that question; and any proposal which neglects to give due and proper consideration to that particular problem ought not to command the assent of parliament or the approval of the people. We know that, under modern conditions, we are obliged to compete in the market of the mother country, not only with the farmers



and producers of the United States, but also with the farmers and producers of Europe as well as those of New Zealand and Australia. It will be impossible for us to compete with them unless we have a modern and efficient cold storage system, and that system can never be thoroughly efficient so long as there is a single broken link in the chain of connection from thq point of production to the markets in the old country. Therefore these essential features, more favourable freight rates, better means of transporting freights, and a system of cold storage seem to me to have been entirely overlooked by this government.
There is another consideration, and my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has dwelt on it. It cannot be denied that the very prosperous times through which Canada in common with the rest of the world, has been passing until within a year ago, have led this government to indulge in enormous expenditures and obligations, the true measure of which is only beginning to be realized. When we find an expenditure of from $175,000,000 to $200,000000 facing us in respect of the construction of the Transcontinental Railway alone, when we see the enormous demands made upon the public treasury from all parts of the country and the somewhat prodigal promises of gentlemen on the treasury benches, when we realize that up to the present we have not developed in their true sense our national ports and that we are only on the threshold of the real development of our inland waterways; when we consider the thousand and one demands for purposes of real national development which must be met within the next few years, we begin to realize that the resources of Canada, great as they are, may be strained, and strained unduly, in the immediate future if we are not careful how far we commit the country to increased expenditure. Look at the estimates of the present year. The government have already brought down estimates amounting to $127,412,724, and if rumour be true we are yet to be confronted with an enormous amount of Supplementary Estimates and perhaps a still more enormous amount for railway subsidies. We are also face to face with this huge expenditure not only on the National Transcontinental, but in almost every department we must be careful how far we commit ourselves in advance. Look for a moment at the terms of this resolution :
That at the Imperial Conference lately held in the city of London, England, the following resolution was unanimously passed:-
That in the opinion of this conference the interests of the empire demand that in so far as practicable, its different portions should be connected by the best possible means of mail communications, travel and transportation; and that to this end it is advisable that Great Britain should he connected with Canada and through Canada with Australia and New Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
Zealand, by the best service available within reasonable cost; that for the purpose of carrying the above project into effect, such financial support as may be necessary should be contributed by Great Britain, Canada, Australia and New Zealand in equitable proportions.
I do not believe that there is any bon. gentleman In this House who dbes not heartily sympathize with the object aimed at. So far as the terms of the resolution are concerned therefore, we need not have any special concern at the moment because our liability is guarded by the expression ' within reasonable cost ' and the whole matter is thus left open. The right hon. gentleman did not mention what be would regard as a reasonable amount this country should contribute. He did not give us any Information as to the amount to which be would be prepared to pledge the credit of the country for the purpose of obtaining a twenty or twenty-one knot service. But even if he did, perhaps we could not place much dependence on it, for if we apply our experience in connection with his estimate of the cost of the Transcontinental, we would be obliged to multiply by fifteen any estimate he would offer. However, the resolution proceeds as follows ;
That it is desirable that steps should be taken with all convenient speed to achieve the results aimed at in the said resolution.
That particular paragraph seems to be entirely unnecessary because it simply states what is proposed in more definite form in the concluding paragraph. The next paragraph is as follows ;
That this House doth hereby endorse the terms of the said resolution, affirming that Canada is prepared to assume her fair share of the necessary financial obligations.
I would have been fairly well satisfied with that paragraph except for the circumstances I have already mentioned, namely, that the Prime Minister and the able advocate of this proposal, my hon. friend from Brandon (Mr. Sifton), have carefully omitted any reference whatever to improvement in the transportation of freight. True, my bon. friend from Brandon (Mr. Sifton), in the concluding part of his speech this session, said this :
So far as Canada is concerned, what may he said to be the argument in favour of it from a commercial standpoint. You can put it in two or three words. At the present time, mail, passenger and freight service of the best and quickest character from here to Great Britain goes through the United States-and from Australia and New Zealand goes across the continent of Europe. It does not go by our own ports or our own territory. In other words, so far as travel and transportation are concerned Canada is on the side street instead of on the main thoroughfare.
He did make allusion to the transportation of freight, but the difficulty I find with his-

proposal is that throughout his speech he strenuously advocates the expenditure of an enormous sum for the improvement of the passenger and mail service but says not one word as to the appropriation of any expenditure whatever for the improvement of the freight service or the establishment of any system of cold storage.
This paragraph of the resolution pledges Canada to assume her fair share of the necessary financial obligations. I see no particular advantage in our pledging ourselves to obligations, the exact nature and extent of which we do not know at present. It has all to come before parliament again in so far as I understand. Even the Prime Minister, in so far as I have been able to comprehend his remarks, did not propose to enter into any definite engagement or to commit Canada to any definite proposal until the project-the plan, as it is called in the last paragraph of the resolution- shall have been submitted to the imperial and colonial parliaments. Of what advantage is .it that the country should pledge itself to an absolutely indefinite and unknown obligation which, if the last paragraph of the resolution means anything, must be submitted to parliament before it can be entered into. There may be some sentimental purpose aimed' at in the paragraph to which I have alluded, but in so far as any practical object is concerned, it seems to me that the resolution might with advantage be modified by omitting it.
