Mr. Speaker, before the House rose I had been considering the individual paragraphs of the proposed resolution. I had pointed out that the second paragraph seems to serve no purpose which is not equally fulfilled by the last paragraph. The second paragraph declares :
That it is desirable that steps should be taken with all convenient speed to achieve the results aimed at in the said resolution.
The last paragraph declares that it is desirable that the several governments should with as little delay as possible agree upon a definite plan for that purpose. This paragraph, therefore, is superfluous.
So far as the third paragraph is concerned, I have pointed out that it is a pledge of financial support to an indefinite expenditure, and is entirely useless unless it is intended to justify the government in committing the country in advance. For that reason I would think that no good purpose would be served by the third paragraph. If everything is to be open to the consideration of parliament when the proposal is eventually submitted, of what value is it to say in this paragraph that Canada is prepared to assume her fair share of the necessary financial obligations ? The necessary financial obligations are to be with-3951
in reasonable cost ; therefore the whole matter, I would suppose, is to be left entirely to the discretion and judgment of parliament when the proposal comes to be submitted. Therefore of what value is it to say in advance that Canada is prepared to assume her fair share of the necessary financial obligations unless the government is now prepared to inform parliament what they consider to be Canada's fair share or the reasonable cost?
I will quote the fourth paragraph :
That in the opinion of this House it is desirable that the governments of Australia, Canada and New Zealand should, with as little delay as possible, agree upon a definite plan for carrying into effect the terms of the resolution of the Imperial Conference, the same to be submitted for the consideration of the imperial and colonial parliaments.
I have no objections to the terms of that paragraph, provided a rider, to which I will refer in a moment, is added which will make it absolutely clear and certain, beyond peradventure, that the government will not take the course of committing the country to some huge expenditure before it comes to this parliament for the purpose of procuring its ratification of that which has been done in advance. The wording of this paragraph leads me to consider for a moment just what the plan may be which the government will eventually propose. I have already pointed out the extreme importance, from my point of view, of fair consideration to lower freight rates and to a system of cold storage, and I am glad to observe that, at the recent Imperial Conference, Mr. Lloyd George apparently took the same view. At page 568 of the report of the Conference I find this :

May I add that at present our connection with this country is by the alternative routes round the cape or through
the Suez oanal ? These are omr princ.ip'T routes and must always remain our great cargo routes, because there is no transhipment.

And, from the point of view of developing trade, they are much more important.
These words indicate his view, of which I was not aware when I spoke on this subject about a year ago. He emphasizes his opinion that one important, perhaps the most important, consideration is the development of trade by the carriage of commodities from one part of the empire to another. Again, at page 577 of the same report, I find Mr. Lloyd George using the following language :
We cannot examine it apart from the question of the carriage of goods too. We must take that into account. It is not only a matter of a fast mail service, but also a question of the cheaper transport of goods and materials from the colonies. I consider that to be a very important item, so far as we are concerned.

Speaking for myself, I consider it to be a very important item indeed, so far as Canada is concerned. Our chief market for our agricultural products is the British market, and is likely to remain the British market for many years to come. To save a cent a bushel on the transportation of 100,000,000 bushels of wheat is to put $1,000,000 into the pockets of the farmers of this country. If by a system of cold storage you enable our perishable products to reach the British market in perfect condition, you confer a corresponding advantage on the producers of these products.
In this connection might I be permitted to make another observation ? It is apparently intended to negotiate for only a 20 or 21 knot service on the Atlantic. As the hon. member for North Toronto has pointed out, the government are only proposing now what their predecessors actually accomplished twelve years ago before they went out of office ; and the proposal of the Prime Minister is subject to this further observation, that if unassisted private enterprise has so improved the service on the Atlantic that instead of a 14 or 15 knot service we now have an 18-knot service, might we not reasonably rely upon the same unassisted private enterprise to bring about in the immediate or early future a 20 or 21-knot service? I will not take up the time of the House further in discussing this subject, but I will conclude by moving the following amendment to the resolution proposed by the Prime Minister :
That the said resolution be amended by striking out the second and third paragraphs and substituting the following
' That this House in expressing its strong sympathy with the object of the said resolution desires to record its opinion that more favourable freight rates and a thoroughly efficient system of cold storage are essential features of any such transportation project.'
And by adding the following paragraph at the end of the said resolution :-
' That, having regard to the very heavy expenditures and obligations in which the present administration has involved the country, the government should not commit Canada to any such plan, or to any contract or expenditure for such purpose until after the same shall have been submitted to and approved by the parliament of Canada.'

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words upon the resolution which has been proposed by the right hon. the Prime Minister. I wish in the first place to express my pleasure at seeing the resolution on the paper. Personally I would have been pleased if the resolution had appeared sooner in the session, for reasons which I will refer to later on ; but I am pleased that the government has been able to see its way clear to make the proposal which the Prime Minister has made. I am not especially concerned in the Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
historical retrospect of my hon. friend the member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) ; at least, in so far as it dealt in criticism of the past action of members of the present government party. In matters of this kind we can at least afford to leave to one side what happened twenty or twenty-five years ago. Conditions have so changed that he would be a strange man indeed whose views in regard to some of these things had not altered with the altering circumstances. I am quite willing to admit that my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) did one service to the resolution when he proved-his remarks were conclusive upon the subject as were also the remarks of the leader of the opposition-that it has been the traditional policy of the Conservative party to favour better means of communication between the different parts of the British empire. That unquestionably has been a part of the policy of the Conservative party, and I trust it is a part of the policy of the party which is now in power. I am satisfied that if this resolution is adopted by this House and if due aud legitimate and proper diligence is shown that in the course of time we shall be able to meet the desires of those loyal British subjects and loyal Canadians who are anxious to see such a project carried into full and effective fruition. I think, however, that our friends on the opposite side of the House in pursuance of the traditional policy of their party should give 'us a little more enthusiastic support than they are giving us upon the present occasion, because while the leader of the opposition may very properly say that there is much in favour of his amendment, yet that amendment can be taken as meaning nothing else than, for the present at least, a negative to the resolution which has been moved by the right lion, the Prime Minister. After all, the position we are in to-day is this :	That the
Prime Minister and his colleagues having attended the imperial conference, and the representatives of all the colonies having passed a certain resolution in regard to improving the transportation system between the different portions of the empire mentioned in the resolution, the question now before the parliament of Canada is : Will the parliament of Canada endorse the action of the imperial conference or will it not ? That is the definite question we have to settle. I am inclined to think that it will be seen upon full consideration that the whole subject is so surrounded with difficulties that it is not possible for the government at the present stage to go into such matters of detail as those to which the leader of the oppositon refers in the first portion of his amendment-the second portion of his amendment, of course, has to do with an entirely different phase of the question. tit will been seen that the effective factors of the problem are such that it is not

possible for the government to come before parliament In regard to a scheme of this kind in the same way as if it were a scheme relating to the internal development of Canada and which was solely and entirely within the jurisdiction of the government and parliament of Canada. We have before us a proposition which has to do with various portions of the empire : Great Britain, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand. You have first to get some kind of a statement of views, some kind of a general proposition to which the parties will agree. The general proposition we have in the resolution of the imperial conference, but then the parties have to find out what can be done ; they have to find out how much it will cost, they have to discuss the question, they have to settle details and arrive at a scheme which each government will be prepared to recommend to its parliament. All that has to be done before you can get any further with the project than it is at present..
Might I point out that my amendment does not touch that part of the resolution.

The position therefore is altered to a considerable extent since the time of the Imperial Confernce. Discussions have taken place and information has been disseminated. It has come to the knowledge of all parties concerned that in all probability such a service as I have deseriDed is a practicable service which could be made and would be the best service that could be obtained for any reasonable expenditure.
Would such a service include the transportation of any of the products of Canada ?

Freight, yes. The ships
on which the estimates were made provided for a capacity of 1,000 tons freight for the Atlantic boats and 3,000 tons for the Pacific boats. I may say that experience shows that a larger capacity than 1,000 tons upon fast Atlantic boats would not be of much service, because taking the year around, the probability is that that is about as much of the class of freight they would take as they could succeed in contracting for. As a matter of fact the very fast boats running from New York do not take anything like 1,000 tons on the average. The Canadian Pacific Railway boats running from Quebec and St. John do somewhat better. Therefore the conference resolution having been passed, as much information as can be gathered has been gathered upon the subject, and if we are able to infer anything as to the attitude of Great Britain, it is that if the colonies are desirous that this plan should be carried out, the colonies should get together, settle upon a definite plan and present it to the imperial government for their acceptance. That obviously is a reasonable position for the British government to take, and therefore it becomes essential that somebody should take the initiative and obviously from Canada's position in relation to the whole scheme and her great interest in successfully carrying it out, it is the logical position that Canada should become the chief promoter in carrying this into effect. Thus what the Prime Minister is asking is that, the resolution having been passed, the general features of the scheme having been accepted in so far as they can be before a definite business proposition is arrived at, the government of Canada should be authorized to take the matter up with Australia and New Zealand, arrive at a definite proposition and then go to the imperial government, get them to agree to the scheme and carry it into definite effect. I cannot see myself that any other plan could be practically proposed or would give any probability of arriving at a successful conclusion.
At the risk of repeating what I have said In this House I shall discuss briefly the cost. Expert shipping men in London were employed for the purpose of arriving at as close an estimate as possible of the cost of such a service upon the Atlantic and

what answer can we make when we are told that, while Canada is developing very rapidly, while she is improving her internal transportation system tremendously, she is still satisfied to remain on a side street, still satisfied to remain dependent for the ordinary interests of business upon the courtesy and good will of our neighbours to the south? It ought not to be so. It seems to me the time has come when Canada can afford what is, in this respect, a necessity for her national growth and development.
And it should be done now. Mr. Speaker, even if you allow, that everything will be done that can be done, and done with all reasonable speed, it will he impossible to bring this service about inside of four years, probably five years. You have to get the several governments together ; there are the interminable discussions between the members of the several governments; the British government has been brought in; the four parliaments have to be consulted. In view of all that is to be done, it is not to be expected that this can be brought into effect inside of four or five years. Then if we are going to do it for this generation, the time has arrived when we ought to make a beginning. Temporary financial difficulties which afflict us at the present time, will not, we hope, remain to trouble us four or five years from now. This temporary financial depression will pass away ; it was a natural thing ; a necessary thing ; a good thing. For, it is as necessary in connection with the business corpus that it should have periods of recuperation as it is in connection with our physical bodies. We cannot keep going at full speed all the time. This necessary lull in business had to come. It has come. It has not hurt Canada seriously. In a year or two we shall have emerged from it, and I think that, if we have then been afraid to begin the steps necessary to bring this great project into effect, every one will feel that we have made a very serious mistake. I do not desire to be understood as advocating a reckless financial policy. I am not on my feet for the purpose of critising the financial policy of the government ; but I am free to say that if. at the end of four or five years, in consequence of arrangements made in pursuance of this resolution, we shall be called upon to pay the subsidy for the purpose of securing this service, I think that some of the expenditures which this parliament is authorizing might well be cut out for the purposes of furnishing the means for this subsidy. Under any circumstances, many of the things we are called upon to do now, we shall not be called on to do then. We are accomplishing great works, they are passing into the region of things accomplished, and what we have to do is look to the future. For my part I am satisfied that my hon. friends opposite can hardly expect the House to take the position that after the representatives of Canada Mr. SIFTON.
have gone to the imperial conference and become parties to the resolution adopted by that conference, the House should decline to endorse the position they took. And I am convinced my right hon. friend, the First Minister, can confidently ask the House to stand by the position he took at the conference.

1.	The provision of fast mail services on the several routes; and

These resolutions were passed almost unanimously in these meetings of commercial men assembled from all parts of the empire. So that the proposition which the government brings down is not a new one. It is true that it is a somewhat advanced position for this government to take. It is to be regretted that this is not a very opportune time to talk of devoting large sums to be taken out of the public treasury to any enterprises at all. I could only wish that a fraction of the amount that is being sunk, for the present, at all events in the Grand Trunk Pacific, could have been withheld in order that w7e might have a subsidized line of steamships to carry the products of Canada to different parts of the British empire. That is a project that is worthy of the greatest consideration, and as a citizen of Canada and of the empire I desire to discuss this question entirely free from all party prejudice as I believe that this side of the House has always held the banner in regard to being the imperialistic party, if there is such in Canada, and that it has always desired to improve the relations between the mother country and the colonies. That being the case, we could not oppose the spirit of the resolution as brought down and which embodies the view of the late Colonial Conference. The amendment moved by my hon. friend tbe leader ol' tbe opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden)
I think does not change the resolution in any particular. Very few7 of our ow7n citizens who go across the ocean want to go in very fast ships, hut the proper transportation of the products which are daily going out of Canada means dollars and cents in the pocket of every farmer iu Canada. So that the first consideration should he given to the transportation of our products in a cheap, efficient and safe way. in a way that will

preserve them in the best condition so that when they arrive on the British market, or on any of the colonial markets, it will be found that they will bring the highest prices. Therefore, I think the rider that has been proposed by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition is one that we might w7ell adopt. I trust that the right hon. leader of the government will see his way to join with my hon. friend the leader of the opposition in this and that we may have a united House on w7hat is really an imperial question. Ret this resolution, as amended by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition he the unanimous voice of this House. I think it would have a great effect throughout the empire. It would he doing something to consolidate the empire and in my opinion it would be a great step iu advance for the commercial interests of Canada and of the1 empire as a whole. It is my intention to support the resolution as amended by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition. I trust that the right hon. leader of the House will see his way to incorporate these few words in the resolution so that it may go out to the world, to Great Britain and the colonies, that we are on this empire matter comparatively" a unit in this country and that when it comes to discussing these broad imperial questions in a business way we do not allow small-minded politics to creep In, but are prepared to do our utmost to further the object which we all have so much at heart-the unification, consolidation and development of the greatest empire that the world has ever seen. If it is the desire of this House to contribute to that end I hope that the resolution, as amended by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, will he adopted, and I trust that the same spirit that has been displayed iu the discussion so far may characterize it up to the finish and that we may present a united front 'upon this question. I have spoken of the chambers of commerce of the empire. They held their fifth meeting in Montreal and their sixth in London. Only yesterday I saw heralded in the press that the seventh has been called and where has it been called? Away out in the Antipodes, in Australia. The next meeting of the chambers of commerce of the empire will he held in Australia. The limelight will then be turned on the transportation facilities of the empire. Business men from all over the world, from all parts of the empire. will be going to Australia to take part in that great congress and the very question that is before this House to-day will be one that will be agitating every business man, every board of trade, every chamber of commerce throughout the empire because they have all to get there. They will want to get there in the best possible way, they will want to get there expeditiously, safely and in comfort. But I say that we should not sacrifice the con-

sideration of material advantage to that of speed. It is all very well to travel in very fast ships, but it Is a great deal better to travel in comfort and safety. The interests of the navy of Great Britain cannot be any more advanced than by the extension of the mercantile marine to all the seas that couple the various parts of the empire, placing upon them a class of ships that will carry safely and expeditiously both the passengers and trade of the great British empire. It is well known that in times of war the mercantile marine is the first adjunct of the navy and that fact should not be lost sight of in the consideration of a question of this kind. It is a matter that presents itself to the advanced man as one of importance. Every ship that you place upon the ocean not only carries mails, passengers and cargo from one part of the empire to another but is also a source of strength and help in time of stress and danger because it affords safe transport for troops, a means of getting supplies to any part of the earth in a short time, and it is one of the most valuable adjuncts that can be given a nation for its safety, prosperity and welfare. When the vote is taken on this resolution I trust it will be found that both sides of the House with united voice will give their support to what I conceive to be one of the greatest factors for the advancement and consolidation of the British empire in its various constituent parts.

I agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Cockshutt) that we should have unanimity on this resolution, for this certainly is a question which is not controversial. The people of Canada are not so much interested in the contest as to who applied the epithet ' All-Red ' to this project, or as to who were the best friends of this enterprise in the past, as they are in the question :	Who are the
best friends of the enterprise now? He who will demonstrate that fact in this House and in the country will do more to enlist the gratitude of Canadians than one who, for the sake of political controversy, endeavours to make out that one political party was more interested in the project than w7as the other. I regret that the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) imparted a political tinge to this debate. It may be that his combative energies have been so exercised lately that unconsciously polemic controversy comes upwards in his mind-anyhow, the leader of the opposition dispelled the idea that we were to have entire unanimity. I looked to him for moderate counsel so that the House might be united on the question in the manner prayed for by my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt), but instead of coalescence the leader of the opposition introduced an amendment which practically will have the effect of making this a
party question, although in its opening paragraph the amendment does speak of acquiescence in the principle, but not in practical details or in the operation of it as a practical measure. There has been throughout the country-there certainly has been in the maritime ports, where the subject was originally of more Interest than it was in the interior of the country-a difference of opinion as to whether a comparatively slow service of 1G or 17 knots would not better serve the exigencies of the country than a more rapid service of 20 knots or over. That controversy waged in parliament. However, the discussion on that point as a practical issue has almost passed, because of the fact that a 17-knot service has been tried and has been successfully established along commercial lines. Such a service does not require so much of government aid in the way of subsidy, and it may be fairly left to achieve its own part in the commerce of the country. That controversy was not confined to politicians in the Canadian parliament or to opposing views in our commercial centres, but it was taken up by the steamboat companies themselves, and some of these companies which are esteemed to be the most highly advanced and most in touch with the freight and passenger traffic of the Atlantic have rather retrograded from the very fast service of 20, 22 and 23 knots to a service of 1G and 17 knots. The controversy existed between the directors of leading steamship lines who had experience in both directions. The White Star line, which has the largest ships in the Atlantic service, have gone back from the ' Oceanic ' of 20 or 21 knots to the ' Republic ' of 16 or 17 knots, and they are building monster ships which are not intended to attain a very high speed. The Hamburg-American line, which was the first to produce a fast ship, have also retrograded and they have built four enormous boats which make a speed of 17 or 18 knots. The ' Kaiserin Augusta,' 25,000 tons and accommodation for 3,000 passengers, is an 18-knot boat, and the ' Amerika,' the ' President Grant ' and the 'President Lincoln' are of similar speed. Some of the White Star boats now run to Southampton instead of to Liverpool ; they have enormous capacity with moderate speed and large passenger accommodation fitted up with all the adjuncts to luxury which modern travel requires. I may say that the experience of this present year has to a large extent justified those who build large ships of great capacity and comparatively slow, because the reflux of passenger traffic in the immense number of continental Europeans who have gone from the United States back to their native land has, on the return voyages filled all the space that was previously occupied by light cargo, and great difficulty has been found even on those enor-

moils boats in providing accommodation for the middle class and steerage passengers. In the minds of a number of gentlemen in this House, and in the mind of the public generally, the ' Mauretania ' and the ' Lusitania ' have set up the standard of what a fast Atlantic ship should be. The British government furnished the Cunard Company with a large amount of money at a low rate of interest, and also gave them a large subsidy, so that they might obtain the prestige of having the fastest ships on the Atlantic, the German builders having wrested from the British builders the reputation for constructing the fastest, best appointed and most luxuriously fitted passenger i-jjiips. But it was not only sentiment that prompted the British people to the desire to have the fastest ships, nor was it altogether that these fast ships would be a powerful adjunct in war. There was the further inducement that the prestige of building the very fastest ships was of immense advantage to the British shipbuilders, whose trade was waning and who, in consequence of regaining their reputation, would have the advantage of securing orders from foreign owners who wanted vessels of that class. The competition was between the British and German builders as to the cost of production as well as to the turning out of the fastest and most economical ships. The ' Mauretania ' and the ' Lusitania ' are of great size, of great speed, of luxurious furnishing, hut they are very costly. Many who would otherwise advocate a fast Canadian line have been deterred from this advocacy through the belief that vessels equal to the ' Lusitania ' and the ' Mauretania ' would be necessary for the Canadian trade. It is a fallacy to suppose that we need vessels of that extremely costly type. The Cunard Company have, in addition to these steamers, vessels of less speed and power and cost, but of greater capacity for the carriage of freight. I believe the great lines usually run cargo boats in conjunction with their fast boats. The North German Lloyds has been spoken of. They were the pioneers in using very fast steamers. They have on the Atlantic to-day four steamers of 23 knots, which are fitted equal to the Cunard steamers, have all the modern appliances for comfort, and make the trip from Cherbourg to New York In six days. They are interchangeable with regard to berths and accommodation, the one with the other, which gives them an immense advantage. They have lately put on the New York route a steamer called the ' Kronprintzessin Cecile,' about 700 feet in length by about 70 feet broad. A ship with a little more horse-power, say 5,000, would make the passage from Halifax to a port on the western coast of England in four days, summer and winter, and there is no other port in America from which a service of that kind could Mr. WM. be maintained. Four steamers of that size and power would be sufficient to maintain such a service continuously summer and winter, because at Halifax they would not be delayed by the tides, but could proceed at any time to the ocean. Where speed is the prime factor, there is no route between Halifax and a southern port on the west coast of England. A remark made by the hon. leader of the opposition has been enlarged upon

that these boats could not carry perishable freight. I think that is the substance of the hon. gentleman's amendment.

BORDEN If the hon gentleman will pardon me. I was not speaking of ships of any particular kind. I was merely desiring to emphasize the point, which the hon. gentleman has already remarked upon, that there should be facilities for carrying freight.

I listened attentively to my hon friend the leader of the opposition. and although he did not expressly state it, the whole course of his remarks, and also of his amendment, tended to the position that this is a comparative question, not an absolute one, and therefore it would

be better to do something else than to do immediately what is proposed by the government. And one of the stated reasons was that the farmers might have the advantage of shipping their ordinary agricultural products, and also their perishable goods. Now, there is nothing to prevent cold storage accommodation being provided on these ships. If that were done, fancy products, such as fruit and other things, could be carried in these ships much better than by any line of freight steamers that could be subsidized or invented; because the great element would be speed. A great many products that could not be sent by an ordinary freight line, even with cold storage, could be sent by a fast line. Merchants and others passing over the line would see opportunities for increasing business, and the English market for our products would be very much extended, because they could be carried by this fast line to the best market in the world, which they have not hitherto been able to reach because of the want of rapid transit. With regard to the remark of the premier of New Zealand, that he stipulated that freight should be carried on the Pacific steamers, I am not going to speak in regard to the Pacific end of this project, as some of our friends from British Columbia are going to deal with that feature of the subject. I will merely say that if a fast line were maintained for so long a voyage as from Vancouver to Australia, it would be impossible for it to carry any great burden of freight. The amount of coal that would be necessary to maintain a vessel at a speed of 18 or 20 knots on the Pacific, would exclude any amount of heavy freight, and only a small space could be reserved for the more valuable and compact goods. Therefore for the future heavy freight would have to be carried by another kind of ship.
The hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) this afternoon expressed anxiety for our fellow citizens of the empire in South Africa. It is a good way out of the line of travel from Vancouver to Australia, but it shows his cosmopolitan regard for sentiment and his love for the old flag ; but I can assure him that the British public have well provided for the trade of South Africa and onwards from there to Australia ; they have steamers of very large size, with good passenger accommodation and that is a trade which they intend to build to its utmost capacity. There is in that country a very strong English sentiment, a sentiment to deal with the mother country. That has been well provided for and the lines well established. I think my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) and I can afford to leave our co-citizens of the empire in South Africa to the kindness of the people of England and to the care of those companies which are at present engaged in the South African trade.
It was hoped that the introduction of the turbine engine would solve a great many questions, but unfortunately the turbine engine is not more economical in the consumption of coal than the old style of engine. It is only on vessels of very high power that there is economy in the turbine and therefore the anticipation that the turbines would permit of longer voyages with the same supply of coal has not been fulfilled. Various comjDanles have been experimenting ; the German companies have adhered to the old reciprocating type, some of the British lines have adopted the turbine and the British government has been experimenting with oil fuel. But these experiments are not yet completed and it is not possible to state any results. Many interested people thought that the turbine engine would solve the problem of coal carrying capacity but as yet that has not been accomplished.
Great Britain has a great interest in this project. The leader of the opposition and the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) called that a sentimental interest. I cannot say where the bounds between sentiment and material interest lie, but it is surely true that the amount of advantage to' Great Britain will determine the amount which Great Britain will contribute to this joint project. It is not merely a question of distance but it is also a question of safety. Great Britain is looking constantly to securing fast merchant ships to supplement the navy, as was well remarked by my hon. friend from Brantford, and this line will afford useful ships for this purpose when required. It is also of great advantage to the British government to have a safe and rapid line of communication available in time of exigency, away from Europe, which would not be menaced by the navy of hostile powers. There is great rivalry as to which shall be the predominant naval power and the further the line of communication is carried away from Europe and the passage of the Suez canal, the safer are the British possessions in the east and the wide stretching British commerce to be found in every sea. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) and the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) have perhaps not looked up the statistics of the immense damage inflicted on British commerce in the short war of independence with the United States and the war with the United States in 1812, when American privateers pushed right up to the British channel and captured whole fleets ) of merchantmen owing to their speed. I recommend my friends to study these subjects at their leisure and give their views at some later stage because they tend to show the immense importance of this subject to the British empire, and also that a liberal participation in this plan is essential to the efficient government and holding of British

colonial possessions. We are not looking for war. The leader of the oppposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) said it was extremely necessary that the farmers should have cheap and rapid accommodation on ships equipped with cold storage and lower rates of freight for their products. The rates of freight from Canada to Great Britain to-day are extremely low on heavy goods. My friends will remember that there are hundreds of thousands of tons of shipping laid up in England at the present time because the vessels are not able to obtain remunerative rates of freights. This government also has subsidized lines of steamers to carry freight with some regularity to compete with freight carried on the great lines from the United States. The government has been liberal in providing for this service, and there has been no complaint, by the leader of the opposition or anybody else, on the ground of excessive freights from Canada to the old country. I would like to see our shipments to Great Britain increase, I would like to see every facility afforded to the farmers, I would like to see cold storages established at every point where it would be of advantage. But the government has not protected that particular interest. I would also like ito see the farmers of Ontario make more frequent passages to the old country and establish agencies under then' own control for the distribution of their products there so that they would reap the whole advantage from their sale. I had remarked that this project must be dealt with comparatively. Well, we know the cost of this somewhat definitely ; also there are limitations under which it will be necessary for Canada to assent to any proposals that are not fair or adequate. Only the other day, we passed a measure to extend a railway to Hudson bay, involving an expenditure of about a hundred millions. I did not hear any of these eloquent voices on the other side raised against that. We had the project of the Georgian bay canal involving a sum, we are told, of a hundred millions.
I did not hear about that.
Did not the hon. gentleman hear it stated that it would cost a hundred millions for the Georgian Bay canal ?
I did not hear the Minister of Railways say it was going through.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman was out. But I am only speaking in round numbers. I have understood that the Hudson Bay proposal would cost something like a hundred millions.
Oh, my no ! I did not hear that.
I heard no objection to the building of the Hudson Bay Railway.
I was in favour of it for my part.

Very well, then the hon. gentleman is committed to it whatever it may cost. And it was supposed to cost a large amount of money. And there was no opposition to that proposal. But here is a proposal within extremely small limitations. Formerly it was supposed to involve an expenditure of $500,000 to $700,000 annually. This proposal as stated by my hon. friend will not involve more than $1,000,000. This affects the interests of eastern Canada, it affects the interests of all the continent through which this line of communication passes ; it affects the interests of the people on the western ocean ; all are interested in this proposal, and nobody, up to the present time, has shown that any disadvantages are to accrue from it. When the expenditure is so limited, why should we have an amendment declaring that this is injudicious or inexpedient at the present time, especially when we have embarked upon proposals that will cost a large amount of money, and more especially when one of the routes to be provided, that by Hudson bay, is open it is said by some, for two months in the year, and by some for four. Here is a route that is opened the whole year round. It opens possibilities greater than any body has been able to prophesy. If we consider the possibilities of the development of Canada we shall give to a project which helps in the realization of those possibilities the hearty and unanimous assent of this House, backed by the enthusiasm of a growing and progressive people.

I do not intend to go into this subject in great detail, as we are trying to end this debate and close the session with as little delay as possible. Nor do I intend to go into the historical phase of the question of the fast Atlantic service. It is pretty well known to the people of Canada that during the past twelve or fifteen years, or perhaps more, this question has been fully discussed. I shall discuss the question from the standpoint of to-day, and consider it in the light of conditions as they exist. The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) says he is sorry that the government is not receiving the enthusiastic support in this measure which he would expect it to receive. Well, it did not occur to me, while the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) was addressing the House upon this project, that that right hon. gentleman was over-enthusiastic with regard to it himself. If ever I saw the Prime Minister handle a question with a pair of tongs I saw him do so to-day. The

hon. member for Brandon, I notice, differed -with the Prime Minister with respect to the speed of these vessels upon the Atlantic. If I understood the Prime Minister correctly, that right hon. gentleman advocated a 20-kuot service. But the hon. member for Brandon still insists that this service should be by vessels of 24 knots an hour. This is a difference of opinion between the Prime Minister and member for Brandon with regard to one of the most important things in this scheme. It seems to me also that the hon. member (Mr. Sif-ton) has not been able to convert certain other members of the cabinet. The leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) read an extract from a speech made on this subject by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher). And I have every reason to believe that the Minister of Agriculture entertains the same view with regard to this service as he did when he made that speech. So, the hon. member for Brandon need not complain about the attitude of the opposition when he lias not been able to win even members of the cabinet to his own view upon this project which lies so near his heart. I said that I did not.intend to go into the historical aspect of this question. But it is necessary that I should refer briefly to the fact that the sum of $750,000 was voted, I believe, by the former administration to aid this fast Atlantic service. At that time, the service on the Atlantic was very poor. The time occupied between Liverpool and Canada was about double the time taken by the steamers of to-day. During these years, private enterprise, with the improvement of conditions, has given us pretty nearly what was laid out in the terms and conditions of the contract it was then desired to enter into. But, more than that, I would point out that this government, as stated by the hon. member for Brandon, is paying out pretty nearly the amount which the former administration proposed to provide for the fast Atlantic service. According to the figures given by the hon. gentleman, this government is paying $680,000 per annum to carry the mails, and, I suppose, subsidize the steamship service upon the Atlantic, which is pretty nearly as much as the amount voted under the former administration. I am glad that through the enterprise of two corporations, we have to-day an efficient service on the Atlantic without the expenditure of an enormous sum. That could hardly have been expected at the time the contract I referred to, as made by a former adminis-tation. was voted upon in this House.
This question we are discussing not only embodies a fast Atlantic service on the Atlantic, which is the most important from our standpoint, but it also embodies the putting of faster trains on the railways crossing the continent-that would apply
to the Canadian Pacific Railway-and a better steamship service on the Pacific ocean between Vancouver, New Zealand and Australia. We have to look at this matter entirely from the standpoint of carrying mails and passengers, and cannot expect that vessels, such as we intend to put on the Atlantic, which have a speed of 24 knots an hour, will be of the slightest advantage to the people as far as freights are concerned.
I shall not take up the time of this House referring at any length to the sentimental aspect of the question. I wish to endorse the words uttered by Premier Deakin, of Australia, and telegraphed to 'this country via London by the Associated Press a day or two ago :
London, July 7.-A despatch from Melbourne says that Premier Deakin, commenting on Sir Wilfrid Laurier's request for Australia's cooperation as to the All-Red route, says the Commonwealth must have a definite financial proposal before he can advise action. The whole question had now narrowed down to cost, as the sentimental benefits were admitted long ago.
That is the position I take. The sentimental benefits which would arise from the bringing closer together the various parts of the empire are admitted. And while I am prepared to criticise the resolution submitted to this House, I do not want to be considered any the less a loyal subject of the empire ; I do not think I will he, and, in fact, I do not care whether I am so considered or not. So far as the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) is concerned, what he proposes is a different scheme from what the Prime Minister brings down. The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) thinks that $1,000,000 is a very small thing with which to charge the country for all time to come. Well, considering all the heavy expenditure to which the government has committed us, in view of the excellent service we have on the Atlantic at preseut, I think this proposed extra expenditure of $1,000,000 per year is a very serious one. Capitalize that amount of interest at 3j) per cent and you have a capital expenditure of $30,000,000, besides the subsidy we are now paying of $680,000 per year. If this government is going into a project which will involve the borrowing of $30,000,000, I think the project is one not to be at all likely lightly considered.
The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) referred to the great development in Germany, which he attributed to their enterprise in subsidizing fast steamships. My own view is that the great development of Germany is not due to her fast Atlantic steamships, although that service may have been a factor to some small extent. But the fact is that some years ago, when the craze was on, each country was competing with the other as to which should have the

fastest Atlantic service. Tlie 1 Lucania ' and the ' Campania ' were built by the Cunarcl line and were the fastest steamers afloat. Then the Germans came on with faster steamers. A few years ago the great financier, Mr. Plerpout Morgan, appeared on the scene and attempted to consolidate certain British and American lines. That caused a sort of spasm in Great Britain, and for fear that the competition created by this great amalgamation would drive British passenger vessels of the fastest type fi-om the Atlantic, and under the influence of that alarm, the British government subsidized two steamers bu'ilt by the Cunard line, the ' Mauretania ' and ' Lusitania,' hut that these vessels have been an unqualified success is questioned. While we have the ' Campania ' and ' Lucania ' on the Atlantic it has been demonstrated that a great many people prefer to travel by slower vessels. From what I have been able to learn, this fast Atlantic travel is more of a fad than anything else. Where two vessels, such as the 'Mauretania' and 'Lusitania,' have been built, there have been twenty-five or thirty others built, more commodious and comfortable vessels, which run seventeen or eighteen knots an hour, and these have taken the business. The Cunard line, many years after they had the ' Campania ' and ' Lucania ' on the Atlantic, built two steamers, the ' Caronia ' and ' Carmania,' which are always crowded with passengers. To suppose that every one who travels on the Atlantic wants to save half a day or a day is simply a fad. W hile some may think the saving of a day of great importance, a great number of the traveling public do not. I have said what the Cunard line have done ; other lines have done the same. The Ham-burg-American owns the ' Deutschland,' built for the New York to Liverpool business. She has been put on the New York and Mediterranian service during the winter time. Then the company have built and worked successfully vessels of great capacity which make slower time, such as the ' President Lincoln,' ' President Grant ' and 'Amerika.' Probably the ' Amerlka ' is the most popular, and of the White Star line the ' Cedric ' and ' Baltic ' and ' Arabic ' are among the most popular. Other companies have not pinned their faith to the extreme type of fast Atlantic vessels. Comfort and security count for something with certain people who travel on the Atlantic.
My right hon. friend the First Minister figured out that a 20-knot service would make the trip in five days across the Atlantic. Well, steamships plying to Great Britain at present take five and a-half days from Liverpool to Rimousk'i and six to Montreal. Are we going to pay this extra $1,000,000 for the purpose of saving half a day or a day? In my opinion, the scheme is not practicable. There is no demand for It. The time is not opportune for consider-Mr. KEMP.
ing it. Twelve years ago the conditions were entirely different. Since then we have been able to secure, on a commercial basis, a service, furnished voluntarily by people well posted in the trade, which is certainly as good as the desired service in many respects.
The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sif-ton) said it would take time, after passing the resolution, to bring all the parties together and decide on a joint agreement, and that it would be five years before we can have the ships on the ocean. I believe that in three years, or in four years at any rate, we will have a 20-knot service on the Atlantic. We have at the present time an all-red route, so called. 1 will not quarrel with the premier or any one else who wishes to have the credit of having invented that name. It is a matter of very little importance to me what you call it, but we have an all-red line from Great Britain to Canada and from Canada to Australia and New Zealand. Only to-day I saw a gentleman who had recently come from Australia on the steamers which are plying on the Pacific which service is being improved. He came across in a ship of 7,000 tons, he had a pleasant voyage and the passengers were well satisfied with the treatment they received and the accommodation they had on that vessel. I endorse what has been said by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) regarding the importance of freight traffic. If we have this amount of money to spend and if we feel that we ought to spend it in this way we would be doing something which would be of far greater service to this country if we did something in the direction of obtaining better freight rates for the products of Canada and of extending the cold storage facilities in a way that will make them of greater benefit to producers than they are at the present time. I do not want to be stampeded into endorsing the vague plan suggested by this resolution. I do not understand how the premier expected this resolution to go through the House unanimously. The time has come when we should stop this sort of thing. The time has come when we should get estimates accompanied by a little more information with respect to matters of this kind. The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) states that some steps ought to be taken but I would like to ask that hon. gentleman as I would like to ask the premier what steps have been taken by the government of Great Britain, New Zealand and Australia. I do not know why we should be expected to take the initiative any more than these other governments. I think that the advantage it would be to save a day or possibly only half a day in the voyage across the ocean has been very much over-estimated. Viewing it from the standpoint that these vessels will be entirely

for the purpose of carrying passengers, that a very small portion of the people travel by the Atlantic or travel at all, and that a great many people prefer such vessels as are on the Atlantic at the present time,
I think we should encourage the people who have had the enterprise to do what has been done upon the Atlantic, who have given such a splendid service, rather than create competition by government aid which would discourage men from going on in the future and continuing the splendid work which they have done in the past. I believe that if we are ,iust a little cautious in regard to this matter, a little more sensible, we will have, in the next five years, upon the Atlantic, a far better service than we will have by the voting of $1,000,000, as is proposed by the hon. member for Brandon. Therefore. I will have great pleasure in supporting the amendment of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance).
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if there be some possible differenceof opinion on this side of the House on details of this question, as suggested, it is quite evident that there must be larger and greater differences of opinion among hon. gentlemen opposite. I take it that the speech of the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) was made in support of this fast line scheme, possibly with some modification of the words, the changing of the phraseology here and there, the dotting of the i's or the crossing of the t's, but the hon. gentleman who has just spoken (Mr. Kemp) has given us his reasons for voting against the whole scheme. Therefore, we must assume, if he is going to vote with the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) on this question, that they have a common ground and that they are really placing themselves in opposition to this whole scheme. If that is not the meaning of the proposition of my. hon. friends opposite I must confess that 4 am unable to see what their purpose is by the amendment which they have presented to the House, because a certain portion of the amendment distinctly declares that you must do nothing immediately. You must not commit yourself to anything, you must come back and tell the House what you have in your mind before you agree to anything. Let us suppose that delegates from this government go to meet the government of New Zealand or of Australia and that they do as my hon. friend the leader of the opposition suggests; they would go there with instructions that they could agree to nothing, commit the government to nothing, bind Canada to nothing, and that would mean the absolute obstruction of this whole scheme. If the whole scheme is a dream and a bad one that position is justifiable, but I do not think that my hon. friends would like to take that position, and certainly that was not the line 396
of action taken by hon. gentlemen opposite
Was it the intention of the resolution as proposed that the country should be committed to a definite plan and to an expenditure without coming back to parliament ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, what was intended to he accomplished was that this House should first declare its approval of the principle of the fast line service forming part of the All-Red line between England and Australia and New Zealand. My hon. friends opposite say that there is a difference of opinion on this side as to whether that should be a 24 knot or a 20 knot service. I do not see any difficulty on that score. Every one of us, I am sure, would be glad to get a 24-knot service if we could get it at a price which would he reasonably within our ability to pay, but if we cannot get a 24-knot service without paying a price that would seem to us to be excessive then I suppose we would all be very pleased to have, at a moderate price, a substantial improvement upon the service that we already have. Whether you have a 20-knot service, a 21. a 23, or a 24-knot service is a matter of detail and a question of price.
I do not see why there should be this division of opinion in the House to-day. My hon friend from Brantford expressed the view very strongly that we should be unanimous, that there should be no difference whatever. He wishes to be counted among the enthusiastic advocates of this All-Red scheme. I share his feeling that there is no good reason for a difference of opinion. If the principle generally that it is desirable to have a faster service on the Atlantic and . a faster service on the Pacific is a principle which we all recognize to be a good one, then I see no reason for the amendment of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition.
We are told that this is not a new question. Very true; and if it is not a new question, if it be one that the House has considered again and again, there can be no reason for complaining that there is not ample time to consider it. If we had brought forward something that was entirely new there might be just cause for complaint on that score. This is not a case in which we are called upon to deal with details. Why should my hon. friend the leaden of the opposition think it necessary or expedient to import into this discussion and into an amendment the question of cold storage or freight rates ? These are important questions, truly, but they are not necessarily part of the present side of the discussion; certainly, they are not necessary in the form of an amendment to a resolution which does not profess to deal with details but in which we are content to ask parliament to assert the general principle of the approval of this policy. So, I think
EDITION	|

my hon. friend has made a mistake, from our point of view, in insisting that this matter shall be dealt with now as one of detail. As far as the question of a freight service is concerned no one disputes for a moment that the transportation question, in relation to the products of the country, is more important than the question of a passenger service. My hon. friend's amendment would imply that no attention had been given to the question of the freight business of the country. On the contrary, everybody knows that this government has liberally supported the establishment of lines for the development of the freight business of the country. A number of steamship lines are to-day engaged in that very line of business under grants in aid given by this government with the approval of parliament.
The question of freight has been considered, the question of freight will continue to be considered and therefore it is not necessary to assume, when we ask that the principle of a fast line should be affirmed, that we are ignoring or neglecting or not considering the development of the freight business of the country. There has been great progress made on Canadian railways in the separation of passenger and freight traffic and we can see similar development in our ocean carrying trade. It is not many years since the very best railways in the country ran mixed trains where you would have a passenger car and a cattle car following the same engine, but to-day the cattle car is to be found on a cattle train, the lumber and the coarser freight is carried on a train specially intended for that pur. pose, and the passenger train is operated as a passenger train absolutely distinct from the freight business. A further development is that on many trains there are only first-class cars, and although we have not yet come to it to any extent in Canada it is a quite common thing in the United States to see passenger trains made up entirely of pullmans. I have seen a cattle steamer leaving the port of Halifax which carried His Excellency the Governor General of the day.
Nothing wrong in that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Nothing wrong at all except to point to the fact that the passenger steamer of to-day does not as a rule carry cattle. It was the only ship His Excellency could avail of in these days, and like a sensible man he took it and no doubt he .would do so to-day under similar conditions. But the point I am making is that owing to the development in the steamship service these conditions do not now exist. The passenger business is being separated from the coarser freight business, and even in what might be called moderately fast steamers comparatively small quantities of freight are carried. I remember crossing I Mr. FIELDING.
on the ' Campania ' which was then the crack boat of the Cunard fleet, and the commander told me he did not want more than 1,500 tons of freight, because anything more interfered with his coal capacity for attaining high speed, and the comfort of his passengers. And so on these fast ships will not carry low grade freight at all, although of course cold storage accommodation will be necessary because that is a specialized freight which can stand a higher rate. It is possible to combine cold storage freight with a fast steamship service, but it is not possible to combine with a fast service the carriage of low grade and bulky commodities. There is a tendency to-day. as we know, for many passengers to take what might be called moderately fast steamers.
Large ships.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. There is no doubt that a great many transatlantic passengers prefer boats like the ' Baltic,' the ' Car-mania,' and the ' Caronia, which are of moderate speed and which while carrying passengers with a high degree of comfort also carry a considerable quantity of freight. But the steamship line which will have its ' Car-mania,' ' Caronia ' and ' Baltic ' will have also other very fast boats and without which the line could hardly keep up its reputation. My hon. friend from Brandon (Mr. Sifton) said that these very fast boats act as an advertisement, and from that point of view it is desirable that we should have them on the Canadian service. A nation, no less than an individual engaged in business, must attend to its advertising, and if we have steamers of not less than 20 knots, or possibly of 22 knots or 23 or 24 knots if we can get them, I feel satisfied that by bringing through Canada a large stream of first-class passengers who now go to New York, it will have the effect of advertising Canada amongst the people whom we desire should know the vast resources of our country. My hon. friends who are in business advertise in newspapers and speqd their money freely, but they seldom can associate a given customer with a given advertisement although they do know that business comes and that if they cease to advertise business will also cease. I believe that even from the point of view of the advertisement it would be well for Canada to have a few of these moderately fast steamers, as fast as we can get. I feel interested in the matter naturally from the point of view of the lower provinces. I sympathize most heartily with my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Roche) in his remarks about the great advantages of the port of Halifax.
I have always felt that in all probability, if some day we are to have one port all the year, that port would be Halifax. I have felt that if in the meantime we are to have a winter port probably Halifax would be found the most advantageous, and that the

summer port would undoubtedly have to be Quebec if tbe ships are of too great draft to permit of them going to Montreal. But while I warmly advocate the claims of Halifax I recognize frankly that this is a question which we must leave to be considered from a broad national point of view. I would be perfectly content, speaking for myself, that if a company should be found to take up this enterprise they should settle for themselves on commercial lines the point of departure in Europe and the point at which their steamers should arrive in Canada. If as a result these steamers should come to my own home in Halifax, well and good, but if. because of the application of sound commercial principles to the enterprise, the ships, will go to some other port, then we shall have to be content.
I shall not detain the House further, but naturally feeling a great deal of interest in the question. I thought I might say a few words. I believe that the time is not ripe for this parliament to deal with it as a question of detail, and that all that remains for us to do at the present time is to reaffirm the resolution of the imperial conference. I am sorry my hon. friend the leader of the opposition feels it necessary to introduce that amendment. It seems to me to be unnecessary and I would hope that he could see his way to withdraw it.
As to the financial side of the question, I regret that hon. gentlemen opposite have taken such a pessimistic view. Either they want this service or they do not, and if they do want it is is a pity they should seek to alarm financiers by the story that this is a gross extravagance and that Canada cannot afford it. Canada undoubtedly has many obligations; we have great works in hand, and we have other great works which have claims upon hs. This is a time toi Canada to exercise all due caution, but it is not a time for timidity. It is a time for Canada to have faith in herself, and while we should hesitate to spend any money wastefully on services which are not calculated to advance tlie best interests of the country, let us say to ourselves and to the people abroad : we have faith in Canada, we believe she is going to pass quickly through this little temporary depression which is less here than in any other part of the civilized world ; we believe that Canada is able to undertake the various responsibilities which her condition calls for.
and tnat the credit of Canada in the future will be upheld as it has been in the past.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. W. DANIEL (St. John, N.B.).
speechtext:
It is gratifying to be able in this parliament to speak to a question which cannot m anv sense of the term be called a party question. We have already heard of the inception of what is called the All-Red route, which was conceived and tried to be started many years ago ; and we all know that even at the present time we have
39Gi
an all-red route from England to Australia and Hong Kong through this country.
I listened very carefully to-day to the speech of the right hon. the Prime Minister I have also read very carefully the resolution which he proposed at the imperial conference and the remarks which he made in support of that resolution. As it gives in a short space and rather definitely the scheme which he urged, I will read it:
That in the opinion of this conference the interests of the empire demand that in so tar as possible its different portions should be connected by the best possible means of mail communication, travel and transportation; that to this end steps should immediately be taken to establish a fast service from Great Britain to Canada, and through Canada to Australia and New Zealand, and also to China, and Japan; that such service on the Atlantic, ocean should be carried on by means of steamships, equal in speed and character to the-best now in existence, and upon the Pacific.-ocean by steamships of a speed of not less-than 18 'knots, and in other respects as nearly equal to the Atlantic ships as circumstances-will permit; that for the purpose of carrying, the above project into effect, such financial support as may be necessary should he contributed by Great Britain, Canada, Australia and New Zealand in equitable proportions.
This resolution, which, with slight modifications, was endorsed and carried by that imperial conference, was not for a service of twenty or twenty-one knots across the Atlantic. It was for a service equal to the best on the Atlantic at the present time. Therefore, 1 was very much puzzled when I heard the right hon. the Prime Minister in introducing these resolutions to-day, speak, not of a twenty-four or twenty-five knot service across the Atlantic, but of a twenty or twenty-one knot service, and I asked myself why we should go through all this formality for a twenty or a twenty-one knot service ? Already we have an eighteen knot service on the Atlantic, and in a very few years we shall probably have a twenty knot service at the hands of the same companies who now give us an eighteen knot service, and at very little if any extra cost to this country. So that it appears to me that if we are looking forward to a twenty knot service on the Atlantic ocean, the members of that imperial conference who endorsed the resolution introduced by our Prime Minister, when they come to read the statement of the Prime Minister in this House to-day that he is only seeking to promote a twenty knot service across the Atlantic, must come to the conclusion that we as a parliament are not keeping faith with the other members of that conference, who voted not for a twenty knot service, but for a twenty-four knot service across the Atlantic ocean. The eighteen knot service applied wholly to the Pacific ocean. Therefore it seems

to me that the Prime Minister has put us rather in a quandary.
Speaking personally, I am quite in accord with the resolution which was passed at the imperial conference, and which is brought before us to-day ; and, for the reasons which have already been given, we can only tell by experiment whether such a service on the Atlantic would be justified or not. We all know that such a service cannot be commercially successful. It is not commercially successful at the present time, even with the steamships running to the port of New York and having the SO,-000,000 people of the United States to draw upon. But if we are going to carry out the resolution of the imperial conference, we have to put on the Atlantic ocean a service equal to the best at present plying on that ocean anywhere. That means a twenty-four knot service, or all our work will be of no effect, and we cannot be considered as carrying out in good faith the undertaking of our representative. Then comes the question of freight. We all know that so far as this country is concerned, the freight business is more important than the' passenger business ; and I may say in passing that the greatest usefulness of speed in crossing the Atlantic is neither for freight nor passengers, but for the mails, and there is no doubt that it is of very great advantage to have a quick mail service. Except with regard to certain classes of freight, like express freight and perishable goods, the matter of speed need not be taken into consideration in connection with freight ; it is not a matter of importance. I am speaking, of course, in a comparative sense ; therefore when we speak of bringing into force a twenty-four knot service, we cannot consider freight at all, but onlv mails and passengers. I would like to call the attention of the House to a remark made by the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sif-tonj when referring to this matter. He says that we already pay about $600,000. and we have our service on the Atlantic and on the Pacific, and that to pay $1,000,000 or a little more for a twenty-four knot service imply llleau tlle addition of say $400,000 a year. Mr. Speaker, I do not think there can be two opinions in the province of British Columbia, where we have seen some fairly rapid strides made in navigation, as to the advantage of this project to the western part of Canada and our own Pacific province. We have to-day operating from British Columbia ports to Australia, New Zealand, Yokohama and- Hong Ivong a number of lines, and the question of a much better Pacific service is one of great importance. The line of demarcation between the speeches of hon. gentlemen on this side and hon. gentlemen opposite on this question is well drawn. The resolution of the Prime Minister means action immediately upon a question which is of

importance to all parts of Canada, while our hon. friends opposite say to wait, or if not to wait, that a cold storage route is the proper route. The difference between the two propositions is that one is all red, which means fast, and the other is an ice cream route, which means anything going slow. Our hon. friends opposite are prepared to accept the cold storage route, but that is not the route which is wanted at present in Canada. From British Columbia we ship all kinds of produce to Australian and Asiatic ports, but we carry very few passengers indeed. 1 believe that Canada is shipping from her ports less than 6 per cent of the passengers carried from North America to European ports and to Australian and Asiatic ports. At present we have the Union Steamship Company from Vancouver and Victoria to Sydney and we have the Australian servi.ce from Vancouver and Victoria to Auckland, both very poor services, with the result that very few people travel by that line. Last summer X saw with my own eyes many people who were not able to secure transportation on the boats leaving Vancouver for Australia; they had either to go via San Francisco or wait for another boat. I talk with people arriving from Australia by every boat and ask them about the Union Steamship Company, the present line between Australia and British Columbia, and they are all of one mind in saying that it is as poor a service as is operated on salt water to-day. In face of the fact that it is a very poor service the boats are usually full, both first-class and second-class, and they are carrying a considerable line of freight. I trust that the All-Red route will consist also of a line of steamers from British Columbia ports to Yokohama, Nagasaki, Manilla or wherever it may be on the Asiatic side. We have at present the Canadian Pacific Railway ' Empress ' line, which has done very good work indeed. There is also the Pacific Mail Steamship line. There never was a time in the history of any country in matters of transportation when it was so urgent that a first-class line of steamers should be established. We should have them from Canada to all ports on the Pacific coast. There is not a good up-to-date line of steamers operating there to-day. The Canadian Pacific Railway have beautiful boats, but they are not doing the trade there they should do. They should have much larger and faster boats, and any Canadian Pacific Rail way official operating out of Vancouver will say as I do, that we cannot afford to wait, as the member for East Toronto suggested, if we are to hold our supremacy on the sea. Now is the time to act, and now is the time for this resolution to be carried into effect. What does the resolution of the leader of the opposition mean? That nothing can be done, not even a telegram
can be sent, not an emissary can be sent to Australia, New Zealand or Great Britain to work up this All-Red route plan until parliament sanctions it.
Now, we are sanctioning the principle of it, and I trust we shall go so far as to not only sanction the principle-for that principle is accepted and admitted by all-but shall take practical steps which, in a short time, will result in a better service on the Pacific; concerning the Atlantic I do not speak. What does it mean, this carrying of passengers from British ports to Canada, across Canada and from our Pacific ports to Australia and New Zealand? It means that thousands of people will come into our country and will have the opportunity of seeing for themselves the possibilities of our country. It means that these people coming into our country will spend thousands and millions of dollars. There is no better trade in the world than the tourist trade of the world. We have demonstrated that conclusively in Vancouver, where our tourist trade has been the means of very considerable advancement for our city. So, I say, we cannot afford to take the position laid down by the leader of the opposition when he says: You should not consider this question until you have further data
