I would not have spoken on this subject at all considering the stage of the session, had it not been for one remark made by the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) which has been so conspicuously accentuated and illustrated by the hon. gentleman (Mr. McPherson) who has just taken his seat. In voting on this motion and amendment, I occupy this position: I have the honour to represent a constituency which, I venture to say, is as strongly imperialistic in its opinions and ideas as any constituency in the Dominion of Canada; I feel very strongly that, no matter what else I may do in this House, if in any way by any action or vote of mine I should show want of confidence that this union would continue, or any unwillingness on my part to do all in my power to continue to' perpetuate and strengthen this union, it would be utterly futile for me to appear again before my constituents. Therefore, it is that, when such a motion is before the House, and when such an amendment is moved by the leader of the opposition, and when the hon. member for Brandon, who has been supposed throughout the country to be the father of this scheme -though it appears most unjustly supposed, because, as shown by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) the scheme is older than its reputed father, but at any rate he must be admitted to be a father-inlaw of the scheme-when that hon. gentleman was careful to define the position occupied by the government on this scheme,

I think it necessary to give the reason why I cannot vote for the motion and why I am compelled to support the amendment.
In my humble judgment, the whole question is in a nutshell. Both sides of this House are in thorough accord as to the propriety, the necessity and duty of doing everything we can to bind the empire together. One side of the House say it is to be done in one way and the other side says another way. I believe the government is entirely wrong. I shall give my vote simply on the ground that hon. gentlemen opposite are entirely mistaken in their choice of the way to bind the empire together and that the mode they have adopted is exactly the one which an enemy of the empire, one desiring to see it dismembered, would prefer.
The resolution submitted by the leader of the government is ambiguous. It may be read one way or the other. But the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) has kindly instructed this House as to the true meaning of that motion, and it is solely on the speech of that hon. gentleman that I feel compelled to vote against the original resolution. Discussing the various advan tages which the proposed line would give the empire, the hon. gentleman was good enough to tell us that the freight and. cold storage service was a mere matter of detail to be looked after later on. To my mind the freight and storage service is the crucial point of the whole case, and there is nothing more to be said in favour of the resolution after this expression of opinion from the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton).
If we are to spend one and a half million dollars, we should get something in return, and when the hon. member for Brandon says that freight and cold storage are simply matters of detail, we must conclude that the expenditure of SI,500,000 a year is for a fast passenger service.
My hon. friend the leader of the opposition, on the other hand, says that whatever we are to give should have for its primary object the best means of bringing the products of the empire to the markets of the empire. Incidentally the passenger question must of course arise, and in the ships which primarily are to bring our products to the markets of the empire, we will do the best we can for the passengers. But the hon. member for Brandon ignores freight and cold storage altogether as,the primary object of the resolution. The $1,500,000 per year is to secure a fast passenger service. Incidentally he will do the best he can to secure freight; and if the rosiest dreams of the hon. friend should be realized, we will be able to carry 1,000 tons of freight on each of these mammoth steamers. Canada at the present time, with all the obligations she has to bear, is to be asked to pay $1,500,000 per year for. its fast steamship service for passenger traffic. Well as an imperialist, I am not going to pay that
for a passenger service. I am prepared to do whatever is necessary to bring the empire closer together by facilitating a better interchange of products, but I am not going to pay that amount simply for a faster passenger service.
My hon. friend from Brandon pointed out that we are at present paying $679,000 a year for the service we have. I presume the greater part is paid under the guise of postal subsidies, and therefore, he. says, all we are asked to pay is $1,000,000 additional per year. But if we are to subtract the $679,000 on the one hand, we must subtract whatever advantage and service we are getting for that on the other hand, because it is not to be presumed that we are paying that $679,000 per year for nothing.
I have always understood that the mail subsidies were practically subsidies to enable the steamship lines to give us a last service which they could not do without such, assistance. No one will pretend that we are paying all this money merely toi the carriage of our mail bags. If we are, we are paying a great deal too much and are being robbed. What we are paying for is not merely the carriage of the mails but indirectly to subsidize these steamship lines which have improved so much in the last ten or fifteen years. If we were to stop the payment of that $679,000 a year, does any one suppose we would have the same efficient steamship service ? It is not to be supposed that we are going to withdraw our present subsidies from those lines which have done so much to promote trade between this country and the motherland. We are asked now by the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton)-and that is his interpretation of the resolution submitted to the House-to pay annually $1,500,000 to some company, without knowing to what company or of whom, it will be composed or what service it will give. All we know is that $1,500,000 per year we shall pay tor passenger service, and incidentally a little freight, and the maximum freight which the hon. member for Brandon can suggest is 1,000 tons to each ship.
Then what kind of a steam service are we to have? The First Minister and the hon. member for Brandon are contradictory in their views. The one says that 20 knots per hour will do, but the other insists on 25 knots per hour; and should we vote this resolution, we will not know whether this annual subsidy of $1,500,000 is to be for a 20-knot or a 25-knot service. If a 20-knot service, that will not smt my hon. friend from Brandon. If a 25-knot service, that is beyond anything the First Minister dreams of. When these gentlemen differ so much, we are justified in asking that the government should decide what it wants and adjust its domestic differences before asking the House to vote. But suppose the scheme should be estab-

lished and suppose we are given the best steamships that can be got, running* at 25 knots an hour across the Atlantic and Pacific, what do we get in return for our $1,500,000 annual subsidy? How many Canadians are going to travel on these fast steamers? Is it not a fact that the faster the steamer the higher the rates? The majority of the people who will pay the particularly high rates will come from the neighbouring republic; and the practical result will be that we will be paying $1,500,000 a year in order that our neighbours to the south may have an opportunity of travelling through the beautiful route down the St. Lawrence to reach the old country by a class of steamers which the people of Canada cannot afford to patronize. In my constituency, you will get very few men who can afford to travel on these expensive boats. I find there are very few of my constituents who will ever be able to send any of their products to the old country by these boats which are limited, as a maximum, to 1,000 tons a trip. Therefore, as representing one constituency, I feel that I am bound to ask what the people of that constituency are going to get in consideration of this grant of a million and a half to which every one who is the head of a family must contribute his share. I am as anxious as any one to support anything that will tend to bind the empire together, but I want some common sense basis for an expenditure of $1,500,000. If any man is an enemy to the maintenance of the empire, if any man wishes to see this empire dismembered, if any man wishes to create a feeling throughout this Dominion of Canada, into which people are pouring from all corners of the earth, that will cause Canadians, including this conglomerate population, to become dissatisfied with the present conditions, he will bring resolutions before this House that will compel the people to pay large sums of money for considerations the value of which we do not know.
The resolution says that it shall be a fair sum.

1. LOGAN (Cumberland). Mr. Speaker. It is a matter of regret that the resolution now before the House and which was moved by the right hon. the hirst Minister; a resolution of extreme importance to all Canada, should meet with the opposition of our friends on the other side of the House. The 'All-Red route' so called, important though it is to every part of the British empire is surely of special importance to our Dominion. Were I an Australian I do not know that I would be so enthusiastic over a proposal to give a large subvention for this steamship service, but as a Canadian living in Canada which is so to speak the half-way house of the empire, I feel that interests vital to our country are wrapt up in the successful accomplishment of the policy enunciated by the right hon. gentleman. It is a matter of common knowledge and I may add a matter of general disappointment to Canadians that travellers to the American continent from the motherland do not patronize to any great extent the existing Canadian seamship lines.
I venture to say that not three per cent of all the travelling Englishmen, Irishmen, and Scotchmen who come to Canada enter the Dominion by a Canadian port. They reach us by the gateway of New York ; thev first see a great city; their eyes first rest on a foreign land teeming with millions of people, and finally they get to Canada by a side door. It is a good deal like viewing a small chapel when one has seen the vast cathedral of St. Peters at Rome. One reason therefore why I support this project so cordially is, that it will be an advertisement for Canada and that it may exert an educative influence upon the people of the old land to-

help them to a correct understanding of the actual conditions of our country, and in some degree to a knowledge of our people and our aspirations as British subjects. Ask nine Englishmen out of ten if the Halifax route or the St. Lawrence route is as safe as the New York route, and their answers will be that our ports are set in dense fog banks, that the ice coming down from the Arctic fields constitutes a danger to navigation. and that the River St. Lawrence is full of hazards. And yet, the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) proved conclusively by the facts which he gave us in the budget debate that the Canadian route is far safer than any other and that so far as absence of danger to navigation is concerned it is incomparatively the best.
We have not had a single accident on the St. Lawrence route for three years.

As my hon. friend remarks there has not been an accident on the St. Lawrence route for three years and the same remark is true of the Halifas route. Speaking on a former occasion in this House, I cited as an illustration of the inexcusable ignorance of people on the other side of the Atlantic with regard to Canadian ports, that a merchant in this city who had ordered goods in England to be sent to him by the Canadian Pacific Railway steamers for his Christmas trade, received word from the British manufacturers that they were sending the goods via New York as the Canadian ports were all frozen up. 1 regret that this is not an isolated instance and that it merely expresses the general opinion to be found on the other side. Such has been my experience when travelling in England and such has been the experience of others. The people of the old land seem to think that while we have a magnificent country in the summer, and while we have great seaports in Halifax, St. John. Montreal and elsewhere, yet in winter these ports are frozen and inaccessible from the ocean. Hence it is that had we this ' All-Red ' route with great vessels plying on the Atlantic subsidized by the imperial government, by the Canadian government, and by the Australian and New Zealand governments, it would be the best advertisement in the world that Canada is not a land of ice and snow, and that even in winter there are Canadian ports to which these magnificent steamers can ply successfully. I quite appreciate, Mr. Speaker, that this late hour of the session is not a time for long speeches, and so I shall be brief. I have already expressed my regret that the members of the great Conservative party in this House did not rise to the occasion, and pledge to the government the assurance of their support in the carrying out of this imperial project. It will be difficult enough to secure the All-Red route and to get subventions from the different governments even if
we had unanimity here, but how much more difficult will it be to bring the scheme to successful fruition when it is proclaimed to the other governments of the great colonies that His Majesty's opposition in Canada have moved in opposition to this scheme. I am honoured Sir, to be the successor in the representation of Cumberland, of Sir Charles Tupper, one of Canada's greatest sons, and the thought occurs to me to-night that were Sir Charles Tupper at this moment leading the opposition, the .attitude of his followers on this great imperial question would be far different from what it is. When the present government came to power in 1896, Sir Charles Tupper wrote to Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Prime Minister, that, if he as Prime Minister of Canada would strive for the fast Atlantic service which had been initiated by the Conservative government then he might count on cordial assistance from the Conservative party. In 1897, when this government completed a contract for a fast steamship service with Peterson, Tate & Co., the first man who spoke from the opposition benches was Sir Charles Tupper, and although he expressed himself .as not agreeing wiith the contract in all its, details he declared that he did not want to have it understood for a moment that he was opposing this scheme which he had so much at heart.
He should have waited for three years and then presented his congratulations.

Sir Charles Tupper was too big a man and too patriotic a Canadian not to congratulate his political opponents when he thought they deserved congratulation and hence he did not wait for three years. Sir Charles Tupper had his heart and soul in this project of a fast Atlantic service and when he introduced his scheme to the parliament of Canada there was no question raised as to his presenting it in all its detail. I read in the debates of 1896, some interesting remarks made by my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster). Let me hark back to his words of that slate to contrast them with his words of this afternoon. He was criticising Mr. Dobell, then a minister of the Crown, in connection with this very subject, and the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) said :
He is opposed to the fast line because it is costly and it cannot be given to the government cheap. Yet the hon. gentleman himself and thousands of Canadians almost every year go down to New York and take the best berths in the fast steamers from that port to Liverpool, and they do not get them cheap.
I would commend these words to my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) in the light of his statement this afternoon that Canadians travel by the existing Canadian routes. The statement was made this afternoon, and it has not been contradicted, that only 6 per cent of the travel between Liverpool and Canada

is on Canadian ships. Is not that a lamentable state of affairs? My hon. friend the member for North Toronto, contending that they knew a good thing and wanted it and were prepared to pay for it, said :
They know a good thing, they want it, and they are prepared to pay for it. Would they not be willing to pay an equal price, if they sailed by a fast steamer from Quebec as by New York? But the hon. gentleman is opposed to a 20-knot service, chiefly because the people would not be able to get a $75 passage.
Let me quote some further words of the hon. member, a. question had been raised in reference to the carrying of freight, and the hon. member spoke as follows :
The hon. gentleman, as a result of his investigations, will not be able to avoid the extreme difficulty of providing ample freight capacity and a rapid service in the same vessel. The more closely the hon. gentleman inquires into the matter, the more he will be satisfied that the government have only a limited range of choice as to the quantity of freight that can be carried, if the main idea of having a fast service is maintained.

I think lie will find out that unless he is prepared to very nearly double the tonnage of the vessels as compared with the tonnage of tenders for which we called, he will not he able to accomplish any very much larger scope of freight combined with the speed that is necessary for making it in reality a fast service. The hon. gentleman went on to speak on the same lines on which the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) spoke this afternoon, saying that if we established this fast service^ for passengers and for certain kinds of freight and for mails, it would not be long before tbe freight service would follow the passenger service. But, I think what takes place is this, and what takes place under these peculiar conditions where these tenders are now, is that fast freight vessels follow in the wake of a fast line such as we are contemplating to put on.

These are details of the question. What we are asked to do here to-night is to endorse the position taken by the right bon. the First Minister at the Imperial Conference in favour of an All-Red route throughout the empire.
I have before me an interview given to the ' Canadian Gazette ' by tbe distinguished statesman, Sir Charles Tupper, immediately after the First Minister placed Ms resolution before the Imperial Conference. Did Sir Charles Tupper greet it with captious criticism? Did he say : We must have a certain amount of room for freight and a certain amount of room for cold stox-age? No. As a big Canadian, he expressed himself as very strongly in favour of the
124(85

scheme. It was a matter in which he had always taken the greatest possible interest, as he naturally would, having been a pioneer in the movement. He said that the All-Red route as now put forward was simply completing the carrying out of an arrangement that was made by his government when he was Premier of Canada; but the contract then made with the Allan line was prevented from coming Into operation by the refusal of the Earl of Aberdeen. then Governor General of Canada, to authorize the signature to the contract. The contract was made by a government of which the hon. member for North Toronto was a member-actually made to be signed by the Governor General without submission to parliament, and Sir Charles Tupper said Lord Aberdeen refused to ratify It.
The hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Kemp) is very frank in this matter. He is against this scheme absolutely, without any qualification. He seems to think that fast travel is a fad, saying that the fast steamers of the German lines were put on at a time when everybody had a fad for fast travelling. I will undertake to say that he could not book a berth on any of those steamers within three months. Everybody knows that they are the most popular steamers that cross the Atlantic to-day. He says the time will come when people will go back to the slower vessels. He might as well talk of abandoning fast trains and going back to slow freightt trains or stage coaches. The tendency of the age is for faster travel, whether on land or sea, and my hon. friend must know that. I know that he knows it, because before taking his seat he said : Our present service is an 18-knot service ; leave it alone, and in three or four years the companies will give us a 21-knot service. If that is going out of style, if this fast travel is only a fad, if people are going back to the old slow travel, why are the Canadian companies going to put on 21-knot steamers Inside of four years ?
This scheme appeals to us in many ways. As a great imperial proposition, it brings the different parts of the empire closer together. I do not agree with those gentleman who say that we can do greater service to the empire by being able to sell our products to the different parts of the empire ; we can become greater imperialists by coming in closer touch with the rest of the people in the empire. This All-Red route will put Canada upon the main postroad of empire. Thousands of people travelling from England away to the east, or from the east to the motherland will pass through this magnificent country, will see the great harbours on the Pacific, the unequalled scenery of the Rockies, the oceans of wheat growing on the prairies of the west, will see the great provinces of Ontario and Quebec ;
in summer they will pass down the magnificent St. Lawrence river and in winter will go through the maritime provinces with their magnificent resources and potentialities and will sail out of a harbour unequalled in the world. This will be an advertisement for our country to our friends at home, and not only will it bring us nearer the man in London, but it will bring us nearer to the man who lives in Sydney or in Melbourne or in Auckland. To-day almost 99 per cent of those who travel between New Zealand or Australia and England go by the way of the Suez canal, and not via the Canadian route. If tills line is established in such a way as we hope, it will mean that not only will we become better acquainted with people in the motherland but we will become better acquainted with our brothers in the more distant parts of the empire.
I regret very much that the proposition is not definite enough to establish Halifax, or St. John if you like, as the Canadian port for use all the year around. Then people would not wonder when travelling whether they were going to Quebec or Halifax or to St. John, tliey would know that they would go to one port all the year around. It would be : All aboard for Halifax or all aboard for St. John at Liverpool at all seasons of the year. It may not be possible to do this but it will at any rate mean that during a great portion of the year this magnificent service will be through the maritime provinces. The maritime provinces will no longer be reached by a switchback railway, they will be on the main line from the old land to the far east. We will be able to show travellers when they enter Halifax the great harbour which is the pride of our province. They will be able to sec the little province of Nova Scotia of which we, its sons, are so justly proud. They will be able to see the great province of New Brunswick and to realize that away down east of the great provinces in which we are to-day, there are provinces well worthy the admiration of* every true friend of the empire.
We spend $680,000 a year in subsidies. I am not here to say that that money is thrown away. I think a considerable portion of it is well spent. Some of it, I am afraid, is not, but is it not better to spend a million and a half and get a sure benefit than to spend $680,000 for doubtful benefit ? We are sure that if this All-Red route is established it will be a great benefit to every province of Canada. There will, no doubt, be accommodation for certain lines of freight but we cannot, as shown by the hon. member for Toronto ten yeaTS ago, make it a freight and passenger service at the same time, although we may provide for some classes of fast freight, express parcels and mails. For these reasons I am very heartily in favour of the resolution

which has been moved by the First Minister.
Our friends opposite are the most slireik-ing imperialists that have ever been known to live until they have to pay for-it. When it comes down to giving a preference on British goods entering Canada they take it with a wry face and in private and on public platforms in some parts of the country, they deprecate giving that preference. They are immense imperialists, but when it comes to giving a million and a half dollars out of the taxes to establish an All-Red route to bring all parts of the empire closer together, to cement the heart and the outlying limbs of the empire, these gentlemen throw in resolutions about cheaper freight, cold storage and one thing and another, all for the one purpose, to defeat the resolution introduced by the First Minister.
I congratulate the First Minister on the scheme which he had the honour of introducing at the imperial conference. It matters not whether he is the author of the name ' All-Red route,' or the author of the scheme, he moved the resolution before the imperial conference of this empire and to him should be given that credit. I can only say in conclusion that if our hon. friends opposite had met this resolution as Sir Charles Tupper would have met it, as the big men who were at the head of that party twenty or twenty-five years ago would have received it, they would have strengthened the hands of the government of Canada, they would have strengthened the hands of the imperial government, and their action would have been a great inducements to the governments of New Zealand and Australia to grant their subventions towards this scheme which means so much not only to Great Britain but to all parts of the empire.

Mr. Speaker, I support this resolution of the right hon. the Prime Minister because I believe it to be commercially important to the Dominion of Canada. The subject-matter of the resolution has been treated under different phases, along different lines. Some have viewed it as an imperial question and others as a commercial proposition. I take it that it is solely in the interests of the different parts of the empire and that it will mean a great deal in the building up of the Dominion. The time has come when water routes are to be given their proper place in the consideration of the great national questions. I have already in this House declared myself strongly in favour of the improvement of the water routes of Canada. I believe that the construction of the Georgian Bay canal is a very live question /or the parliament and people of Canada and I trust that before many months, or years at most have elapsed, we will have some definite announcement with reference to the construc-

*
tion of water routes in this Diminion. It is also of vital interest to the Dominion of Canada that we should improve in the best possible way the transportation facilities between Europe and the Dominion.
In connection with this resolution,I would add a word in favour of a project, that is receiving the attention of the British parliament. that is to include a port in Ireland as one of the features in the All-Red route. I do this not simply because I am proud to say a word on behalf of Ireland, not only as an Irish Canadian, but because I believe the project can not be successfully carried out without a thorough, studied consideration of the advantages of a port in Ireland as a means of shortening the Atlantic passage. Therefore, I have double pleasure in suporting this motion, because ultimately Ireland will receive a great measure of justice in the consideration of this question. I am opposed to the amendment because I believe that its main object is to defeat the motion before the House.

Before the vote is taken, I wish to claim the attention of the House for a short time; and I do it because of certain things that have transpired since the right hon. gentleman introduced the resolution this morning, and also because of certain differences of opinion as to the meaning of the resolution and the amendment. I listened with interest to the speech of my hon. friend from Brandon (Mr. Sifton). But the House 'could not but ask: What scheme is it we are asked to endorse? My hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Logan) made a very strong appeal to the opposition to support the government scheme. The vital question with me is: What is, at the present moment, the gov eminent scheme? I know that the scheme was as proposed by the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) at the imperial conference. That was a scheme of 24-knot service on the Atlantic and 22-knot service on the Pacific. I know what the scheme was as proposed by my right hon. friend this morning-it was a scheme of 20 knots or 21 knots for the Atlantic and IS knots, if it could be had, on the Pacific. But, when the master of ceremonies came upon the scene and gave the only authoritative pronouncement, and with greater, though limited, information, the scheme he outlined was one of 24 knots on the Atlantic and 22 knots on the Pacific. Now, when heated appeals are made to this side of the House to support the government scheme, I ask myself: Which is the government scheme? Who is the master of this craft? The hon. member for Brandon gave us what may be called a matured opinion. In the speech he delivered a few months ago in this House, he declared that he had been commissioned by the Prime Minister to take this matter up in England and gather

information. To-day, he told us that he had gathered that informaion. He knew exactly the scheme that was proposed. It was the scheme of 24 knots on the Atlantic and 22 knots on the Pacific: it involved a subsidy of $5,000,000 a year, and Canada's contribution to that subsidy was to be from $500,000 to $700,000 in round figures. He declared that he had gone over to the old country, and, as no one else seemed to be doing anything about it from the public point of view, he had set himself to make these inquiries; he had talked with members of the government, with financial men, with shipbuilding experts; he had had computations made of revenue, of cost, of deficit; and had arrived at the conclusion which he announced here to-day without an if or an an as the scheme which was known to everybody who was intimately connected with it. And yet, the Prime Minister this morning did not know of that. He had not taken counsel with the hon. member for Brandon, and made the mistake of coming down to a 20-knot service on the Atlantic and 18-knot service on the Pacific. Again I ask myself: Who is the authority and what is the scheme?	.
Now, why was there nobody to get in formation? If the thing was not to go absolutely by default why was it necessary that the hou. member for Brandon should go across the water and make these investigations? One of the schemes of the imperial conference of last year was the establishment of a secretariat, under Lord Elgin, whose duty it was to take up unfinished resolutions and unfinished proceedings, pursue the investigations and report the information to the different governments, so that these governments would have the duty of placing this information before their councils, and, if thought necessary, before their parliaments. That secretariat has been organized; I cannot but think that that secretariat has been at work. Is the hon. member for Brandon a member of that secretariat? Or is it that that part of the organization of the imperial conference of last year, heralded to us as having been established by Lord Elgin in connection with the colonial office, has done nothing in reference to this, the largest piece of unfinished business which was before the conference? I cannot but think that that secretariat has done its duty; that it has been making investigations; that it has been taking the opinion of experts, and that it is giving this information to the imperial government, for every once in a while we see intimations that the imperial government is considering the matter, is taking counsel with reference to it, and we are told, time and time again, that it is more favourably inclined to it on account of the information it has received. Now, the Prime Minister should have done what the j hon. member for Brandon did, only more '
so. They have employed him, they have authorized him, and he-as shown by his own statement to-day-having made the inquiries, the Prime Minister should have placed the information before us and given us such facts and calculations of cost, revenue and expenditure, of such commercial avenues as would be opened up by this scheme, as have been gathered by the hon. gentleman into whose hands he committed the matter and the secretariat whose duty it was to follow out this unfinished business in the way I have described. And yet my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier) did nothing of that kind when he came before us to-day.
Now, that is the first thing I wish to call tile attention of the House to; and the second thing is this: We have had rather a remarkable change within the last few hours in the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite. In the 1907 conference, my right hon. friend never made a plea for freight, or cold storage, or reasonable freight rates. I have read his whole speech through-it does not take long to do it-and there is not a suggestion in favour of any consideration of these important points. He does not recognize their importance. He gives way to the statement made by Sir Joseph Ward that the 22-knot service on the Pacific is necessary in order to satisfy New Zealand's -wants, and, by implication, cuts out the employment of the service for fruits and perishable commodities of any kind.
When he brought this matter before the House this morning, he never mentioned, he never thought of the immense importance to this country of the cheap transport of its products. He never seemed to have had sympathy with or to have thought of the matter until it was brought up by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. K. L. Borden). Then it certainly developed into a most important thing under the manipulation of the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) and of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding). Then it became the word for every speaker on the other side that we must have regard to the moving of the products of the country, to the cheapening of rates and the furnishing of cold storage facilities. The resolution of my hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden) has done this much. It has wakened hon. gentleman opposite to a realization of the fact that there is a farmers and producers side to this question as well as the side of the nabob and millionaire who travel and pay large sums for every luxury and comfort on their passage.
)But there is another strange difference of opinion. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) blurted it out and so did the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Macpherson). What was the plain statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) ? Each of these gentlemen wanted-what ? The

approval of this House to the resolution of the right hon. the First Minister, or, as they put it, the approval of the scheme of the government. It would take a Philadelphia lawyer to tell what is the scheme of the government. Who has the best of it ? Is it the member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) or the Prime 'Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurer) ? The one speaks as Prime Minister but the other speaks with a voice which sounds very much like a solid and supported authority. The Minister of Finance and the member for Vancouver say : Support the scheme of the government; give it your endorsation. For what purpose ? As the Minister of Finance says, you could not bind Canada to anything unless parliament gave its sanction to this resolution. The member for Vancouver said : What is the use of going over there and talking to the delegates of Australia or New Zealand, you would not be liable to make any binding agreement with them. What these gentlemen believe is that if the resolution passes, the Prime Minister will have the authority to go to Australia and New Zealand and Great Britain and make hard and fast contracts and bring them down to this House-make these contracts with the authority of this parliament behind him and quoting the support of this parliament in his negotiations with these countries. But if I understood the Prime Minister at all rightly this morning, he declared in so many words that it was not a part of his resolution to make it possible for any contract to be agreed upon between Canada and the other parties, that all these things must be brought down to parliament, and be subject to the open and free discussion and approval of parliament. Did I understand my right hon. friend aright ? He nods his assent. Then we may have been a little over cautious, as far as he is concerned, when we wanted to make it still more binding that we should not be bound to any financial responsibility and be prevented from obtaining the consent of the House before being bound. But my hon. friend the Minister of Finance has an absolutely different idea. He cried out with indignation : Unless you give your approval, we could not bind Canada to anything. Well it is the opinion of this side that we shall have to back up the First Minister in opposition to the Minister of Finance and his followers and help the First Minster to insist on the point that this parliament shall not be bound by any agreement or contract, that we shall be free, from the compulsion of a contract, and that the government shall not be in the position of coming down to this House and forcing its supporters to carry through the contract because this bad authorized the government to make it and make it final. We are supporting the First Minister against the Minister of Finance and those who look upon the adoption of this resolution as necessary

to bind Canada. I think that is a fair criticism. We must have things clear in our minds.
Wjth reference to the resolution itself, my hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Mac-pherson) was in a dense fog. No darkness ever encompassed the Pacific ocean, so dramatically alluded to by the hon. gentleman this morning, so dense as that which enveloped him when he was trying to grasp the meaning of the resolution introduced by the right hon. the First Minister. He seemed to be impressed with the idea that you could not speak to Australia at all, that you could not pay two cents for postage to carry a document to Australia, that no steps could be taken and no expenditures made unless this resolution of the First Minister, as he intepreted it, was passed. Why, the hon. gentleman surely can read English. What do you find ? You find this expressly stated in the resolution of the First Minister :
That in the opinion of this House it is desirable that the governments of Australia, Canada and New Zealand should, with as little delay as possible, agree upon a definite plan for carrying into effect the terms of the said resolution of the imperial conference, the same to be submitted for the consideration of -the imperial and colonial -parliaments.
That is to be found in the Prime Minister's resolution-this resolution, one-third of which is supported by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden). Therefore the opposition and the First Minister, whatever the hon. member for Vancouver may say, are agreed entirely in saying that the government should not delay, that the government should negotiate with Australia, New Zealand and Great Britain, and as soon as possible agree upon a definite plan, and then bring it to this parliament and let us discuss it. But the member for Vancouver says: Ah, you you should show sympathy with this. You should be more enthusiastic, says the member for Brandon, What can we do more ? The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) who has been making his eulogy, long past date, of that great Canadian Sir Charles Tupper, said that if Sir Charles Tupper were here, you would not find him talking this kind of politics. Well, Sir Charles Tupper would be supporting the Prime Minister against some of his recalcitrant followers who want to push him further than he says he is willing to go. 'Sir Charles Tupper expressed his strong agreement with the Prime Minister in the idea which the latter brought before the imperial conference. That is what Sir Charles Tupper, that large Canadian would do were he here. That is what he did in London by interview. But what does my hon. friend the leader of the opposition propose ? He proposes :

That this House, in expressing its strong sympathy with the object of the said resolution-
Do you want anything more ? Even the big Canadian, Sir Charles Tupper, used almost the same words. He said . strong support.' My hon. friend says ' strong sympathy.' That is better than strong support. It takes in the heart and vital organs. It is sentiment as well as force, and it is therefore stronger than the other. Let the member for Vancouver possess his soul with patience, let the member for Cumberland do likewise-if the resolution passes as amended by my hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden), you have a strong expression of sympathy with the resolution of my right hon. friend and you have the imperative command of this House not to delay negotiations, to make them as speedily as possible, to settle on a definite plan, to bring it as quickly as possible to this parliament, and we will take it into consideration. What the amendment of my hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden) does is this :	It calls to mind,
and it was a timely calling to mind, that in the midst of this lavish expenditure which lias been, the lavish expenditure which is now going on and the lavish expenditure which is in contemplation it is well, if you propose to spend so many millions more, that you shall heed the great imperative necessity of this country which is to get the producer, within the smallest cost and at the greatest speed, to the market where lie must sell his products. To do that you have to have cold storage, and you have to have reasonable freight rates and that is all that this amendment in that respect calls for. It does call for that and why you should not call for that ? To my mind it was not necessary for the right hon. gentleman to put that resolution before the House. He had just as much authority-he and his government-to go into the closest negotiations with the parties to this matter, to get a definite plan, to get all information, all results, all consequences, all the advantages from the plan so concerted between the contracting parties, as far as the plan was concerned then he had a perfect right to bring that to this parliament and then parliament would have something to devote its attention to instead of the airy and contraditory nothings which are banded about between the right hon. gentleman and some of his followers. I would not give a doit, or anything in the way of heavy expenditures, if we are not going to get something which was really excellent for the money. The Prime Minister seems to be willing to take a twenty knot service, or may be a little less than a 20-knot service or any old thing that he can get, and pay well for it. This is a very important crisis with reference to what I consider the greatest of all elements in the permanence and progress of the British empire. This is the
first attempt at co-operation amongst the great members of the British family. What is involved ? Forty or fifty million dollars is involved. John Bull & Co., represented by the old country, by Canada, by Australia and by New Zealand, have in contemplation the putting of $50,000,000 of their good money into a certain scheme, I say it is of the utmost importance that all the strength of investigation, of business talents, of clean cut judgment and the most serious consideration should be given to the bases of the project into which John Bull and these parts of the company propose to put $50,000,000 of their good money. Rush into a scheme that shall be unfortunate, rush into a scheme that shall be unsuccessful and you damn for ever co-operation between John Bull & Co. It is of the utmost importance, therefore, that time for investigation, that the clearest expert opinion, the best commercial opinion and the best statesmanship should be lavished upon the foundations and building up of the plan upon which we propose to get into this new venture with $50,000,000 of our good money. It is because it is not in that position that I am opposed to having this country bound any more than it is to-day until we have these foundations and until we have this superstructure as well. The hon. Minister of Finance with jaunty courage as some men would call it, but which I would not designate as courage but rather as temerity, is willing to go into any expenditures at all and he piteously appeals to this side of the House and says that it would be a pity if we gave a black eye>
to the credit of this country. My hon. friend would have done better if he had thought of that every year in the last six years of his financial administration. He would have done well to have thought of that when, at first with reluctance, but afterwards with heels that clipped it as quickly as those of any of his supporters, he rushed into expenditures for all kinds of inexcusable things in order that patronage and political strength might be given to the party [DOT] which he is trying to lead.

What are they ?
Mr. FOSTER, One of the most comical things I think I ever witnessed in parliament I witnessed this afternoon when this learned, responsible and accomplished expert in the line of expenditures and steamship building hardened his face like flint and shouted out: We will take the responsibility, when $40,000,000 or $50,000,000 was spoken of. It is courage like that, based upon strength and stability like that, that helps us over the steep and difficult places in parliament and keeps our abiding faith in our country still within our bosoms when oftentimes we *would be discouraged. But let the Finance Minister not turn to this side of the House if he is so anxious not

to give to the credit of this country a black eye. He must think of his own misdeeds. He did preach economy in the days of his novitiate, he did, in the maritime provinces declare aganst the extreme extravagance of the party that he wished to dispose, but that hon. gentleman repudiated, the very moment he got into the saddle, the professions of his novitiate and entered upon a course of reckless public expenditure which has brought the credit of Canada close up to the breaking point. The Finance Minister, as the financial head of this country, for the time being in control, should have known his business better, should have had something to do with experts' and something to do with foundation processes when he came, in 1903. before this parliament and pledged his faith as a minister, and pledged this country as the Finance Minister, that it would cost, for building the Transcontinental Railway from Winnipeg down to Moncton, the sum of $52,000,000. To-da.v he is face to face, with a market which is none too favourable, with an expenditure for that same line of railway of $160,000,000 or $170,000,000. That is something which gives Canadian credit not the best standing in the markets of London where moneys are to be raised, where financial men look keenly and carefully into the resources and into the prospectus and statements which are made by the government and especially by the financial head of the government in Canada. My hon. frind the Minister of Finance said he thousht that we wanted to be solid against the scheme. We were once the imperialists ; where are we now ? Does he not know the obivious retort ? Once he was a repealer ; where is he now ? Once he advocated a commercial policy which opened the arms of Canada to the United States and which barred with all the power of a discriminative tariff Great Britain and every colony of Great Britain out of this country as far as trade privileges were concerned. That is the hon. gentleman who thinks it safe and prudent to raise a question as to the loyalty of this great Dominion ; to raise a question as to imperial preference and the imperial relations. I do not wish to take up the time of the House longer.
Hear, hear.

I am very glad that hon. gentlemen opposite show by their applause that they would like me to continue, and on some other occasion and in cooler climatic conditions I will afford these gentlemen the pleasure they desire.
It were comical, were it not so serious, to note the efforts of my hon. friends opposite to kill this project while they pretend to be in favour of it.
Oh.
That's all the thanks we get for supporting you.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Foster! is perhaps not aware that in his verbose extravagance he does not weigh his own words, and probably he does not remember that not five minutes ago he used these very words : I am opposed to have this country saddled with this new burden.

I did say that, but I coupled with it the condition that I was opposed to having the country burdened with the financial responsibility contemplated unless we had the definite plans and the basis for it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Let my hon. friend have whatever comfort he can take from that. The hon. gentleman is opposed to this project unless we have a definite plan, but I had understood that hon. gentlemen opposite were in favour of the idea and that they were anxious to have it investigated, although now they say they are opposed to it.
Do you say we are opposed to investigation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. Foster) has all along shown that he does not want this scheme, but, if he will permit me to say so, he has not had the manliness to come forward and declare it boldly. The hon. gentleman wants to know what is the scheme before the House. Well, I spoke with perfect candour, and I stated that there were more ways than one to approach the subject, and that there was more than one kind of steamer afloat on the ocean. The hon. gentleman asks : Is this the scheme of the member for Brandon or is it the scheme of the Prime Minister, as if there was any difference whatever between the scheme of the member for Brandon and the scheme of the Prime Minister. My hon. friend knows the English language even better than I, and here are the words of the resolution :
That we are in favour of a steamship service by the best service available within reasonable cost.
Mark, with reasonable cost. If we can have a 24-knot service we are in favour of it if we can have it within reasonable cost ; if we can have a 25-lmot service, or a 26-knot service, or a 27-knot service, or the best service on the ocean, we are in favour of it, provided we can get it at reasonable cost.
That's right.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I referred this afternoon to the ' Mauretania ' and the ' Lusitania,' and the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) spoke as if that was the type of steamer we had in mind at the conference.

The memory of the hon. gentleman is defective ; he knows that the conference sat in May, 1907, and the ' Mauretania ' and the ' Lusitania ' were not then launched, so that we could not have had them before us for purposes of comparison. I stated to-day that if we could have steamers like the ' Mauretania ' and the ' Lusitania ' that is what we would desire, but I spoke honestly as to the difficulty, and I said that it had* not yet been proven that these two great steamers were a commercial success.
I pointed out that while steamers of this type were what we aimed at, we might not be able to have them if they could not be obtained within reasonable cost. There are none so blind as those who do not wish to see, and there is no one who can be so blind as my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) on occasion. No one will accuse him of being naturally dense, but when he does want to be d^ense he will not exercise his power of discernment, and he can be denser than anybody I know of. Let us judge the policy of the opposition by the amendment they have moved. There are two propositions in that amendment, the last of which means nothing, because the difference between it and the proposition of the government is merely the difference between tweedledum and tweedledee. But there is another idea in the amendment, and I will mention it as an example of how ridiculous sensible men can sometimes be. This All-Ited route is acknowledged to be a splendid project, a project which excites the pride of all Canadians and of all British subjects. What does the opposition say with regard to it? They say : Stop here ; do not go any further in this imperial project until you have made arrangements for cold storage. Never was there such a big beginning and such a small ending. Is it possible that these gentlemen opposite, who claim that their party has attained to dignified statesmanship, should came down to resolve that in a project so vast you must not undertake it until you have provided for cold storage? Why do they not ask us to provide that the steamers shall have funnels and boilers? Is there any well equipped steamer to-day that is not provided with cold storage facilities as well as with a rudder and a mast? Do these hon. gentlemen opposite really believe that when we were contemplating this imperial steamship service, which is calculated to bind the British empire together, we ever thought the steamers would not be equipped with cold storage? Has it come to this? Is not such an idea too small for grown up men? Let me comfort my hon. friends opposite by telling them that it certainly does mean cold storage, for does not the resolution say in so many words that it means the best service available? Is there any kind of first-class service afloat on the Atlantic which is not provided with cold storage?
Why, cold storage accommodation is just as necessary as the boilers in the ships. But my hon. friend from North Toronto, and the hon. leader of the opposition as well, have let the cat out of the bag and have -given us the true intent which moved them to this amendment. The leader of the opposition told us in his speech that there was something in this project not very pleasant for the farmers of Ontario and of the country generally, who do not travel in these luxurious steamers, but who want cheap freight rates for their products.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I notice that the sentiment is responded to on the other side of the House. There are more ways than one of providing cheap freight for the producers of this country. It is not altogether a matter of affording cheap transportation rates. The farmers will realize that whetn we provide the steamship service we have In mind we will be doing something to benefit the farmers of Canada. And here let me say that if there is one thing men should be ashamed of it is to endeavour to introduce class prejudices into a question of this kind. Let me point out that when we have these great steamers afloat on the ocean, and when we are carrying people from all parts of the world to our shores, we will be doing a good deal for the farmers of Canada.
I do not always agree with my hon. friend from North Toronto, but I must give credit to whom credit is due. We must give credit even to some persons whom I will not name, though it is not due; therefore I give credit to my hon. friend from North Toronto. My hon. friend during the present session made use of an expression which at the time seemed to me a little audacious, but which on the whole was correct. He said that in Switzerland they exported scenery. The expression was audacious, but there is merit in it. It meant that the scenery of Switzerland attracted to that country every year thousands of tourists. This is what he calls exporting scenery, and this is what we want to do-export the scenery of Canada. We are going to export it to Europe; we are also_going to export it to the Orient: and this is in accordance with the views of my hon. friend. My hon. friend this morning made it a reproach to me that I brought this resolution before the imperial conference on the last day of the sitting. I do not know that it matters very much, as to the merits of this resolution, whether it was brought on the first day or the last day of the conference. Does my hon. friend want to make that an argument against the resolution ? Did it occur to my hon. friend that, because the matter was brought before the conference on the last day of its sitting, it took the conference by surprise? Who expressed any surprise that the matter was brought up ?
Llo.vd George.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Lloyd George did not express any surprise; lie only complained that he had not seen the resolution. He did not say that the idea was new to him. Does anybody suppose that at a conference of that kind, when members were meeting each other day after day, this matter had not been discussed informally between them? Does anybody suppose that this matter was brought before the conference suddenly, without a word of discussion or explanation, beforehand? If the matter had not already been discussed, the moment the resolution was brought before the conference, everybody would have said: This is new to us; we must have time to consider it. Mr. Lloyd George complained only that he had not seen the resolution; but neither he nor anybody else complained that they were taken by surprise. No, Sir; the resolution was presented at the right moment: and. what we want now is to have the assurance of the Canadian parliament that it will do its share when called on. I do not pretend to say for one moment, if we are authorized by this parliament to ask Australia and New Zealand for their co-operation in this scheme, that we can bind the Canadian parliament to do this or that; but we want to go to Australia and New Zealand with the moral certainty, affirmed by the Canadian parliament, that we have behind us the whole Canadian people.
House divided on amendment of Mr. R. L. Borden.

Before we go into Supply I would call the attention of the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) to the fact that a report of the Debates Committee was brought before the House on April 23rd last, but no motion has been made to have that report adopted by the House. If I am well informed, it was delayed because of an expression of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), but it was to have beeu brought forward later on. Since then, a later report, made by the same com-

mittee, and involving exactly the same principle, has been brought before the House and adopted. I would now ask my right hon. friend if nothing can be done to have the pending report also adopted by the House. This is one of these reports of committees which are generally treated with respect by this House, and I think it is due to the Committee on Debates that this report should be brought before the House and acted upon. I imagine that the answer to my question will be that the chairman of the Debates Committee should bring the matter forward. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Gervais) is not here to-day. I do not know whether he will be here before the end of the session or not. I call the attention of my right hon. friend to the fact that it will seem like a slur on the Debates Committee if its report is not acted upon before the end of the session.

I must say, in justice to the chairman of the Debates Committee, that he has called my attention to this report more than once, but I have always understood that the matter was enngaging the attention of the Committee on Internal Economy.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance).
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The matter is engaging the attention of the Committee on Internal Economy, and in one form or other it will be brought to the notice of the House, either by the report of the committee being called up or by some other proposition, at an early day. ['I would remind my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) that, as I have already stated, since this report was brought down, a later and analogous report from the very same committee has been adopted by the House.']
Has any printed statement of the Inspector General been distributed?

I am about to distribute it now. 1 could not do it before because it required a motion of the House, but I am going to read the document and shall ask permission of the committee to lay the report on the table and it will be immediately distributed.
I regret very much that I shall be obliged to detain the committee for some little time at such a late period of the session, but I think the committee will agree with nje that
I should not allow this session to close without making reference to the report of the Civil Service Commission, so far as it affects the Department of Militia, especially as my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) saw flt to give force to this report by reading very extensively from it those portions which refer to the Militia Department, thereby, I suppose, adopting the views therein expressed. I might have brought the matter up on the occasion when the report of that commission was under discussion ; but as I did not wish to discuss it generally, I thought it would be better that I should do so on the motion to go into supply upon the estimates for civil government. It so happened however that the estimates for civil government of my department were passed at a moment when, by agreement on both sides, there was no debate, when it was desirable to get the estimates through in order to facilitate the payment of the clerks in the service. Therefore I must ask, Mr. Chairman, your indulgence while I refer to that portion of the civil service report which deals with the Department of Militia. I believe it was understood that this item was reserved in order that any matter pertinent to the Militia Department should be open for discussion. I do not intend to go into a general discussion of the work of the Civil Service Commission, but I cannot help thinking that commission did not do its work in as workmanlike 'manner ias was the work of the commission of 1892. I have carefully read the report and the evidence of the commission-the evidence taken by the commission of 1892 as well as that taken by the commission of 1907 and the report now under consideration. I observe that in 1892 the commission was very careful to prepare a list of the questions which were submitted to all the leading officials of the various departments some time before they were to be examined in order to give them every opportunity of being prepared to answer those questions. Perhaps I had better read a short extract from the report of the Civil Service Commission of 1892 because the idea is better expressed there than I can do it. It reads as follows :
In order to fully carry out the duties entrusted to them, the first step which the commissioners took, after electing Mr. Hague chairman, was the preparation of a carefully considered schedule of questions on the above subject. A copy of these was transmitted to the deputy head or other responsible officer of each department with the request that answers shall, he prepared and submitted when the officers in question shall be called on to give evidence before the commission. This method of procedure had the eSect of obtaining accurate information in matters of detail and also of shortening to some extent the time occupied in the inquiry.
Nothing of this kind was done by the recent commission. On the contrary, it seems

to me, from reading the questions which were put, that there was frequently an evident intention to take the officers by surprise. At any rate no opportunity to prepare was given them. It seems to me that the questions were frequently leading and that there is every indication that the commissioners approached their task with their minds made up and not with the desire or expectation of learning anything from the evidence they were taking, which would enable them to reach a sound conclusion. It impresses me in that way, and in reading over the evidence taken in the different departments, I cannot but observe how differently the different departments were treated. I cannot help thinking that, perhaps without intention-we will hope without intention-the chairman of that commission was. let us say. unconsciously influenced by the fact that he had Keen an officer of the Dominion government for thirty or forty years and had been Deputy Finance Minister for something over thirty years and had thereby been brought in contact with the Important officers in the different departments. This, one would have thought, would have' given him possibly more special qualifications for judging tile condition of the civil service, and undoubtedly it did. But, on the other hand, there were the jealousies and the difficulties which had arisen during those thirty years of office between him and other officials, and I presume that the chairman, being human, went into the work of chairmanship of this commission with a good many prejudices and possibly with some old grudges wdiich have found vent in the report laid before the House in the manner of the questions put to the different witnesses.
I am not going to quote generally from the evidence, but I want to accentuate the observations which I have just made, by referring the committee to the evidence to be found in the first volume of the evidence, at pages 180, 183 and 184. I would suggest to any lion, gentleman who wishes to spend an amusing half hour that he read the evidence taken by the commission from the officers of the Department of Finance. It will not be forgotten, Mr. Chairman, that the chairman of this commission had been for thirty years Deputy Minister of Finance. I will give you tw7o or three sample questions to show you how gently he treated his own department, the department in which he was formerly deputy minister. At page 180 I find this question put by the chairman to the present Deputy Minister of Finance, Mr. Boville :
Q. You worked your way up through every grade by promotion examination until you became deputy minister?-A. Yes.
Then, Mr. Fyshe says :
Q. Have you passed several promotion examinations?-A. One was all I had to take.
Sir FREDERICK BORDEN
Then, at page 183, this question is asked by the chairman :
Q. As a rule your employees are all healthy ? -A. Yes.
Q. And scarcely without exception they are of good character?-A. The employees of the Department of Finance are of the highest character.
By Mr. Fyshe:
Q. Are you more careful in your selection? -A. We are very careful in selection.
Q. And your political head does not give you any trouble?-A. None whatever. He is very reasonable and very careful to give us as good material as he possibly can obtain.
A little later on; the chairman-the exDeputy Minister of Finance-says :
Who is being examined?
The present deputy minister, Mr. Boville, who had grown up in the department.
Who appointed the chairman?

Well, I did not, but I am responsible.
Q. In consequence of the training they received many former officials of the Finance Department have succeeded in outside life?- A. Yes.
Q. Mr. Ross left the department?-A. Yes, Mr. Chipman left the department.
Q. To become chief factor for the Hudson Bay Company?-A. Mr. Baker left the department in your time, Mr. Courtney.
The Chairman.-Yes. The Finance Department has trained up a lot of men.
The Witness.-Mr. Tabor is now a lawyer in Dawson.
A regular mutual admiration society. Here was Paul sitting at the feet of Gamaliel. I had a little curiosity to look up the length of time that these gentlemen had been in this wonderful department in which so many men have been trained for such important positions and this is what I found : Mr. Chipman was in the Finance Department from July 1, 1880, to February 7, 1881. and you will see what miracles were per-pormed in that short time. I find that Mr. Ross, who was taken out of this department and given the position of general manager of a bank, was in the department exactly eighteen months, from July 1, 1901, to January 1. 1903. So you will observe that the department is able almost to perform miracles, that it is a wonderful training school. A man goes in, remains six months and is eligible for any position ! But there is one question from which probably a different meaning was intended to be taken from that which might be taken. The chairman says:
Q. And while men have constantly left the department you have had no applications from any who have retired to come back again?-[DOT] A. No.

No, oiice having escaped they never want to return. However, I do not intend to deal with the matter in this way. I have simply given the committee this as a sample brick to indicate the method of investigation and the kind of frivolous questions with which these gentlemen occupied themselves in dealing with a serious question.
Were they as gentle with the Department of Militia and Defence?

Not quite, as I shall show you. The Militia Department can, I suppose, fairly be called a technical department. It is a department in which the expenditure of money is based upon the policy of the country. Parliament deliberately decides how large the militia shall be, what amount of money shall be expended upon it, and what shall be the policy with regard to the development and carrying out of the defence of this country. 1 have read over the orders in council by which this commission was appointed and I have looked in vain for any authority given by that order in council to these gentlemen to constitute themselves a committee to investigate and criticise the policy deliberately adopted by the parliament of this country. It is not their's. Therefore, I venture to think that these gentlemen have made a very grave mistake in arrogating to themselves the right to make such an investigation, particularly as they are notoriously, absolutely and utterly ignorant of the first principles which govern military matters. But, they rushed in and we have before us, in the report of the commission, portions of which have been read to this House, from the bottom of page 37 down to the middle of page 42. what might be fairly described,
I think, as an indictment against the administration of the militia services, beginning I with the criticism of the policy of parliament in increasing the vote from $3,500,000 to $6,500,000 between the years 1903-4 and the years 1907-8 and ending with the conclusion that the efficiency of the militia is less than it was ten or fifteen years ago. I propose, as briefly as may be, to deal with some of the matters referred to in this report.
As I shall quote to some extent from the memorandum of Major General Lake, Inspector General upon that portion of the report of the Civil iService Commission. 1908. which deals with the administration of the militia, I propose with the consent of the committee to lay this memorandum on the table, and I shall distribute copies to hon. gentlemen. I may say that when the report of the Civil Service Commissioners appeared, General Lake was very much surprised and he at once came to see me and he said he would be very glad indeed to prepare an answer which I gave him authority to do. Everybody knows who General Lake
is, and everybody will agree with me that his opinion on the militia of Canada is worth more than perhaps that of any other living man. General Lake has served in Canada now about 9 years; he served as Quarter-Master General under the late government from 1893 until that government went out of power, and then on till 1898 under the present administration. Since 1904 he has been chief of the General Staff. He has served in India and he has served for a number of years in the war office. He was assistant quarter-master general at the war office during the whole of the South African war and he had under his control and was responsible for the transport of that great army which left the shores of Great Britain and which was safely landed, I believe, without the loss of a single man. I think I am correct in saying that his department of the War Office is the only one that has not been criticised in connection with the South African war. I think I may venture to put forward the memorandum of General Lake on a military matter as against the report of the Civil Service Commissioners. While the Civil Service Commission was sitting I called upon the chairman of the commission and suggested to him that as military work was somewhat technical perhaps he would like to examine some other officers-he had then examined General Lake and the present deputy minister who had only at that time been four months in office as deptuy although he had previously been in the department as director of medical service-and I said I would like very much. if the commissioners would do me the favour of allowing me to see the questions and answers which they had received. I was received very pleasantly by Mr. Courtney and while he did not promise absolutely to do so he gave me to understand that he would. But a day or two afterwards I received from him the following letter :
Civil Service Commission,
October 24, 1907.
Dear Sir Frederick Borden,-Yesterday I talked over with my colleagues the purport of our interview of last Saturday, and, while we considered it very desirable to do all in our power to make our inquiries as complete and perfect as possible yet it was felt that to let the evidence get out before the production of the report would be unsatisfactory. The commission instituted a comparison between the expenditure of 19031904 and that of 1908-1909, as they say for 'specific reasons'; and they go on to point out that the Militia law was changed about 1904. An attempt is made to show that the change in the law resulted in placing the Militia Department absolutely under the control of the military branch and that therefore, in some way not fully explained, the expenditure ran up from three and a half millions in 1904 to six and a half millions. The commissioners say :
Your commissioners have made a comparison between these two_ years for specific reasons. In 1904 there was introduced into parliament an Aet respecting the Militia and Defence of
