Canada, which in many particulars was a new departure from the former Act. In the Act of 1901 by section 6 it is enacted:-
The Governor in Council may appoint a deputy of the minister and such other officers as are necessary for carrying on the business of the department, all of whom shall hold office during pleasure.
In all the Act which has over 140 sections, no other reference is made to the deputy, and it is a curious circumstance that while the appointments of certain officials are permissive certain others are mandatory.
You will expect, as a logical inference from this statement, that in the old law, the law which preceded that of 1904, elaborate references were made to the deputy minister, and you will he surprised when I produce the law of 1904 and the law of 1886, to find that the language in both is precisely the same. I am reading now from the statute of 1904, which is the present law, and in which section C says :
The Governor in Council may appoint a deputy of the minister and such other officers as are necessary for carrying on the business of the department, all of whom shall hold office during pleasure.
Now, let me read from the law of 1886. It is this :
The Governor in Council may appoint a deputy of the Minister of Militia and Defence, and such other officers as are necessary for carrying on the business of the department, all of whom shall hold office during pleasure.
The one is copied verbation from the other ; and yet these gentlemen never took the trouble to look at the statute, because they were afraid, I suppose, that they might find that the very foundation of their theory did not exist. They go on to say that the creation of the militia council brought the military authority forward and substituted it for the civil ; and they say that this is proved by the fact that the headings of the reports of the Militia Department have changed-that whereas in the old days, before this iniquitous law was enacted, the report was headed as follows : ' Department of Militia and Defence year ended so-and-so ; ' now the heading is only : * Report of Militia Council for the Dominion of Canada for the year ending so-and-so ; ' and they say that this is a proof that ' the department has been swallowed up by the militia council.' Now, the report of 1904, the last report, is under two heads-first, part 1, that is, the report of the deputy minister ; next, part 2, the report of the General Commanding. Under the head of the deputy minister comes the report as to the civil side of the department under the heading of the general officer commanding, all the district officers of the Dominion are included. It would be just as sensible to say that the department was swallowed up by the general officer commanding in the old days, and much more
so, as to say that the department has lost its identity through the existence of the militia council. But these gentlemen venture upon somewhat dangerous ground for novices. They undertake to say that the militia council is more powerful and has assumed more authority in Canada than the army council in Great Britain. I shall read an extract from General Lake's memorandum on that point as it will be accepted as more authoritative than anything I could say. General Lake says :
It is rather a pity that the commissioners should have commented unfavourably upon the increased expenditure without thinking it necessary to make any reference to these reasons for that increase, which are matters of policy approved by parliament.
On the contrary, they seem to wish to attribute the whole of it to the assumption by the militia council of what they designate as the ' control ' of the Militia Department. A parallel is drawn between the Army Council at the War Office in London and the Militia Council at Ottawa, in which it is argued with somewhat scant acquaintance with the organization of the War Office, that the Army Council is 'entirely distinct' from the War Office, whereas the Militia Council has ' swallowed up' the Militia Department. To any one who knows the War Office, the former statement is wide of the truth.
An attempt is also made to show that parliamentary control is more fully assured in England than in Canada. Parliament is supreme in both cases, and the weakness of the contention advanced by the commissioners will be recognized when it is remembered that the Militia Council is by law (para. 7, Militia Act) purely advisory to the minister, and cannot act without his direct assent (see order in council of December 7, 1904), whereas the letters patent of February 6, 1904, which created the Army Council, not only vested in the latter all tbie prerogative powers of the Crown previously exercised by the Secretary of State or the Commander in Chief, but gave to any three of its members authority to exercise its full powers.
That is literally true and yet this selfconstituted military critic has the effrontry to say that the militia council has assumed control and absolutely possesses by Act of parliament greater control than does the army council itself. The militia council has no control whatever. The militia council, as the Act prescribes, is purely advisory, it is simply a convenient method by which the minister brings to his aid different members of the department, four officers and two members of the civil staff. The Militia Department is peculiar in this respect, it is different from such a great department, for instance, as that of the Interior, which has its geological branch, its Indian branch its land branch, and so on, all absolutely and entirely distinct. The Militia Department has its intelligence branch, with its chief of general staff, its adjutant general, looking after the troops, the training, &c., the quarter-master general, looking af-

ter the stores and supplies, and the Master General of Ordnance, and of course the deputy minister of the department as the other departments have. But these different departments or branches are inter-dependent, they are in a sense inseparable, and in order to have successful administration you must have those different departments in perfect accord and perfect touch. You must have continuity of purpose, you must have co-operation among the different branches of the service and you must have co-ordination or you will experience very great difficulty. That is the object for which the army council was conceived, but of course, the army council has received very much greater power. That is the object I had in copying the present plan on which the war office is administered, by introducing the idea of having in Canada a militia council. The system has worked admirably, better than I expected and I hope it will always be continued.
Why in the world did the commission go so far afield to invent a cause for the increase of expenditure when they had actually before them in the evidence of General Lake and in the evidence of the deputy minister, the reasons for the increase? 'The reasons are known to everybody who will stop to think. They are as follows: During the year 1903-4 this country assumed the responsibility of taking over and maintaining the garrisons of Halifax and Esquimau. That meant an expenditure of one and a half to t wo million dollars. There is more than one-half of the total amount of the increase at once. The militia, under the new law, was paid nearly twice as much in the latter years as in the former years. That would account for from a quarter to half a million. The militia had been increased enormously in its numerical strength between 1903-4 and 1907-8. They might also have taken note of a charge of $200,000 on account of customs which is simply a cross entry. Between these different amounts you get the full three millions. I have a statement here which will give this exactly. The expenditures on account of the headquarter staff and district staff, the permanent force, exclusive of Halifax and Esquimalt, and their pay, provisions and supplies for the permanent force, clothing for the permanent force, transport of staff and permanent force' amounted in 1903-4, to $649,000, and in 1907-8 to $1,253, i 00. The strength of the permanent force, exclusive of Halifax and Esquimalt, has been increased from 853 to 1,656. Now, take the expenditure of the active militia, for training, clothing, grants, etc. In 1903-4 the total expenditure under this head was $1,077,000 ; in 1907-8 it was $1,562,000. The number of men of all ranks-paid in 1903-4 was 33,751 and in 1907-8 42,612. On rifle ranges and camp grounds Sir FREDERICK BORDEN.
there was nearly $200,000 more spent in 1907-8 than in 1903-4-and I suppose no one will quarrel with that expenditure. On ordnance, field guns and rifles the expenditure in 1903-4 was $487,000 and in 1907-8 $718,000. On warlike stores the expenditures were much the same. On account of garrison at Halifax and Esquimalt there was no expenditure in 1903-4 except $109,987, which was the amount the Canadian government contributed to the British government for the maintenance of Esquimalt. I have here an interesting statement showing that in 1895-6 the output of the cartridge factory was only 672,000 rounds, while in 1903-4 it was 6,352,000 rounds and in 1907-8 10,500,000 rounds, with a very large number of shells of the most expensive kind. These figures show an output in 1903-4 eight times greater than in 1895-6 and in 1907-8 fifteen times greater. In these items I have included the vote for customs, as I have already mentioned.

I wish to give the evidence of a man above the suspicion of writing or saying what is not absolutely correct :
The commissioners refer to the prevalence of desertion in the permanent corps and attribute it mainly to a want of sympathy between officers of the permanent corps and the men. It may be remarked that the reasons given by Major General Lake

In bis evidence, mind you, which they would not take any notice of :
-were, the demand and high pay given for labour everywhere, the smallness of the establishments, poor barracks, no change of station and the occasional failure on the part of the government to keep faith with the men. (f) That ' the desertions have been one in three.'
This statement was approximately true for 1905, but there has been much improvement since then. For 1906 the figures were one in six. For 1907 they were one in nine, and many of these men rejoin froip desertion and reduce the proportion.

The commissioners consider that the appointment of an inspector general is of but little benefit to the militia, and recommend that, when vacant, it be not filled. They state that, in Great Britain, the appointment was made for reasons which do not exist in Canada. They do not give those reasons, and it is, therefore, impossible to judge how far the commissioners' contention holds good.
But it may be remarked that the committee of 1904

That is the English committee, the Esher committee as ,it is called,
-on whose report the present War Office organization was adopted, were very insistent upon the need for an inspector general; indeed, they said that effective inspection was 4 absolutely imperative.' And the appointment is at present filled in England by one
of the ablest soldiers in the army '(General dir John French).
An inspector general was appointed in Canada because the arguments used by the War Office Reorganization Committee (and detailed in their report) were concurred in, and it was considered essential to provide for inspection by a highly qualified officer, competent to speak with authority upon all military questions, who should insure, first, that the directions of the Militia Council were faithfully and uniformly carried out throughout the militia force (especially that the instruction given in the various military schools should be uniform) ^pd, second, should report to the Militia Council upon the practical results of the measures adopted by it. Thorough and competent inspection is, at least, as necessary in the militia as in any business concern.
At this moment General Lake is the inspector general and he is engaged in making a most careful inspection of every branch of the militia from beginning to end, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, for the benefit of this country and so that this parliament at its next session will be able to see exactly what that able, experienced, competent, fearless officer thinks of our militia force. General Lake came out here in 1904 as chief of the general staff to assist in the reorganization of the militia, to inaugurate not a new policy, but improvements in the general plan of the militia, and I thought it was fitting that a man of his capability and experience should occupy the position of inspector general before he leaves this country for I regret to say his term of office will be up in a few months. I thought he should have an opportunity to see whether the system he inaugurated is effective and is being properly carried out so as to inform the minister as to what changes in it he would suggest. That is a duty that all inspectors general will have to perform. It would be extremely difficult to get as able a man as General Lake. I believe men can be got of sufficient ability and sufficient honesty to fill the position advantageously in the interest of the country, and of all the positions in the militia I believe this is one we can at least do without.

4.	There is also a daily journal in which all issues are entered and thence transferred to the general ledger, and the department is debited with the receipt and credited with thet issues.
The general or store ledger consists of debit and credit pages and shows at the top of the debit page every article in store charge. At the end of each month the receipts for that month on the debit page are totalled up and added to the balance brought forward from the preceding month. Issues for the month are deducted and the result shows the balance in hand at the depot.
A monthly return from each depot is forwarded to headquarters showing all transactions. including each issue and receipt, accompanied by the authority for such issue or receipt. The checking clerk at headquarters sees that the balances on hand at the end of the preceding month are correctly carried forward to the current month and that the number of articles received or issued correspond with the authority for such receipts or issues.
Should any entry appear with no authority submitted it would, be at once challenged. It will thus he seen how complete the system of checking and accounting is.
5.	No issues are allowed to he made by any ordnance officer except on written authority, and such authority is governed by regulations as to clothing and all other equipment and the same authority is given for all receipts from inspection stores.

It is in order, apparently, that they may propose, as a preferable arrangement, ' that the expenditure (on the militia) should be increased according to the growth of the population and be put on a per capita basis/ If this means anything, it must apparently mean that the requirements of the defence of the country do not affect the question. No matter how imminent or how great the danger may ibe, the expenditure is only to increase in the same ratio as the population- no matter if the danger decreases or disappears altogether, the expenditure is to go on increasing because the population does. Their reasoning may embody some economical doctrine, but it is hardly common sense. The only reasonable plan is to regard military expenditure as an insurance against national danger, the amount of that insurance being decided by the extent and imminence of the danger and by the degree to which the nation can afford, and is willing, to insure itself.
I had intended dealing in my statement in defence of the department against the outrageous, extraordinary and unjustifiable attack of this commission, with a number of other points mentioned by the commission, but time will not permit me to do so. These tables give some idea of the present state of efficiency of the militia which has been branded by this commission as being less efficient than it was fifteen years ago. The objects of the militia are, as we know, three-fold, the maintenance of the civil power within onr own borders, the repelling of any attack from without and the assisting when the parliament of Canada sees fit to undertake it. or whenever it may be necessary, of the mother country. The militia of Canada has performed great services for this country. It -is a very old institution, and it has done its work well. One essential difference between the militia of to-day and of the time prior to 1895-1896 is that in the past on every occasion when an armed service was required in Canada, it was necessary that the imperial troops should take the initiative. We had not the departments necessary, our force was not a self-contained force ; but to-day, the militia of Canada is in a position to place in the field a considerable number of men and to take the initiative itself and probably do so effectively until assistance could come, if it were necessary, from the mother country. Now, it seems to me that those of us who take an interest, a broader interest, in our future, and recognize the imperial obligation or duty, ought to feel proud that we are in that position and are no longer, as we were up to a very few years ago, absolutely dependent upon the mother country. It should be some comfort to those of us who think-though I do not believe there are many such within the sound of my voice -that this country should subscribe a sum of money for the maintenance of the British navy to know that, while we do not possess a fleet, we possess at least the nucleus of an army, with all the departments necessary and able materially to assist the mother country if it were necessary to do so. It is absolutely in our own power to say whether we shall do so or not, but it is a great thing to have the power. I would like to read a sentence or two which I have taken from the budget speech of Sir Alexander Galt when Finance Minister of Canada in .Tune, 1806,-before confederation. These are the notable words to which he gave utterance and which are as applicable to-day as they were then :
We must all feel that the security of the country is to be found in its own power, not in the forbearance of another or in the discharge of duty by another, but by its own ability to maintain our independence and safety.
These are sentiments which, I believe, every man in this committee, every man in this House, every man in this country, will subscribe to.
I shall not detain the committee further. I hope I have succeeded in answering some
of the very unjust statements which have been made. I hope I have been able to satisfy the committee that the increase in expenditure is justifiable and that it is not due in the slightest respect to the reasons alleged by the commission-the change in the law in 1904 by which an advisory board, a militia council, was established. I hope I have been able to satisfy the committee that this country has something to show for money that is being expended. I hold that an inefficient militia is an undesirable thing ; I would rather spend no money at all on the militia-I would rather wipe out the militia altogether-than have a militia that is a mere pretense and therefore absolutely worthless. You can have that by spending one or two millions, but you cannot by such an expenditure provide anything at all adequate for the services required for a country like this, and for a people occupying the responsible position which we occupy as Canadians, as people responsible for the enormous territory which we administer and as the most important member of the great British empire to which we are proud to belong. I am proud to feel and to know that the money which has been spent in the department has resulted in bringing about great efficiency; and I believe that a very small portion, if any, of the money has been improvidently spent. I invite the closest inspection-and we have had some of it already-into the expenditures that have taken place in that department-we welcome it. I consider that our system of purchasing is as good as any system in any government, and will compare favourably with the system of many large business establishments.
I thank the committee for their great patience. I would not have trespassed so long, but for the fact that the forbearance of hon. members has shown that they feel that I * should be privileged at least to state my side of this case.

At this early hour in the morning, and very late stage of the session, it would be very much out of place for me to devote any length of time in criticism of the speech of the Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Frederick Borden). But I will say this : though I have been in the House for over a quarter of a century I never saw at this stage of the session such an exhibition by any minister of the Crown, one at the head of a department whose expenditure is very heavy and increasing rapidly for years. The minister has devoted about two hours and a half, not to defending the expenditure, not to showing that it was wise and economical, that it was beneficial to the country, but simply attacking the Royal Commission which he himself helped to appoint, a commission that, I frankly confess, I always thought was composed of able men, eminent men. men of high aims and great ability. They did their work accord-

hig to their lights ; they gave the .benefit of their time to the country and to this House ; and now the Minister of Militia who assisted by order in council to appoint these men as a royal commission has taken up two hours ahd a half to abuse and condemn them, and very little to defend the expenditure of his department. I have here in brief an account of some of the increases in the Militia department which, as it is in more condensed form than anything I could offer, may fairly be quoted in dealing with this subject. I have taken this from the Montreal ' Gazette ' of some time ago :
In 1896 the cost of the Militia Department was $2,193,372, of which $1,000,000 was for arms and accoutrements. In 1906 this had grown to $5,664,192, an increase of 158 per cent. Of the latter amount only $1,299,875 was for arms, &c. The balance of $1,291,124 covered the same expenditures as the $1,193,372 spent in 1896, the expenditure for administration purposes having increased by 360 per cent.
Is the militia three times as efficient or three times as numerous as it was in 1896?
An idea of how this vast increase has been created may be gained from a comparison of the cost of the headquarters staff at Ottawa in the two years. This was the staff in 1896:

Feathers come higth.
The head quarters staff at Ottawa has grown from eight officials, costing $16,300 per year, to twenty-three officials costing $73,425. These are all the items I intend dealing with to-night but they are a fair sample of the iucrease of expenditure all along the line, and I am quite sure that the people of this country, especially the agricultural class, will not be inclined to congratulate the minister when they are properly informed of the rapid increase in our militia expenditure. I am not denying that in many respects the militia are very much better, but I am not prepared to admit that up to a few years ago we had practically no militia at all. We had some in 1885 when the Northwest rebellion was quelled, and in 1866 when the Fenian raid was repulsed and in 1871, and at various times before this heavy increase of expenditure we certainly had some kind of militia which we found very useful.

I did not say that we had no militia or that it had not done good work. II said the militia had done good work always, but we had none of the departments or branches which go to make up an army and always relied on the Imperial troops and officers who happened to be in Canada at the time.
iMr. SPROULE. I understood the minister to say that we had simply a militia in name and nothing more.
No, no.

Who was it did good service for the country then ?
Sir FREDERICK BORDE-N. I did not say that. iMy hon. friend is doing me an injustice.
I do not wish to do my hon. friend an injustice hut that was my understanding of what he said.
That was not what I intended saying.
I always thought that in practice our militia proved themselves efficient every time their services were called upon.
So they did?

The expenditure has grown very rapidly iand we are not getting full value for it. It is too late however in the session and the hour is too late to criticise in any detail, and we shall have to content ourselves with taking some other opportunity in the future to discuss our military expenditure and force at greater length. But let me say with regard to the

commission, that it comes with had grace from a minister who helped to appoint them, to take up two and a half hours of our time in abusing these men after they have done their work so faithfully. The hon. gentleman has put the commission on trial and they have been quartered to the Queen's taste.
Experimental farms, $130,000.
As we shall have supplementary estimates on these various subjects, it might be understood that any member of this House who desires to discuss any of these questions may do so.
I am quite willing.
I know that my hon. friend from Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) is anxious to speak on the same item.
